Preface

The field of cardiovascular medicine has undergone tremendous evolution over the last number of decades. From reliance on auscultation and clinical examination to now, a deluge of diagnostic information that has aided more informed treatment decision making and improved clinical outcomes. To date, the clinician has managed to integrate the ever-growing information into practice but in the last number of years, data are outstripping the capacity of a physician to process it. In addition, there is an increasing awareness of the richness of information that is embedded within imaging data, which extends beyond what the human eye can process and extract. Artificial intelligence and machine learning have rapidly transformed every aspect of our lives and are now being explored and implemented in a number of aspects of cardiovascular medicine.
Machine Learning in Cardiovascular Medicine is one of the first textbooks to highlight the ever-expanding applications of machine and deep learning within cardiovascular medicine. In this book, the editors have compiled an excellent overview of the current applications of machine learning for clinical data analysis, as well as highlighted the recent advances in deep learning for cardiovascular image analysis. From traditional to state-of-the-art algorithms, the first few chapters set the technical foundation for understanding the inner workings of these algorithms as well as appreciating available metrics for the evaluation of their performance for a specific clinical task. The book then delves into current applications of machine learning: from its role in natural language processing to various imaging modalities such as CT, MRI, and Echocardiography. The editors have provided a tour de force go to reference for all those in the field. Importantly, the editors seek to also expose the many limitations in the space and also the ethical challenges that we will all be facing as we seek to implement and refine these tools in our clinical practice. To do so, they have assembled an incredible group of authors with expertise in every aspect of artificial intelligence and cardiovascular medicine. As Andrew Ng famously stated: “As leaders, it is incumbent on all of us to make sure we are building a world in which every individual has an opportunity to thrive. Understanding what AI can do and how it fits into your strategy is the beginning, not the end, of that process,” this book is a perfect fit to educate the clinical and research communities regarding current, and potential, future applications of artificial intelligence within cardiovascular medicine.
Jonathon A. Leipsic, M.D., F.R.C.P.C., F.S.C.C.T.

Introduction

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a topic for discussion within various medical domains, and especially within the cardiovascular community. The availability of large multidimensional datasets within medicine offers a framework for significant advances with the appropriate harnessing of AI. The integration of AI can occur throughout the continuum of medicine; from basic laboratory discovery to clinical application and healthcare delivery. Yet, integrating AI within medicine has been met with both excitement and skepticism. By understanding how AI works and developing an appreciation for both its limitations and strengths, clinicians can harness its power to streamline workflow and improve patient care. AI provides an opportunity to improve upon research methodologies, beyond what are currently available using traditional statistical approaches. Further, computers scientists and data analysts can provide solutions, but often lack easy access to clinical insight that may help focus their efforts. This textbook provides the platform to bring these two disciplines together.
Machine Learning in Cardiovascular Medicine addresses the ever-expanding applications of AI, and specifically machine learning (ML), in healthcare and within cardiovascular medicine. AI was initially born out of the need to solve nonlinear and combinatorially complex tasks. Over time, AI has transformed innumerable aspects of human life; the development of augmented reality, autonomous driving, robotics, as well as sophisticated predictive modeling are just a few examples of how AI has sparked the current innovative climate within the industry sector. While the industrial applications of ML are nearly ubiquitous, its introduction into the medical field has been much more gradual. The landscape, however, is rapidly changing as a result of the availability of computational power as well as the creation of large repositories of datasets. The computer science and medical communities are increasingly streamlining efforts at harnessing the potential of ML in order to solve complex tasks and optimize day-to-day workflow in the healthcare sector. This book is focused on emphasizing ML for biomedical applications and aims at providing a comprehensive summary of the past and present of AI, basics of ML as well as clinical applications of ML within cardiovascular medicine for predictive analytics and precision medicine.
Subhi J. Al'Aref, M.D., F.A.C.C.

Chapter 1: Technological advances within digital medicine

Ahmed M. Altibi1, Subhi J. Al’Aref2, and Pegah Khosravi3     1Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Harvard University, Boston, MA, United States     2Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, Little Rock, AR, United States     3Computational Oncology, Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY, United States

Abstract

Contemporary advances within digital medicine have gradually changed the landscape of healthcare and biomedical research. Over decades, significant innovations have been witnessed in various aspects of digital medicine, including mobile health (mHealth) applications, telehealth, wearable healthcare technologies, and robotics. mHealth technology utilized artificial intelligence to mitigate the two major barriers for cardiac health promotion: (i) global deficit of healthcare professionals and (ii) ever-growing cost of healthcare services. mHealth applications have been used in preventative, diagnostic, and therapeutic aspects of medicine. Smartphone-based EKG and “pocket” echocardiography are two pioneering examples in diagnostic cardiology. Wearable technologies rely on implemented sensors to monitor for an array of physiologic parameters, such as vital signs, cardiac electrical activity, and physical activity metrics (e.g., steps count and energy expenditure). Fitness trackers and smartwatches, the most popular and commercially available wearable devices, solely play preventative role via self-quantifying of health metrics. To the contrary, other wearables are enabled to deploy therapeutic interventions—such as the wearable cardioverter defibrillator which can provide a life-saving shock in cases of dysrhythmias. Finally, advances in robotics and robotic-assisted interventions (e.g., percutaneous coronary interventions, peripheral vascular interventions, and catheter-based ablation of arrhythmias) have enhanced procedural accuracy, improved quality of clinical outcomes, and minimized occupational hazards associated with interventional cardiology.

Introduction

Technological advances within digital medicine have been gradually changing the landscape of healthcare and biomedical research. Since William Withering utilized digitalis 250 years ago, from Foxglove plant, to treat “dropsy” (congestive heart failure) (
In this chapter, we provide an overview of the key advances in digital technologies impacting healthcare in cardiovascular medicine, including: (i) wearable healthcare technology, (ii) mobile health and telehealth, and (iii) robotic technology. A plethora of wearable technologies currently exists and can be broadly classified into diagnostic versus therapeutic devices. Diagnostic wearables rely on digitized data acquisition for monitoring (e.g., smartwatches and fitness trackers). On the other hand, therapeutic devices have instrumental components enabling them to intervene to prevent, mitigate, or treat certain medical conditions (e.g., wearable cardioverter defibrillators).

Wearable sensing devices

Fitness trackers and smartwatches

Introduction

With the recent technological revolution involving nanocomputers, AI, big data, wireless networks, and cellular networks, the past decade has witnessed an explosion in the utility of wearable optic sensors technologies worldwide (

Devices and sensors

Fitness trackers and Smartwatches are equipped with a multitude of sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, altimeter, barometers, and GPS) that function to record fitness-related metrics such as movement acceleration, steps count, energy expenditure, and physical location for the individual (
In addition to accelerometers, some wearables utilize additional sensors to increase the accuracy of the device, such as gyroscopes, magnetometers, barometers, and altimeters. Gyroscope sensor, or angular rate sensor, functions via sensing the angular velocity (change in rotational angle per unit of time), and hence, provides information on both orientation and rotation (
Finally, photoplethysmogram (PPG) is a noninvasive optical sensing technology that utilizes an infrared light to detect any minor volumetric changes in blood of the peripheral circulation (
Ultimately, the quality of a wearable device depends on the accuracy of its sensors and the algorithms utilized to operate data collected from these sensors. This explains the increased focus in revolutionizing sensory technologies in healthcare wearable devices (

Clinical applications

The ability of optical sensors to detect abnormal heart rhythms has been a topic of interest in healthcare. The Apple Heart Study was designed to evaluate the Apple Watch irregular rhythm notification’s ability to accurately identify atrial fibrillation (AF) – the most common clinically significant arrhythmia (Fig. 1.1) (
In addition to diagnostic and therapeutic applications, wearable devices can be implemented to collect aggregated data as part of large-scale public health research studies (

Wearable cardioverter defibrillator (WCD)

Introduction

Sudden cardiac death (SCD) is responsible for half of all cardiac-related deaths (

How does the WCD function?

The WCD device consists of two main components—a garment and a monitor. The garment is worn under clothing and functions to detect arrhythmias and to deliver life-saving shock when an abnormal heart rhythm is detected—via four sensing and three defibrillating electrodes (

What are the indications for WCD?

Thus far, WCDs are used as bridging/temporizing interventions rather than destination measures substituting for ICDs. Clinical indications for WCDs were initially coined by American Heart Association (AHA) science advisory in 2016. Later, further endorsement was publicized by other scientific bodies (e.g., Heart Rhythm Society) (
  1. • Bridging for interrupted ICD or “pending” ICD implant.
  2. • Following myocardial infarction (MI) or coronary revascularization—with severely reduced ejection fraction (EF) (<35%).
  3. • Following new diagnosis of nonischemic cardiomyopathy—with severely reduced EF (<35%).
ICD “interruption” refers to the state where an implanted ICD system is extracted for a compelling reason such as device infection or endocarditis—to achieve proper source control (

Does the WCD technology save lives?

WCD therapy has been proven to be highly effective in terminating VT/VF rhythms when worn properly. Studies have shown the first-shock termination rate to be comparable with that for ICDs, ranging between 95% and 100% (
WCD has been shown to be highly efficient in terminating abnormal rhythms. However, many experts have raised concerns that the device is increasingly presumed to be the “de facto” standard of care in certain subsets of patients, despite the inconclusive evidence. The evidence to support an overall mortality benefit and cost-effectiveness is still limited. This becomes important knowing that leasing a LifeVest costs ≥ $3000 per month (

Mobile health in cardiovascular medicine

Introduction

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death globally among all ethnic and racial groups and is responsible for one in every four deaths in the United States (A nationwide framework for surveillance of cardiovascular and chronic lung diseases, 2011;
mHealth incorporates all medical services and public health activities enabled via mobile devices. It is estimated that there are more than 300,000 mobile health applications available in the market—the majority are not FDA approved. Strikingly, more than 600 of these commercially available smartphone applications are specifically designed to improve adherence to therapy (
In the era of miniaturization, great strides have also been made to revolutionize current diagnostic and imaging modalities by integrating AI systems in the vicinity of mobile health technologies. Smartphone-based electrocardiogram (EKG) and “pocket” echocardiography are two pioneering examples for this integration in diagnostic cardiology (

Smartphone-based electrocardiogram (EKG)

Over the past decade, mHealth technologies have witnessed a tremendous leap in the applicability of mHealth in the monitoring of chronic diseases (
The use of smartphones for cardiac rhythm monitoring is another leap for EKG development and utilization. Currently, there are two types of smartphone technologies used to detect and monitor heart rhythms: (i) PPG, and (ii) Single-lead platform technology (
Over time, this technology has progressed to the more promising “single-lead” smartphone-based EKG—first FDA-approved in 2012. Single-lead technology combines an external EKG sensor with a smartphone application to generate a one lead rhythm strip (
AliveCor Kardia is currently the most clinically validated mobile-based EKG technology. Studies have shown AliveCor to be highly sensitive (98%) and specific (97%) in capturing abnormal heart rhythms, such as AF (
Interestingly, the world’s first six-lead smartphone-enabled EKG was pioneered by Kardia in 2019. This functions via incorporating an innovative third electrode to allow visibility into certain arrhythmias that were previously undetected with single-lead EKG (Fig. 1.4). (

Pocket-echocardiography

Echocardiography is the primary imaging modality to assess cardiac function and to diagnose a multitude of cardiac conditions. The fundamental concept of “portable” echocardiography goes back to the 1970s when the “ultrasonic” stethoscope first appeared (
“Pocket” echocardiography machines are smartphone-sized devices that provide diagnostic quality 2D with or without color Doppler imaging in real-time (
The introduction of pocket echocardiography devices in clinical practice has raised questions over the diagnostic capacity of these devices when compared to the standard transthoracic echocardiography (sTTE) (
In view of the increased evidence to support the valuable diagnostic utility of pocket echocardiography, the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) released special recommendations for healthcare providers on the use of pocket-size imaging devices (

Robotic technology in cardiology

Robotic technology has been used in medicine for several decades, primarily in surgical (
The past few years have witnessed advances in robotic technology within cardiovascular medicine; leading to a wider utilization in both investigative and therapeutic domains (

Robotics in PCI

When Andreas Gruntzig performed the first-in-human coronary angioplasty in 1977 in Zurich, Switzerland, the landscape of cardiovascular medicine was transformed forever (
However, technical hurdles remain to deem certain complex coronary lesions ineligible for robotic interventions (e.g., bifurcated coronary lesions, severely calcified lesions, and chronic total occlusions), hampering global implementation of robotics in catheterization laboratories (

Robotics in PVI

Similar to PCI, peripheral vascular interventions (PVIs) have also been associated with increased risk for hazardous radiation exposure and orthopedic injuries. In fact, PVIs had been associated with a significantly greater (1.4 folds) radiation risk for operator as compared to PCI. Currently, two robotic systems are FDA-approved for PVIs: (i) CorPath 200 system (Corindus Vascular Robotics, MA, USA), and (ii) Magellan System (Auris Surgical Robotics Inc., CA, USA). The RAPID (Robotic-Assisted Peripheral Intervention for Peripheral Artery Disease) trial was a prospective single-arm trial to assess the feasibility and safety of CorPath robotic technology in femoropopliteal PVIs (

Robotics in electrophysiology

Catheter-based ablation has become one of the preferred treatment modalities for sustained arrhythmias (i.e., atrial fibrillation) (

Future perspectives

Contemporary robotic-assisted cardiovascular interventions have enhanced procedural accuracy/precision, improved quality of clinical outcomes, and minimized occupational hazards (i.e., radiation exposure). Future iterations for robotic-assisted devices should take into consideration the technical challenges associated with more complex scenarios (e.g., robotic PCI for bifurcated or severely calcified coronary lesions). Further studies assessing cost-effectiveness of robotics for coronary and peripheral interventions are also warranted.

Conclusions

Innovations in digital cardiovascular technology continue to evolve with recent and ongoing advances in robotic technology, wearable technology, mobile health, telehealth, and others. Digitization of cardiovascular care holds promise to revolutionize diagnostic and imaging modalities, improve precision of therapeutic interventions, and mitigate occupational hazards on healthcare workers. With the powerful AI methods and ML algorithms, digital health technologies have the potential to transform the practice of cardiology. To outdistance the rapidly burgeoning digital medicine, development of ethical and regulatory frameworks ensuring appropriate implementation becomes a necessity (Chapter 18).

Chapter 2: An overview of artificial intelligence: basics and state-of-the-art algorithms

Qi Chang1, Leon Axel2, and Dimitris N. Metaxas1     1Department of Computer Science, Rutgers The State University of New Jersey, Piscataway, NJ, United States     2Department of Radiology, New York University School of Medicine, New York, NY, United States

Abstract

Recently, deep convolutional neural networks have been successfully applied to medical image tasks by taking advantage of a large amount of training data with gold standard annotations. The first part of this chapter introduces several basic, yet critical, concepts regarding machine learning and deep learning, which provide a foundation for understanding of both the development of these algorithms as well as appreciating their current cardiovascular applications. Thereafter, this chapter provides an overview of state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms including Bayesian, Decision Tree, Support Vector Machine, and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).

Keywords

Classification; Convolutional neural network (CNN); Deep learning; Evaluation metric; Machine learning; Regression

Introduction

In the early days of artificial intelligence (AI), the field rapidly tackled and solved problems that were intellectually difficult for humans but were relatively straightforward for computers— problems that could be described by a list of formal, mathematical rules (
The first part of Chapter 2 presents basic concepts within machine learning and AI. Specifically, this chapter will cover basic knowledge on the scope and approach of machine learning, with a focus on specific terms that are often misconstrued within the community. In the second part of this chapter, we will provide an overview of the state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms commonly used in academic research and the industry domain. By discussing various algorithms and approaches, we aim to provide the reader with a platform to navigate through different algorithms and select an approach that is best suited for a specific research or medical task.

Basic concepts

What are AI, machine learning, and deep learning? And what is the difference between them?

John McCarthy, widely recognized as one of the godfathers of AI, defined AI as “the science and engineering of making intelligent machines.” As the name suggests, AI can be loosely interpreted to refer to the incorporation of human intelligence into machines. In machine learning, machines can learn on their own without being explicitly programmed to do so. It also allows for self-modifications based on data in real-time scenarios. In other words, machine learning is the study of computer algorithms that allow computer programs to automatically improve through experience.
Deep learning is one of many approaches to machine learning. Other approaches include decision tree learning, inductive logic programming, clustering, reinforcement learning, and Bayesian networks, among others. Deep learning was loosely inspired by the structure and function of the brain, namely the interconnection of many neurons. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are algorithms that mimic the biological structure of the brain. In ANNs, there are “neurons” which have discrete layers and connections to other “neurons.” Each layer picks out a specific feature to learn, such as curves/edges in image recognition. It’s this layering that gives deep learning its name, depth is created by using multiple layers as opposed to a single layer.
Analogies between human and machine learning (ML) naturally bring to mind the term “AI” and the obvious question: “What’s the difference between AI and machine learning?” There’s no clear consensus on this matter, but most (not all) agree that ML is one form of AI, and that AI is a far broader subject encompassing such areas as robotics, language processing, and computer vision systems. To increase the ambiguity even further, machine learning is being applied with increasing frequency to many of those aforementioned fields. As such, we can conclude by stating that the discipline of ML refers to a specific body of knowledge and an associated set of techniques. It’s fairly clear what is, and what isn’t, machine learning, whereas the same can’t always be said of artificial intelligence. Paraphrasing Tom Mitchell’s often-cited definition, a computer program is said to learn if its performance of a certain task, as measured by a computable score, improves with experience (

Types of machine learning

There are some variations in the available definitions of machine learning algorithms. However, such algorithms are commonly divided into categories according to their purpose, with the main categories being:
  1. • Supervised Learning
  2.     Supervised learning algorithms try to model relationships and dependencies between the target prediction output and the input features, such that one can predict the output values for new data based on those relationships learned from the previous datasets. Here, human experts act as teachers where one feeds the computer with training data containing the input/predictors while providing the correct answers (output); using which the computer should be able to learn underlying patterns. The process of learning from data, and subsequently using the acquired knowledge to inform future decisions, is extremely powerful. Indeed, machine learning is rapidly becoming the engine that powers the modern data-driven economy. Widely used supervised machine learning techniques include Classification and Regression algorithms.
    • Classification: It is a Supervised Learning task where the output is having defined labels (discrete value). It can be either binary or multiclass classification. In binary classification, the model predicts either 0 or 1; yes or no, but in case of multiclass classification, a model predicts more than one class. As an example: Gmail classifies mail in more than one class like social, promotions, updates, and forums. It can either classify one class or multi classes per input or, as in image segmentation, classify classes over each pixel.
    • Regression: It is a Supervised Learning task where the output has a continuous value. The goal here is to predict a value as close as possible to an actual output value, with subsequent model evaluation by calculating an error value. As expected, the smaller the error the greater is the accuracy of a regression model.
  4. • Unsupervised Learning
  5.     In this paradigm, a machine learning model is trained with unlabeled data and without any explicit target output. The computer might be able to discover new knowledge regarding patterns within datasets that humans might have previously neglected. However, these models are particularly useful in cases where the human expert doesn’t know what to look for within the dataset. Such algorithms try to use techniques on the input data to mine for rules, detect patterns, summarize and group the data points, which ultimately helps derive meaningful insights while better describing the data to the end-users. Commonly used unsupervised learning algorithms include K-Means, Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), Autoencoder, and Generative adversarial network (GAN) (
  6. • Semi-supervised Learning
  7.     In the previous two paradigms, either there were no labels for all observations or labels are present for all the observations. Semi-supervised learning falls in between these two methods. In many practical situations, the cost of performing expert labeling is significant. Hence, in the absence of output labels in the majority of observations, semi-supervised algorithms are best suited for model creation. These methods exploit the idea that even though the group memberships of the unlabeled data are unknown, such data carries important information about group parameters.
  8. • Reinforcement Learning
  9.     Reinforcement learning aims at using observations gathered from the interaction with the computationally simulated environment to learn to perform actions that would maximize the reward or minimize the risk. Reinforcement learning algorithms (referred to as the agent) continuously learn from the environment in an iterative fashion (Fig. 2.1). In the process, an agent learns from its experiences until it explores the full range of possible states. Reinforcement Learning allows machines and software agents to automatically determine the ideal behavior within a specific context, to maximize its performance. Simple reward feedback is required for the agent to learn its behavior; this is known as the reinforcement signal. Some applications of the reinforcement learning algorithms are computer played board games (Chess, Go), robotic hands, and self-driving cars.

Machine learning in practice

In the following sections, we will mainly focus on supervised learning tasks, which constitute a majority of the current applications of machine learning, and are the most frequently used methods in the medical domain. A generalized outline for a step-by-step approach to machine learning has been depicted in Fig. 2.2. To have a better understanding of the training process, the following technical terms are explained.

Generalization in machine learning: overfitting versus underfitting

Generalization refers to how well the concepts learned by a machine learning model apply to specific examples not seen by the model when it was learning. The goal of a good machine learning model is to generalize well from the training data to any data from the problem domain. This allows for accurate predictions when applying the model to never seen scenarios/data/patients. The cause of poor performance in machine learning is usually a result of either overfitting or underfitting of the model on the data. Overfitting refers to a phenomenon when the model learns the training data. The model learns both, the information and random noise, in the training data to an extent that it negatively impacts the performance of the model on new data. This means that the noise or random fluctuations in the training data is picked up and learned as concepts by the model. This negatively impacts the model’s ability to generalize as noise being “random” is not replicated in the subsequent data. An overfitted model thus will not perform well on unseen new data.

Dataset split: training versus validation versus testing

Training dataset is the sample of data used to fit/train the model. The validation dataset is used to evaluate a given model. By using this data to fine-tune the model hyperparameters, one could identify the best-fit model. Hence the model occasionally sees this data, but never does it “Learn” from it. The test dataset provides the gold standard which is used to evaluate the trained model. It’s only used once a model is completely trained (using the train and validation sets). The test set is generally what is used to evaluate competing models. This is done to perform an independent validation of the model’s performance.
In addition to this, several sampling can be used to prevent model overfitting. Cross-validation is one of the most commonly used resampling techniques wherein the entire dataset is split into two parts: train and test. Thereafter, the test set is kept aside, while a randomly chosen X% of the train dataset is used as the actual train set while the remaining (100-X)% is used as the validation set (X is a fixed number (typically 80%). The model is then iteratively trained and validated on these different sets. The use of cross-validation avoids overfitting, with K-fold cross-validation being the most popular method, where k-refers to the number of iterations.

Basic evaluation metrics

Evaluation metrics measure the performance of a particular model, which helps with optimal model selection in the testing phase. Different metrics may reflect the different goals when designing the task at hand. For instance, there are different metrics for the tasks of classification, regression, ranking, clustering, topic modeling, etc. Some metrics, such as precision-recall, are useful for multiple tasks. Classification, regression, and ranking are examples of supervised learning, which constitute a majority of machine learning applications. The choice of evaluation metrics heavily impacts the ability of the model to learn from the data. Hence, depending upon the characteristics of the dataset and the problem statement, the choice of an evaluation metric is made (Table 2.1).
  1. • Model Accuracy
  2.     Model accuracy in terms of classification models can be defined as the ratio of correctly classified samples to the total number of samples:

  5. Table 2.1

    Confusion matrix.
  7.     Or for binary classification models, the accuracy can be defined as:
  9.     The use of the accuracy metric is justified when the number of examples for each class is somewhat balanced. However, when the dataset is imbalanced, accuracy should not be relied upon as it can be misleading. In those cases, metrics such as precision, recall, or F1 should be used.
  10. • Precision and Recall
  11.     In a classification task, the precision for a class is the number of true positives divided by the total number of elements “labeled by the model” as belonging to the positive class:
  13.     Recall is defined as the number of true positives divided by the total number of elements that actually belong to the positive class:
  15.     In simple terms, high precision means that an algorithm returned substantially more relevant results than irrelevant ones, while high recall means that an algorithm returned most of the relevant results.
  16. • F1 Score
  17.     The F1 score is the harmonic mean of the precision and recall, where an F1 score reaches its best value at 1 and worst at 0.
  19.     In segmentation tasks, F1 score is also referred to as the Dice Coefficient.
  20. • ROC Curve and AUC (Area under the ROC Curve)
  21.     A receiver operating characteristic curve, or ROC curve, is a graphical plot that illustrates the diagnostic ability of a binary classifier system as its discrimination threshold is varied. The ROC curve is created by plotting the true positive rate (TPR) against the false positive rate (FPR) at various threshold settings. The ROC curve is a two-dimensional depiction of classifier performance. To compare classifiers, we may want to reduce ROC performance to a single scalar value representing an expected performance. A common method is to calculate the area under the ROC curve, abbreviated as AUC (Fig. 2.4). An excellent model has AUC close to 1 which means it has good measure of separability. A poor model has AUC close to 0 which means it has a poor measure of separability. In fact, an AUC of zero means that a specific model is reciprocating the result: it is predicting 0s as 1s and 1s as 0s. Finally, when AUC is equal to 0.5, it means the model has no class separation capacity at all.

    22. State-of-the-art algorithms

    Bayesian machine learning

    Bayesian machine learning allows for the influence of prior knowledge and experience regarding the format and structure of a constructed model, independent of what the data tells us. This is especially useful when a particular dataset is too small to confidently train a particular model on probability theory. Bayes’ theorem describes the probability of an event, based on prior knowledge of conditions that might be related to the event.
    Here, P(A) and P(B) are independent probabilities of event A and B, respectively. P(A|B) means probability of observing A, given that event B has happened. In Bayesian machine learning, we use the Bayes’ theorem to infer model parameters (theta) from data (D):
    is a term that generally cannot be computed, but since it is just a normalizing constant, it doesn’t matter that much. When comparing models, one is mainly interested in expressions containing theta, because stays the same for each model. is an estimation of model parameters based on expert opinion or previous experience. Most often, expert opinion is inconclusive and in the setting of ample data this expert opinion has minimal influence on model parameters. Inference should converge to probable theta as long as its not zero. is called the likelihood of data given model parameters. The formula for likelihood is model-specific. Scientists often use likelihood for evaluation of models: a model that gives higher likelihood to real data is better. Finally, is a probability distribution over model parameters obtained from prior beliefs and data.

    Decision tree

    Decision Trees are a type of Supervised Machine Learning where the data is continuously split according to a certain parameter. The tree can be explained by two entities, namely decision nodes and leaves. The leaves are the decisions or the final outcomes. And the decision nodes are where the data is split. A single decision tree is often not as performant as linear regression, logistic regression, etc. However, by introducing random forests and boosting, it can result in dramatic improvements in prediction accuracy at the expense of some loss in interpretation. Among decision support tools, decision trees have several advantages. Decision trees (
    1. • Are simple to understand and interpret. People can intuitively understand decision tree models after a brief explanation.
    2. • Have value even with relatively smaller datasets. Important insights can be generated based on experts describing a situation (its alternatives, probabilities, and costs) and their preference for outcomes.
    3. • Help determine worst, best, and expected values for different scenarios.
    4. • Use a white box model, if a given result is provided by a model.
    5. • Can be combined with other decision techniques.

    Decision tree versus random forest

    If there was a way to generate a very large number of trees, averaging out their solutions, then one would likely get an answer that is going to be very close to the true answer. Enter the random forest—a collection of decision trees with a single, aggregated result. Random forests are commonly reported as the most accurate learning algorithm. Random forests reduce the variance seen in decision trees by:
    1. • Using different samples for training,
    2. • Specifying random feature subsets,
    3. • Building and combining small (shallow) trees.

    Random forest versus boosting

    Like random forests, gradient boosting is a set of decision trees. The two main differences are:
    1. • How trees are built: random forests build each tree independently while gradient boosting builds one tree at a time. This additive model (ensemble) works in a forward, stagewise manner, introducing a weak learner to improve the shortcomings of existing weak learners.
    2. • Combining results: random forests combine results at the end of the process (by averaging or “majority rules”), while gradient boosting combines results along the way.

    Regression

    Regression is based on a hypothesis that can be linear, quadratic, polynomial, nonlinear, etc. The hypothesis is a function based on some hidden parameters and input values. In the training phase, the hidden parameters are optimized while the input values are presented in the training. The process that does the optimization is the gradient descent algorithm. If one is using neural networks, then there is an additional need for a back-propagation algorithm to compute gradient at each layer. Once the hypothesis parameters are trained (when they gave least error during the training), then the same hypothesis with the trained parameters is used with new input values to predict outcomes that will again be real values.

    Linear regression versus logistic regression

    1. • In case of Linear Regression, the outcome is continuous while in the case of Logistic Regression the outcome is discrete (not continuous).
    2. • Linear Regression is a regression algorithm for Machine Learning while Logistic Regression is a classification algorithm for machine learning.

    Support vector machine

    Support Vector Machine, abbreviated as SVM, can be used for both regression and classification tasks. The objective of the support vector machine algorithm is to find a hyperplane in an N-dimensional space that distinctly classifies the data points. To separate the two classes of data points, there are many possible hyperplanes that could be chosen. The objective is to find a plane that has the maximum margin, i.e., the maximum distance between data points of both classes. Maximizing the margin distance provides some reinforcement, so that future data points can be classified with more confidence. The loss function that helps maximize the margin is the hinge loss:
    where t the target label, and the model parameters.

    Deep learning and neural networks

    Why neural networks work?

    Since the inception of deep learning, few ideas have generated as much impact as convolutional neural networks (CNNs or ConvNets). Inspired by the experiments of David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel on the visual cortex (
    The Neural Network layers are inspired by the basic structure of the brain. The computational unit of the brain is a neuron. Approximately 86 billion neurons can be found in the human nervous system, and they are connected with approximately 1014–1015 synapses (

    Typical deep learning pipeline

    The training of a deep learning task is similar to that of ML tasks, like classification, segmentation, or clustering. All pipeline steps are built upon a general framework, for instance, Tensorflow (
    In the data preprocessing stage, the input data are collected and cleaned, while at this stage the ground truth is also defined and the quality of the data is validated. During the training stage, the prepared images and labels (if exist) are sent into a predefined convolutional neural network. Based on the output of the network, it calculates the loss function while the backpropagation will send the loss back to achieve optimal weights for each of the network layers. One Epoch is when an entire dataset is passed forward and backward through the neural network only once. Iterations are the number of batches needed to complete one epoch. During the testing stage, the platform should verify the test dataset, and decide which model is the best.

    Neural network versus convolutional neural network

    Convolutional Neural Networks are very similar to ordinary Neural Networks: they are made up of neurons that have learnable weights and biases. Each neuron receives some input, performs a dot product, and optionally follows it with a nonlinearity. The whole network still expresses a single differentiable score function: from the raw image pixels on one end to class scores at the other end. In addition, CNNs still have a loss function (e.g., SVM/Softmax) on the last (fully connected) layer, and all the tips/tricks that have been developed for learning regular Neural Networks still apply. Convolutional Neural Network architectures make the explicit assumption that the inputs are images, which allows us to encode certain properties into the architecture. Such a step allows efficient implementation of the forward function, as a result of vastly reduced parameters in the network.

    Convolutional neural network layers

    1. • Convolutional Layer
    2.     The convolutional (conv) layer is the core building block of a Convolutional Network (ConvNet) that does most of the computational heavy lifting. The conv layer’s parameters consist of a set of learnable filters. Every filter is spatially small (in terms of width and height) but extends through the full depth of the input volume. For example, a typical filter on a first layer of a ConvNet might have a size of 5 × 5 × 3 (i.e., 5-pixel width and height, and 3 because images have a depth of 3, which are the color channels). During the forward pass, one slides (more precisely, convolves) each filter across the width and height of the input volume and computes dot products between the entries of the filter and the input at any position. As one slides the filter over the width and height of the input volume, a 2-dimensional activation map is produced that gives the responses of that filter at every spatial position. Intuitively, the network will learn filters that activate when they see some type of visual feature such as an edge of some orientation or a blotch of some color on the first layer, or eventually entire honeycomb or wheellike patterns on higher layers of the network. Now, there will be an entire set of filters in each conv layer (e.g., 12 filters), and each of them will produce a separate two-dimensional activation map. Finally, these activation maps are stacked along the depth dimension thereby producing the output volume.
    3. • Pooling Layer
    4.     It is common to periodically insert a pooling layer in-between successive conv layers in a ConvNet architecture. Its function is to progressively reduce the spatial size of the representation to reduce the number of parameters and computation in the network, and hence to also control for overfitting. The Pooling Layer operates independently on every depth slice of the input and resizes it spatially, using the MAX operation. The most common form is a pooling layer with filters of size 2 × 2 applied with a stride of 2 downsamples every depth slice in the input, and by 2 along both width and height, discarding 75% of the activations. Every MAX operation would, in this scenario, be taking a max over 4 numbers (little 2 × 2 region in some depth slice).
    5. • Normalization Layer
    6.     Many types of normalization layers have been proposed for use in ConvNet architectures, sometimes with the intention of implementing inhibition schemes observed in the biological brain.
    7. • Fully connected layer
    8.     Neurons in a fully connected layer have full connections to all activations in the previous layer, as seen in regular neural networks. Their activations can hence be computed with a matrix multiplication followed by a bias offset.
    9. • Activation layer
    10.     Every activation function (or nonlinearity) takes a single number and performs a certain fixed mathematical operation on it. There are several activation functions one may encounter in practice:
      • Sigmoid Activation Layer: It takes a real-valued number and “squashes” it into a range between 0 and 1. In particular, large negative numbers become 0 and large positive numbers become 1. The mathematical form is: .
      • Tanh Activation Layer: It squashes a real-valued number to the range [-1, 1]. Like the sigmoid neuron, its activations saturate, but unlike the sigmoid neuron its output is zero-centered. Therefore, in practice the tanh nonlinearity is always preferred to the sigmoid nonlinearity. The mathematical form is: .
      • ReLU Activation Layer: The Rectified Linear Unit has become very popular in the last few years. It computes the function . In other words, the activation is simply thresholded at zero.
      • Leaky ReLU Activation Layer: Instead of the function being zero when x < 0, a leaky ReLU will instead have a small negative slope (of 0.01, or so). That is, the function computes , where is a small constant.

    Convolutional neural network architectures

    The machine learning community has persisted in its effort at innovating a variety of neural network layers to achieve higher performance. Different settings and combination of layers significantly affect accuracy and performance. In this section, we discuss how these are commonly stacked together to form entire ConvNets.
    1. • LeNet
    2.     The first successful applications of Convolutional Networks were developed by Yann LeCun in the 1990s. Of these, the best known is the LeNet architecture that was used to read zip codes, digits, etc.
    3. • AlexNet
    4.     The first work that popularized Convolutional Networks in Computer Vision was the AlexNet, developed by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoff Hinton. The AlexNet was submitted to the ImageNet ILSVRC challenge in 2012 and significantly outperformed the second runner-up (top five error of 16% compared to the runner-up with 26% error). AlexNet had a very similar architecture to LeNet, but was deeper, bigger, and featured Convolutional Layers stacked on top of each other (previously it was common to only have a single Conv layer always immediately followed by a POOL layer).
    5. • ZF Net
    6.     The ILSVRC 2013 winner was a Convolutional Network from Matthew Zeiler and Rob Fergus. It became known as the ZFNet (short for Zeiler and Fergus Net). It was an improvement on AlexNet by tweaking the architecture hyperparameters, in particular by expanding the size of the middle convolutional layers and making the stride and filter size on the first layer smaller.
    8. • GoogLeNet
    9.     The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) 2014 winner was a Convolutional Network from Szegedy et al. from Google. Its main contribution was the development of an Inception Module that dramatically reduced the number of parameters in the network (4M, compared to AlexNet with 60M). Additionally, it used Average Pooling instead of Fully Connected layers at the top of the ConvNet, eliminating a large amount of parameters that do not seem to matter much. There are also several follow-up versions to the GoogLeNet, most recently Inception-v4.
    10. • VGGNet
    11.     The runner-up in ILSVRC 2014 was the network from Karen Simonyan and Andrew Zisserman that became known as the VGGNet. Its main contribution was in showing that the depth of the network is a critical component of good performance. Their best network contained 16 CONV/FC layers and, appealingly, featured an extremely homogeneous architecture that only performed 3 × 3 convolutions and 2 × 2 pooling from the beginning to the end. Their pretrained model is available for plug and play use in Caffe. A downside of the VGGNet is that it is more expensive to evaluate and uses a lot more memory and parameters (140M). Most of these parameters are in the first fully connected layer, and it was since found that these FC layers can be removed with no performance downgrade, significantly reducing the number of necessary parameters.
    12. • ResNet
    13.     Residual Network developed by (

      Conclusions

      The application of traditional and advanced machine learning methods to solve cardiovascular tasks has witnessed significant strides over the past few years. This chapter covers the basic knowledge on the scope and approach of machine learning algorithms, specifically the utilization of convolutional neural networks to medical image tasks. Deep learning promises to revolutionize cardiovascular image analysis, and current efforts are focused at providing tools for interpretation of neural network output, as well as optimization for clinical applications.

    Chapter 3: Machine learning for predictive analytics

    Sehj Kashyap, Kristin M. Corey, Aman Kansal, and Mark Sendak     Duke Institute for Health Innovation, Durham, NC, United States

    Abstract

    Advances in the field of machine learning are enabling the development of new predictive models in the field of cardiovascular medicine. In this chapter, we cover how predictive machine learning models are developed, their recent use-cases in cardiovascular medicine, and limitations for their expanded use in healthcare. Predictive modeling has long been used in medicine, but recently, machine learning methods offer the ability to learn patterns in large and heterogeneous health data for improved predictive modeling. In addition to describing the general methods by which machine learning models are developed, we share their recent applications in electrophysiology, interventional cardiology, heart failure, and preventive cardiovascular care. We conclude with a discussion about issues regarding data quality, generalizability, bias, and interpretability, and how these influence model development and clinical integration.

    Keywords

    Artificial intelligence; Cardiovascular medicine; Clinical decision support; Machine learning; Predictive models

    Introduction

    Predictive models have long been used in medicine for clinical tasks such as risk-stratification, patient prognostication, and treatment planning. The Framingham risk score, ASCVD risk score, and NEWS score are examples of predictive models that use logistic regression and scoring-based methods, and have already been integrated into routine clinical care (
    What is unique about machine learning methods for predictive analytics as compared to traditional methods like statistical modeling and rules-based systems? It is important to acknowledge that there is no well-defined line separating machine learning methods from statistical and rule-based methods (

    Developing a predictive model

    In this section, we highlight four key steps in developing ML predictive models: (1) defining the opportunity, (2) creating the dataset, (3) developing the model, and (4) evaluating model performance. For more detailed outlines for developing machine learning models, we refer readers to the following reviews (

    Defining the opportunity

    The first critical step in developing a machine learning model is to clarify whether there is an opportunity for the intended clinical benefit. As pointed out by several researchers (
     

    Table 3.1

    A summary of key questions that should be asked at the outset of model development to clarify the opportunity of a model-integrated workflow.
    Defining the opportunity

    • What action(s) will be triggered or changed as a result of the model prediction? Can these actions be taken?

    • How much lead time is needed between the prediction time and the window of time over which an outcome is predicted to occur?

    • How will workflows be affected or need to change to utilize the model predictions?

    • Will the benefits realized exceed the costs of taking action?
    Often, a predictive model triggers an action or a series of actions to realize these benefit(s). Identifying what action would be triggered or if those actions could be taken is the first important step. The second step is to determine the minimum lead time required between when the prediction is made and when the outcome occurs to take the identified steps. The range for clinically useful lead times can vary between close to zero, to months or years. For example, predicting an incident episode of atrial fibrillation right before onset could still be useful as an intervention can be rapidly deployed. Third, it is important to consider how workflows may be affected by clinical and operational constraints; what can be done to make taking the desired action as easy as possible in the real-world setting? Finally, will the benefits be realized in the true positive cases identified by the model exceed the costs of taking action on the false-positive cases? How does the model performance compare with and without deployment of the model? If a model predicts cardiac decompensation and triggers intensive care unit (ICU) admission, is the escalation of care for that particular patient the most beneficial use of an ICU bed? These are some of the considerations that need to be thought through before beginning model development work and several authors have proposed doing utility assessments before and during model development (

    Creating the dataset

    After the opportunity has been defined, a dataset is prepared to train a model. Health data can come in many forms or modalities, for example, clinical registry data, medical device data, imaging data, and lab results data (
    Besides mathematically representing health data, it is also useful to organize the data onto a patient timeline. This has been proposed by multiple authors and most recently used in the paper by Rajkomar et al. for scalable deep learning in health (
    Once the data have been gathered, organized, and represented mathematically, data quality checks must be done. These checks can reveal unusual entries in the data that need to be corrected or discarded before model training (
    An important but subtle point is the validity of the labels. Labels are the clinical endpoints that a model is built to predict. If each patient record is converted into a mathematically represented input, the label is the output that the model must learn to map to from the input. If a model is built to detect hyperkalemia from electrocardiograph (ECG) recordings, the input is the ECG recordings and the label is whether that particular ECG reading was taken from a patient with hyperkalemia or not. In clinical medicine, nearly all endpoints to be predicted may have an element of subjective interpretation. For example, cardiac decompensation may be hard to define (

    Chapter 4: Deep learning for biomedical applications

    Jessica De Freitas1,2, Benjamin S. Glicksberg1,2, Kipp W. Johnson2, and Riccardo Miotto1,2     1Hasso Plattner Institute for Digital Health at Mount Sinai, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, United States     2Department of Genetics and Genomic Sciences, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, United States

    Abstract

    The types of data most commonly used for machine learning in biomedical research, including electronic health records, imaging, -omics, sensor data, and medical text, are complex, heterogeneous, poorly annotated, and generally unstructured. However, gaining knowledge and actionable insights from all these data sources is a key challenge in implementing personalized medicine and next-generation healthcare. Deep learning, which describes a class of machine learning algorithms based on neural networks, provides effective opportunities to model, represent, and learn from such complex and heterogeneous sources. Here, we review how this paradigm has already affected healthcare, we note limitations and needs for improved methods and applications, and we discuss the challenges to implement and deploy augmented human intelligence based on deep learning in the clinical domain.

    Keywords

    Augmented human intelligence; Biomedical applications; Biomedical informatics; Deep learning; Digital health; Electronic health records; Genomics; Health monitoring; Neural networks; Personalized healthcare

    Introduction

    Healthcare is approaching a new era where clinical decisions and patient behaviors will be influenced by the analysis of large quantities of biomedical data. On one side, physicians are capturing the status of their treated patients, their thoughts, orders, and outcomes in electronic health records (EHRs), -omics biobanks, and images. On the other side, patients are becoming more aware of the importance of prevention and keeping continuous track of their health status using wearable devices and preventative visits. Advances in machine learning (ML) are then taking advantage of this data in an attempt to supplement clinical medicine.
    However, there are many challenges in making full use of biomedical data, owing to their high-dimensionality, heterogeneity, temporal dependency, sparsity, and irregularity (
    A common approach in biomedical research is to have a domain expert specifying the phenotypes to use in an ad hoc manner. However, the supervised definition of the feature space scales poorly and misses the opportunity to discover novel patterns. Alternatively, representation learning methods allow automatic discovery of representations needed for prediction from the raw data (
    DL, a subfield of ML, has seen a dramatic resurgence in the past 6 years, largely driven by increases in computational power and the availability of massive new datasets. The field has witnessed striking advances in the ability of machines to manipulate data, including images (
    This chapter discusses recent and forthcoming applications of DL in medicine highlighting the key aspects to significantly impact healthcare. We do not aim to provide a comprehensive background on technical details or general application of deep learning (see, e.g.,

    A brief overview on deep learning

    ML is a general-purpose paradigm of artificial intelligence that can learn relationships from the data without the need to define them a priori (
    In contrast, DL is a form of representation learning, that is, a machine is fed with raw data and develops its own representations needed for pattern recognition, which is composed of multiple layers of representations, usually derived with neural networks. These layers are typically arranged sequentially and composed of a large number of basic, nonlinear operations, such that the representation of one layer (beginning with the raw data input) is fed into the next layer and transformed into a more abstract representation (
    Different important advances established DL as the state-of-the-art solution for several tasks. These models can scale to large datasets, mostly because of their ability to run on specialized computing hardware, and continue to improve with more data, enabling them to outperform many classical ML approaches. Easy-to-use software packages have brought these techniques to a broad community of computational scientists. Additionally, recent improvements for regularizations, strategies that aim to reduce generalization error, have made networks more robust, even when the number of parameters is very large. The larger datasets now available are also sufficient for fitting the many parameters characterizing deep neural networks. The convergence of all these factors currently makes DL extremely adaptable and capable of addressing the differences of each domain to which it is applied. Moreover, DL systems can accept multiple data types as input, which is of particular relevance for heterogeneous healthcare data.
    The most common models are trained using supervised learning, in which datasets are composed of input data points (e.g., a brain MRI scan, lab results) and corresponding output data labels (e.g., disease diagnosis, “abnormal” vs. “normal”). Unsupervised (or self-supervised) learning is usually used to draw inferences from datasets consisting of input data without labeled responses and to derive robust representations of the input space. Reinforcement learning, on the other hand, relies on computational agents that learn by trial and error or by expert demonstration and has recently been applied in medicine to learn wound suture for robotic-assisted surgery (

    Deep learning for healthcare

    The application of DL in medicine has been constantly increasing since 2012. Although initial publications only reported pilot studies and proof of concepts, more recent works are considering all the processes leading up to clinical deployment (
    The literature of this growing field is summarized in different excellent review papers and books (e.g.,
    In the following sections, we review a few relevant applications of DL in medicine, in particular related to medical imaging, EHRs, biomedical data, and health monitoring data. For each data type, we provide a comprehensive description of at least one study from the literature and briefly overview other relevant work. To the best of our knowledge, there are only a few applications that harness the ability of DL to combine various data sources or a part of them in a joint representation for medical analysis and prediction. We address this point in the discussion section.

    Clinical imaging

    Some of the greatest success of DL has been in the field of computer vision, which focuses on deriving insight from images and videos, and deals with tasks such as object classification, detection, and segmentation. In the medical domain, computer vision can be used to determine, for example, if a patient’s MRI scan contains an abnormal lesion. CNNs have grown to be central in this field, as they are good in modeling data with natural spatial invariance (i.e., images do not change if rotated or shifted). There are several examples of powerful applications of DL and CNNs in medical image analysis and computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) (
    CNNs were used to create an algorithm for automated detection of diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema in retinal fundus photographs (
    Skin cancer is primarily diagnosed visually, beginning with an initial screening and followed potentially by dermoscopic analysis, a biopsy, and histopathological examination. Automated classification of skin lesions using images promises to accelerate this process and to reduce subjectivity biases. Esteva et al. used a single CNN, trained end to end from images directly, using only pixels and disease labels as inputs to classify skin lesions (
    Zech and Badgeley et al. built deep neural networks to automatically detect pneumonia in chest radiographs (
    In addition to discovery, ML with images can be integrated as part of a “learning healthcare system” to facilitate hospital processes (
    DL has also been used to facilitate the analysis of cell images and tissue samples, where finding a trade-off between imaging quality, speed, noise reduction, and consistency in the analysis is difficult and often is a cause of missed opportunities and biased analysis. Lee et al. used CycleGAN (

    Electronic health records

    EHRs from millions of patients are routinely collected across diverse healthcare institutions. They consist of heterogeneous data elements, including demographic information, diagnosis, laboratory results, medication prescriptions, and free text clinical notes (
    A common approach of ML with EHRs is to have a domain expert designate the patterns to look for (i.e., the learning task and the targets) and to specify clinical variables in an ad hoc manner. Although appropriate in some situations, defining the feature space in a supervised manner does not scale or generalize well and does not allow for the discovery of novel patterns and features. DL can mitigate these limitations by reducing the need of manual feature engineering. In particular, deep neural networks are generally used to process aggregated EHRs, including both structured (e.g., diagnosis, medications, laboratory tests/results, procedures) and unstructured (e.g., free-text clinical notes) data, to obtain vector-based representations that are used for specific clinical inferences.
    In one of the first applications of DL to EHRs, Miotto et al. presented “Deep Patient,” an unsupervised deep feature learning framework to derive a general-purpose patient representation from EHR data that facilitates clinical predictive modeling (
    Fig. 4.4 includes high-level conceptual architecture to derive deep patient representations. All EHRs are first extracted from the clinical data warehouse, preprocessed to identify and normalize clinically relevant phenotypes, and grouped in patient vectors. Each patient can be described by just a single vector or by a sequence of vectors computed in, for example, predefined temporal windows. The collection of vectors obtained from all the patients is used as input of the deep unsupervised neural network to discover a set of high-level general descriptors. Every patient in the data warehouse is then represented using these features and such deep representations can be efficiently and effectively applied to different clinical tasks (

    Chapter 5: Generative adversarial network for cardiovascular imaging

    Mina Rezaei     Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States

    Abstract

    Analysis of cardiac function plays an important role in clinical cardiology for patient management, disease diagnosis, risk evaluation, and treatment decision. Delineation of right- and left-sided cavities, as well as major vessels, is an important step in clinical cardiology for cardiac disease diagnosis. Medical imaging provides a noninvasive diagnostic tool to study cardiac anatomy and detect pathological changes that occur in disease states such as dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and right ventricular dysfunction. The accurate automation of the corresponding task can accelerate the diagnostic part and assist in therapy decisions. In this chapter, we overview recent machine learning approaches that have been applied for automatic cardiac diagnosis based on deep learning and generative adversarial networks and explain the recent application of generative adversarial networks (GANs) for classification, detection, segmentation, registration, image reconstruction, and synthetization mostly in cardiovascular imaging. In continuum, we review the public cardiac dataset with open challenges and conclude the chapter with GAN limitations and future research directions.

    Introduction

    Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death in the United States, being responsible for 840,768 deaths (635,260 cardiac) in 2016 as reported by the American College of Cardiology (
    Cardiac image analysis plays an important role in cardiovascular disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and clinical monitoring. Cardiac imaging can provide useful information for the detection of different pathological conditions such as valvular disease, coronary artery disease, and myocardial disease. Further, imaging is often essential for the evaluation of therapy success. However, it is often difficult to interpret the raw data extracted from images due to the high variability in image quality and structure appearance among various individuals. Fig. 5.1 illustrates the diversity of myocardial tissue, vessels, and atrial/ventricular cavities in the systolic and diastolic phases on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
    Machine learning has been applied to cardiac images and clinical data to improve prediction accuracy and efficiency, which could result in more precise and targeted therapy while streamlining the diagnostic process. For instance, the number of investigations that have utilized machine learning approaches for automating medical image segmentation, for example, cardiac MRI segmentation (
    Generative approaches build models based on prior domain knowledge regarding the appearance and spatial distribution of the different tissue types. In the scenario of supervised learning, a generative model estimates the joint probability distribution of data P(X,Y) between the observed image X and the corresponding segmentation mask or label Y. Examples of popular generative models are Naive Bayes, Hidden Markov Models, Latent Dirichlet Allocation, and Boltzmann Machines. Traditionally, generative probabilistic models have been popular where simple conditionally independent Gaussian models (
    On the contrary, discriminative models directly learn the relationship between the local features of images to specific labels without any domain knowledge. Examples are logistic regression, scalar vector machine, neural networks, nearest neighbor, and conditional random fields. These local features can be raw input pixel values (
    Another popular discriminative model is the neural network, in which the machine learns the hierarchical representation of features (

    Generative adversarial networks

    The GAN framework (

    The generator G implicitly defines a probability distribution Pz as the distribution of the samples (G) obtained by z. Therefore, we would like Eq. (5.3) to converge to a good estimator of Pdata, if given enough capacity and training time. If the discriminator D is trained to optimality before the next generator G updates, then minimizing LG is proven to be equivalent to minimizing the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between Pdata(x) and Pg(z) as mentioned by Goodfellow et al. The desired outcome after training is that samples formed by should approximate the real data distribution Pdata(x).

    Challenges for GAN optimization

    The training procedure by GAN is hard and different from neural networks because we simultaneously optimize the generator and the discriminator for opposing objectives. Therefore, many methods address this problem by proposing variant losses, training with different architecture, or even different optimization algorithm. Another problem by classical GAN is nonconvergence where the model parameters oscillate, destabilize, and never converge. There has been nontrivial progress on how and when one can prove that GANs are globally convergent such as (1) game theory, (2) simplifying assumption, and (3) using normal neural network techniques.
    • (1) Game theory: These techniques try to model GAN training process using notions from game theory. Current studies (
    • (2) Simplifying assumptions: Some studies have shown that by simplifying assumptions of the generator and discriminator, one can move away the nonconvergence problem. For example, the simplified LGQ GAN (
    • (3) Using techniques from normal neural networks: Other studies have shown the success of convergence by applying normal and nonconvex neural networks.
      Mode collapse is one of the hardest problems to solve in GAN. Here, the generator collapses, which produces limited varieties of samples. For example, in ACDC dataset (
      The nonconvergence and mode collapse are often explained as an imbalance between the discriminator and the generator. The obvious solution is to balance their training to avoid overfitting. However, little progress has been made but not due to a lack of effort. Some researchers even believe that this is not a feasible or a desirable goal because a good discriminator gives good feedback. Some of the attention is, therefore, shifted for cost functions with nonvanishing gradients instead.
      In a discriminative model, loss measures the accuracy of the prediction, which is then used to monitor the progress of the training. However, the adversarial loss in GAN measures how well the discriminator is performing compared to the generator. Often, the generator cost increases but the image quality is improving. The next step is to examine the generated images manually to verify the progress. This makes model comparison harder, which in turn leads to difficulties in picking the best model in a single run. It also complicates the tuning process. Therefore, the next sections aim to cover investigations that have aimed at solving this issue.

    Loss-variant GANs

    Another design decision in GANs that significantly impacts performance is the choice of loss function in Eq. (5.3), which is an essential step to match the generated distribution to real data distribution. The objective function of original GAN is to minimize the JSD, wherein the JSD is derived from the Kullback–Liebler divergence (KLD).

    Scalability: As the authors discovered that GANs benefit dramatically from scaling, they introduced two architectural changes to improve scalability (described in detail in the paper’s Appendix B), while at the same time improved conditioning by applying orthogonal regularization to the generator.
    Robustness: The orthogonal regularization applied to the generator makes the model amenable to the “truncation trick” so that fine control of the trade-offs between fidelity and variety is possible by truncating the latent space.
    Stability: The authors discovered and characterized instabilities specific to large-scale GANs and devised solutions to minimize the instabilities, although these involve a relatively high trade-off on performance.
    In addition to its performance boost at 128×128 resolution, BigGAN also outperformed the previous state of the art at 256×256 and 512×512 resolution on ImageNet. The model was also tested on the larger image dataset, JFT-300M, to demonstrate its transferability.

    GAN application in medical imaging

    In this section, we provide an overview of the current state of the art in the application of deep learning algorithms to medical imaging. We cover details of GANs application for cardiovascular imaging. This section focuses on GAN application for canonical tasks such as image synthetization, reconstruction, classification, detection, segmentation, and registration.

    Medical image synthesis

    GANs have been widely proposed for image generation. We can group the GAN-based approaches into two categories: unsupervised generative framework and conditional GANs.
    Unsupervised GAN maps random noise to synthetic, realistically looking images following the training data distribution while the conditional GAN framework has a condition on prior knowledge for both the generator and the discriminator rather than solely utilizing noise. Fig. 5.6 shows the difference between unsupervised GAN and conditional GAN framework. Unsupervised GAN has been widely used to synthesize certain types of medical images either from noise alone or from prior knowledge by setting the conditions of image data for handling imbalanced classes (
    In an unsupervised setting, different GAN frameworks have been implemented for 2D or 3D synthetic image generation. Thereafter, the generated images in addition to the training samples are fed to the deep learning models with the goal of providing balanced, augmented, and diverse data.
    Hence, the diversity gained from synthesized images can introduce more variability into the training set and considerably improve classification results. In continuum, we describe the GAN framework used for generating minority class examples. For instance, Rezaei et al. proposed different 2D and 3D conditional and unsupervised DCGAN for MRI image synthesis to mitigate imbalanced class problem. The researchers then provided different experiments on balanced datasets with GAN generated samples, classical data augmentation, and imbalanced dataset. As expected, the diversity gained from synthesized images introduced more variability into the training set and considerably improved classification results. Figs. 5.7 and 5.8 show different settings by unsupervised and conditional configuration for image synthetization, respectively.

Positron emission tomography (PET) images are frequently used for diagnosis and staging in oncology, and the combined acquisition of PET and CT images is a standard procedure in clinical practice. Furthermore, PET/CT imaging is becoming an important evaluation tool for new drug therapies. However, PET studies are expensive and lead to radiation exposure, which carries an increased risk of future malignancy. Consequently, the imaging community has been working on synthesizing PET images directly from CT data. In this context, GANs have also shown outstanding performance. Initial promising results for synthesizing liver PET images from CT data with conditional GANs have been obtained by
    MRI. PET from MRI has been used for monitoring disease of progression, understanding the physiopathology while evaluating treatment efficacy in multiple sclerosis (MS).     Classification and detection

    Classification is one of the most successful applications of deep neural networks and generative adversarial networks that have been applied to various medical imaging benchmarks. Hierarchical image features can be extracted from a deep neural network and trained with imagewise class labels. GANs have been used for classification problems as well, either using part of the generator and/or discriminator as a feature extractor or directly using the discriminator as a classifier. Examples of classification by conditional GAN on cardiac images are included (
    Computational detection of anomalies from images using supervised algorithms require a large amount of annotated training data—extremely difficult and time consuming to be provided by experts. Unsupervised algorithms, such as GANs, have the potential to be effective in such a setting. The main driving idea of anomaly detection is to train GAN on normal images, so that inference on diseased images would lead to incomplete reconstructions. Such incompleteness is typically associated with the regions of an anomaly.

    Segmentation

    Conditional GANs (cGANs) have the advantage of being able to provide better representations for multimodal data generation because there is a control on the modes of the data being generated. This makes cGANs suitable for image semantic segmentation task, where we condition on an observed image and generate a corresponding output image.

    The 2015 Data Science Bowl challenge aimed at creating a benchmark of machine learning algorithms for the automated measurement of end-systolic and end-diastolic volumes on cardiac MRI. The database includes more than 1000 MRI images in 2D cine frames each containing around 30 images across the cardiac cycle. This dataset was compiled by the National Institutes of Health and the Children’s National Medical Center and is an order of magnitude larger than any cardiac MRI dataset previously released. The competition task had been to create an automated method capable of determining the left ventricular volume at two time points: after systole, when the heart is contracted and the ventricles are at their minimum volume, and after diastole, when the heart is at its largest volume.
