    Challenges, limitations, and future perspectives

    It is clear that deep learning and generative adversarial neural networks are very useful when one is tasked with producing accurate decisions based on complicated datasets. However, there are some major challenges and limitations of GANs that were discussed in Research background section. Emphasis should be placed on technical challenges such as mode collapse, none convergence, lack of interpretability and theoretical underpinnings of many GAN models and techniques, and the resulting difficulty in deciding exactly what it is that makes one model better than another, specifically in medical datasets. Other challenges are a result of difficulties in evaluation and assessment of performance.
    The progress of the GANs model in medical imaging and the clinical dataset is not quite as settled. One issue is that medical images are often three-dimensional, and three-dimensional convolutional neural networks are not as well developed as their 2D counterparts. A significant challenge relates to memory and compute consumption when using CNNs with higher-dimensional imaging data; challenges that researchers are trying various approaches to deal with (treating 3D as stacks of 2Ds, patch- or segment-based training and inference, downscaling, etc.). Other important challenges are related to data, trust, interpretability, workflow integration, and regulations.

    Chapter 6: Natural language processing

    Jake Vasilakes, Sicheng Zhou, and Rui Zhang     Institute for Health Informatics and College of Pharmacy, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, United States

    Abstract

    Natural language processing (NLP) is a subfield of artificial intelligence that is concerned with the automatic understanding of human language by computers. NLP has seen much success in recent years due to increased computing power and the rise of deep learning, and this success has extended into the domains of biomedical and clinical text. NLP has contributed to tasks such as the discovery of drug interactions, the development of clinical decision support systems, and the facilitation of chart review. Part I of this chapter provides an introduction to NLP, some common tasks in the biomedical domain, and the methods for accomplishing these tasks. Part II gives a survey of recent applications of NLP in cardiovascular medicine.

    Introduction to biomedical natural language processing

    It is widely assumed that a key component of intelligence is the ability to understand and use natural language. Natural languages are methods of communication that have developed naturally within human society without explicit planning. These include languages such as English, Chinese, and Pashto. Natural language processing (NLP) is a subfield of artificial intelligence whose goal is to program computers to understand and analyze natural language. The main challenge NLP faces in accomplishing this goal is ambiguity, which abounds in natural language. Words often have multiple meanings (e.g., “duck” in “We saw her duck.”), as do sentences (e.g., “No one does what we do well.”), and ungrammatical English is often still quite meaningful (e.g., “Me want cheeseburger” still gets the point across). Natural language thus stands in contrast to formal language such as computer programming languages and languages of logic. Formal languages are completely unambiguous. For example, a statement in C++ has exactly one meaning and all statements that are not grammatical C++ have no meaning at all.
    To address the ambiguity in natural language, NLP borrows extensively from the fields of linguistics, computer science, and artificial intelligence. Adopting this interdisciplinary approach, NLP has been successful for widely used languages such as English, specifically the “typical” use of English as in news articles and social media posts. However, as the field matures and NLP techniques become more successful, researchers have started applying NLP to various new domains.
    In general, the goal of NLP is to understand what a given collection of texts, called a corpus, is about. The biomedical domain, which includes journal articles and clinical notes from electronic health records (EHRs), is one of the most exciting domains to which NLP has been applied in recent years. NLP has found much success here, having been used to automatically extract knowledge from the biomedical literature, to improve clinical outcomes via clinical decision support, and to discover new drug interactions. However, the analysis of a biomedical corpus (collection of texts) brings forth an additional set of challenges over traditional NLP, in the form of increased ambiguity and patient data privacy.
    Ambiguity is a major challenge in biomedical text. Biomedical text has its own sublanguage, that is, sets of words, phrases, and structures that differ significantly from typical language (
    Patient data privacy is another critical issue for NLP applied to the clinical text. The use of clinical text corpora requires prior approval from institutional review boards (IRBs) and often requires de-identification, the process of removing all protected health information (e.g., names, dates, and addresses) that could allow one to identify the patient discussed in the note. Obtaining IRB approval and data deidentification are lengthy processes that significantly affect the speed with which new clinical NLP systems can be developed. Even once these processes are complete, sharing data across institutions is difficult, which further hampers the development of NLP systems that perform well across clinical sites.
    The above challenges, while specific to biomedical NLP, pose questions that are important for the field of NLP as a whole to answer: How should we approach sentence structure and meaning for ungrammatical or semi-grammatical text? How can we efficiently learn the meanings of previously unseen words? How can we develop NLP systems that respect personal (patient) data privacy? We are a long way from definitive answers to these questions and so these are crucial points to consider when deploying NLP systems in the real world.
    In the following sections, we discuss (1) The typical tasks when working with biomedical NLP and (2) The methods commonly used to address them. We are careful to illustrate where biomedical NLP differs significantly from traditional NLP, why it does so, and any implications.

    Tasks in biomedical NLP

    Creating an NLP model that understands a given corpus requires the completion of a number of tasks, which can be broadly categorized into high-level and low-level tasks. High-level tasks in NLP are often an end in themselves, while low-level tasks are part of the pipeline in addressing a high-level task.

    High-level tasks

    High-level tasks include but are not limited to automatic language translation, summarization, and question answering. The most prevalent high-level task in biomedical NLP, however, is information extraction (IE). IE aims to discover information or knowledge that is, in a sense, hidden within the text. IE is therefore crucial for a variety of time- and life-saving clinical processes. For example, IE can help facilitate chart review by extracting information from clinical notes (

    Named-entity recognition

    The goal of named-entity recognition (NER) is to find all mentions of certain types of concepts or entities in a given corpus. For example, an NER system might find mentions of symptoms and drugs within clinical notes. That is, it reads through the input text and outputs the entity type (symptom or drug or null) of each word. The main hurdle NER must face is polysemy or words with multiple meanings. In cases of polysemy, NER turns to one of two subtasks: word-sense disambiguation (WSD) and acronym disambiguation. The goal of WSD is to determine the intended meaning of a word as used in the text. WSD systems leverage context around the target word as well as syntactic information. For example, the word “cold” is polysemous, having different meanings according to the context and its role in the sentence, e.g., “I feel cold” (adjective) versus “I have a cold” (noun). Acronym/abbreviation disambiguation is related to WSD in that it aims to disambiguate acronyms by finding their correct expansion. For example, “MAP” expands to mitogen-activated protein but also mean arterial pressure.
    Although polysemy is pervasive in text, many of the entities in the biomedical text are much less susceptible to misinterpretation. For example, the word “tamoxifen”, especially in a clinical note, almost certainly refers to the breast cancer drug. In some cases, this means that rather than employ complex context- and syntax-aware methods, biomedical NER can proceed as a simple dictionary lookup. If the given word exists in a list of drugs, then it is annotated as such. For certain entity types, this method works relatively well in practice.

    Entity linking

    Biomedical entities often have a large variety of synonymous terms. For example, vitamin C, l-ascorbic acid, and sodium ascorbate all refer to the same entity. Giving a word or phrase a precise meaning is called grounding and it is often accomplished by the task of entity linking, which links entity mentions (such as those found by NER) to entries in terminology or database. Entity linking serves two purposes: (1) it is a means of normalizing all synonymous mentions into a single form (such as a specific database ID) and (2) it enables access to the other information stored about that entity in the database. For example, by linking the term sodium ascorbate to its PubChem entry 54,670,067, we gain access to its chemical structure, safety information, uses, etc. Entity linking also allows the knowledge generated by an IE system to interface with and inform other biomedical information systems.
    Entity linking also faces issues with ambiguity. Even if the NER or WSD system correctly identifies a word’s meaning, there may be multiple candidate database entries to link to. For example, should “increased mean blood pressure” be linked to the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) entry increased mean arterial pressure (C0520853) or mean arterial pressure increased (C4087413)?

    Relationship extraction

    Relationship extraction (RE) aims to discover relationships between entities in the text. The entities are often obtained by running an NER system beforehand. Using the example of discovering adverse drug reactions, an RE system should discern whether (1) the given symptom is an adverse reaction of the drug, (2) the drug treats the symptom, or (3) the symptom and the drug are unrelated in the text. The output of an RE system is thus a set of triples with a <subject, verb, object> structure, such as <tamoxifen, has_adverse_reaction, chest pain>. RE systems use context, such as the words between the two entities and the sentence structure, to determine whether two entities are related. Both are crucial for an effective RE system as clues in the context can be negated by sentence structure. Take for example the pair of sentences “We reviewed the charts of patients who were administered tamoxifen. It has been reported to cause chest pain but not vomiting.” First notice that the drug name “tamoxifen” does not occur in the second sentence, but is rather referred to by “It.” Resolving the meaning of pronouns like “It” across sentences is a task called anaphora resolution. Second, the context “reported to cause” between the drug (“It”) and the symptom “vomiting” indicates a potential adverse reaction, yet the “but not” indicates the opposite is true. The task of determining the scope of negation words such as this is called negation detection and negation resolution, respectively.
    The set of triples output by an RE system can be considered hypotheses, which can inform real-world clinical outcomes such as those related to pharmacovigilance, precision medicine, and drug repurposing.

    Low-level tasks

    Low-level NLP tasks are those that are not an end in themselves but are rather an integral part of larger NLP systems and crucial to the systems that perform the high-level tasks given earlier. Some low-level tasks are tokenization, sentence boundary detection, part-of-speech tagging, syntactic parsing, and language modeling. Many modern and very capable systems exist to perform these tasks, even given the challenges of biomedical text, so this section will provide only a brief overview.

    Tokenization

    Tokenization is the process of splitting a text into its constituent word instances or tokens. Although in English most tokens are separated by whitespace or certain punctuation marks, biomedical text often contains exceptional tokens such as “q.i.d.” or “L-ascorbic acid.”

    Sentence boundary detection

    Even in grammatical language, determining where a sentence starts and ends can be difficult. The period “.,” which is used in many languages to denote the end of a sentence, occurs in other places, such as in acronyms (M.D.). This ambiguity is increased in clinical note shorthand, which can leave out punctuation altogether. Systems for sentence segmentation thus employ a variety of contextual clues to determine whether a given character, such as a period, is indeed an end-of-sentence marker.

    Part-of-speech tagging

    The part of speech (POS) of a word indicates the role it plays in a sentence, such as verb, noun, and preposition. Knowing a word’s POS can thus provide crucial clues about its meaning. Knowing, for example, that “Buffalo” is being used as a proper noun allows an NER system to narrow down the possible labels for it. POS tagging systems assign one of a number of tags, such as those from the Penn Treebank, to each word in the input.

    Syntactic parsing

    Although POS tagging gives the roles of individual words, syntactic parsing determines how words fit together syntactically. Syntactic parsing can be shallow or deep. Shallow syntactic parsing groups words into phrases, such a noun or verb phrases. Deep syntactic parsing goes a step further by determining how words and phrases fit together to form a grammatical sentence. In both cases, a syntactic parser starts with the POS tags and combines them according to a set of grammatical rules to form a parse tree.
    A deep syntactic parse of the sentence “The patient reports experiencing chest pain.” is given in Fig. 6.1. The structure of a sentence illuminated by a syntactic parse shows how phrases are related to each other and can thus provide crucial clues to an RE system. For example, the parse tree shows that there is indeed a connection via a verb phrase between “The patient” and “chest pain.”

    NLP methods

    A number of methods exist for accomplishing the tasks described in the last section, which can be broadly grouped into rule-based methods and statistical or machine-learning methods. This section describes some common methods in each of these categories.

    Rule-based methods

    As discussed in the introductory section, natural language often breaks the rules of grammaticality. It is therefore impossible to come up with a set of rules that would allow computers to understand every utterance in a given language. Nevertheless, rules can account for a number of linguistic phenomena. Although the general NLP community has generally moved away from the use of rule-based models for analyzing text in favor of more complex machine learning models, biomedical NLP continues to benefit from them. Rule-based systems such as MetaMap (
    One of the most popular and powerful ways to implement rule-based NLP is by using regular expressions (regex). Regex is a small programming language designed to match and extract text. A given regex specifies a pattern to search for and is composed of literal characters and metacharacters. Literal characters allow for exact matches, for example, cat. Metacharacters have special meanings that either match multiple characters or which operate on another character. For example, the period “.” matches any character except newline and the plus “+” means match the previous character one or more times. Thus the regex cat.+ matches the literal string “cat” followed by any number of other characters such as “catamaran,” “catch,” etc.
    There are a number of existing expert-curated biomedical terminologies and ontologies that lend even greater power to pattern matching systems. Resources such as the UMLS (

    Statistical and machine learning methods

    Despite the continued relevance of rule-based models in biomedical NLP, the rise of machine learning (ML), specifically deep learning, has allowed for unprecedented performance on a variety of biomedical NLP tasks. We here describe a few common ML models for NLP, but in general one can think of an ML model for NLP as taking in a collection of numbers representing the text and outputting a collection of probabilities or predictions corresponding to the specified hypotheses (e.g., “at risk of heart attack” vs “not at risk of heart attack”), which can then be used to make a decision.
    Features
    As mentioned earlier, the input to an ML model must be a numerical representation of the input, but what does it mean to represent a word or a sentence numerically? There are a number of specific implementations, but in general the text is transformed into a vector, that is, a list of numbers, that in some way represents its meaning.
    Bag-of-words (BOW) is one of the simplest ways to represent text numerically. Each word in the corpus (collectively called the vocabulary) is assigned a place in a large vector. A “1” is marked down for each word that occurs in a given document. For example, say the vocabulary extracted from a corpus is the following:
    • [the, patient, arrhythmia, doctor, reports, saw]
    Then the following sentences would be represented as
    • The patient reports arrhythmia [1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0]
    • The doctor saw the patient [1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1]
    Note that BOW does not maintain the order of the words, nor does it indicate how many times a word occurs. Additionally, words such as “the” that provide little insight into a document’s meaning are treated the same as more illuminating words, such as “arrhythmia.” Term frequency inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) accounts for variation in word importance by weighting words according to a combination of their frequency in the document and their frequency in the entire corpus (
    Word embeddings or word vectors are one of the most important advances in NLP in recent years. As opposed to BOW and TF-IDF, which represent each word by a single number, word embeddings represent each word as a vector of numbers. Specifically, the numeric vector of a word is computed by a neural network model (discussed later) and is determined by the contexts in which that word occurs in a corpus. The assumption here is that words with similar contexts have similar meanings. In practice, this assumption is a powerful one. When estimated using a sufficiently large amount of text data, word embeddings capture phenomena such as synonymy and analogy surprisingly well. Fig. 6.2 provides a geometric interpretation of how word embeddings capture analogous meanings between words.
    The invention of word embeddings has led to significant advances in NLP across tasks and domains. Indeed, it was a major motivation for the rise of neural network models in NLP. The original word embedding model, Google’s Word2Vec (
    n-Gram language model
    An n-gram language model is one that predicts the next word given the n — 1 previous words using a simple count-and-divide method. The predictive model is estimated for a given sequence of n words by dividing the number of times that sequence occurs in the corpus by the number of times the previous n − 1 words occur in the corpus. For example, say the 4-gram “She fed the dog” occurs two times in a corpus and the 3-gram “She fed the” occurs eight times. Then the probability that the next word is “dog” given “She fed the” is . Language models allow us to compute the overall probability of a series of words, which is useful for a variety of prediction tasks.
    Hidden Markov model
    Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are sequence models. That is, given a sequence of inputs, such as words, an HMM will compute a sequence of outputs of the same length. An HMM model is a graph where nodes are probability distributions over labels and edges give the probability of transitioning from one node to the other. Together, these can be used to compute the probability of a label sequence given the input sequence. Fig. 6.3 illustrates a small HMM for weather given the temperatures over a number of days. According to this model, the temperature is unlikely to change dramatically from 1 day to the next. That is, it is unlikely to go directly from <0°C to >20°C.
    HMMs are often used for tagging tasks such as POS tagging and NER where a given label depends not only on the word in question but also the sequence of labels up to that point (e.g., it is unlikely that a verb follows a preposition).
    Support vector machine
    The support vector machine (SVM) is a model that learns how to separate data points (e.g., words or sentences) into one of two possible classes. As opposed to n-gram models and HMMs, the SVM is a discriminative model in that it does not estimate probabilities of belonging to one class or the other but rather it finds a decision boundary that separates the data points in geometric space (
    SVMs are most often used for prediction: after estimating a decision boundary on a set of data points for which we know the labels, the SVM predicts the labels of any new points by computing which side of the boundary they fall on. SVMs work quite well for a variety of NLP problems and, until recently, were used by many state-of-the-art systems for text classification.
    Neural networks
    The SVM in its standard form is a linear classifier. That is, the decision boundary it finds is always perfectly straight, as shown in Fig. 6.4. However, the classes in many datasets are not separable by a linear boundary. Although it is possible to modify the SVM via something called a kernel function to allow it to estimate a nonlinear decision boundary, it is still limited in its expressivity by the exact kernel function used. Neural network models (NNs), on the other hand, can approximate any function whatsoever, meaning the nonlinear decision boundary they find can be as nuanced as desired (
    NNs are realized in a wide variety of architectures. The neural network in Fig. 6.5 is an example of a feed-forward neural network (FFNN), as the values of each layer are fed directly into the next layer via a linear transformation. Other common NN architectures are the convolutional neural network (CNN) and the recursive neural network (RNN). Illustrations of these architectures are given in Fig. 6.6.
    CNNs (Fig. 6.6A) were originally designed to mimic the human vision system to improve performance on automatic image recognition (
    RNNs (Fig. 6.6B) are different from feed-forward neural networks and CNNs in that they operate over time (
    Standard RNNs are good for transforming an input sequence into an equal length output sequence, such as biomedical text input to word labels for an NER task. To transform between two sequences of unequal length, on the other hand, an encoder-decoder network is used (Fig. 6.7A), which uses a stack of two RNNs (
    Nevertheless, the encoder–decoder architecture described earlier has two issues. First, the entire input sequence is encoded into a single context vector, which is not ideal especially for very long input sequences. Second, the context vector is only made available to the initial state of the decoder, meaning that later decoder states will use it less. To combat these issues, the attention mechanism was developed, which provides a robust way to pass information from the encoder to the decoder (
    Although early uses of attention were in encoder–decoder networks using RNNs, it was later found that the RNNs themselves could be replaced by a modified attention mechanism called self-attention (
    The use of attention and self-attention culminated with the development of Google’s BERT model, short for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (
    The combination of BERT’s performance and the relative ease of fine-tuning it for specific tasks shot it into the spotlight, motivated a variety of modified versions, such as AlBERT (

    Biomedical NLP resources and systems

    The field of biomedical NLP is growing rapidly. As such, many new tools and resources are being developed for performing a variety of NLP tasks on biomedical and clinical text. This section briefly describes a few often used, open-source resources and systems.

    Biomedical terminologies and ontologies

    Summary

    Natural language processing seeks to address a variety of problems, from word tokenization to syntactic parsing to question answering. In the biomedical domain, however, information extraction (IE) is the major focus, and it comprises subtasks such as named-entity recognition (NER), entity linking, and relationship extraction. In general, the NLP methods used for these tasks can be divided into two categories. The first method is rule-based, which employs regular expressions, keyword lists, and other manually defined logic to process the text. Although rule-based methods have largely been discarded by the NLP community in favor of modern machine learning approaches, they still find a home in the biomedical domain, as they are easy to implement, use, and interpret, and in many cases perform competitively with modern approaches. Some notable rule-based systems are MetaMap and SemRep for entity linking and relationship extraction, and NegEx for negation detection. The second category is machine learning methods, which automatically learn to perform NLP tasks by using statistical modeling techniques. Most notably, the explosion of deep neural networks in recent years has motivated a number of powerful models for NLP, including CNNs, RNNs, and transformers, the last of which have shown enormous potential across many tasks and domains. Nevertheless, earlier models such as HMMs and SVMs often perform well in practice.
    A number of existing tools exist for NLP in the biomedical domain. The Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) provides an invaluable and expansive biomedical terminology. The UMLS is used by the aforementioned MetaMap and SemRep to perform entity linking and relationship extraction. Finally, cTAKES, CLAMP, and BioMedICUS are toolkits for biomedical NLP that include functionality for a variety of tasks, from tokenization to relationship extraction.

    Applications of NLP in cardiovascular research

    It is a rising trend to apply NLP in research related to cardiovascular diseases. The American College of Cardiology released the “Roadmap for Innovation” in 2017 that emphasizes the importance of NLP and machine learning in the era of digital health (

    NLP for information extraction

    Extracting information from text data is one of the primary tasks of NLP in the clinical area. The unstructured part of EHRs mainly contains three types of data: real-time data, retrospective data, and clinically irrelevant data (

    Rule-based NLP applications in cardiovascular research

    Researchers have been using NLP for information extraction tasks in clinical settings since the 2000s. Friedlin et al. developed an NLP tool called REgenstrief data eXtraction tool (REX), with the object to extract a list of targeted congestive heart failure (CHF)-related concepts (e.g., CHF, cardiomegaly) from X-ray reports (
    NLP has also been used for cardiovascular disease phenotyping in the EHR.

    Machine learning and deep learning with NLP applications in research

    NLP applications in clinical settings have been evolving from rule-based methods to machine learning and more advanced deep learning methods.

    NLP for clinical decision support

    Clinical decision support (CDS) aims to aid clinicians by providing them with easily accessible health-related information at the point of potential actionable advice. NLP is instrumental in extracting valuable information from unstructured data to represent clinical knowledge and drive CDS interventions that would improve the quality of healthcare (

    NLP for predictive models related to cardiovascular diseases

    The combination of NLP and machine learning methods is promising in the development of models for predicting cardiovascular diseases.

    NLP for cohort identification of cardiovascular diseases

    Cohort identification is another important task in the field of clinical research. It is a vital step for other tasks such as clinical trial screening and recruitment and public health studies. Traditional cohort identification uses structured data such as the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes and billing codes. However, using NLP methods on unstructured clinical texts has shown to better improve cohort identification tasks.

    Conclusion

    In summary, NLP applications in cardiovascular diseases have been developed for various tasks in processing and analyzing clinical texts, and a few of them have been applied in real practice. Currently, the major goals of NLP applications in clinical research are to extract and classify the target information of patients. NLP methods have evolved from rule-based methods to conventional machine learning-based methods. Most recently, advanced deep learning techniques, especially transformers such as BERT, have led to unprecedented advances in NLP, and have the potential to radically change how we approach NLP problems by removing the need for vast amounts of task-specific training data. There are still challenges and opportunities for NLP tasks in cardiovascular diseases. In the future, NLP will continue to play vital roles in both clinical research and clinical practice.

    Chapter 7: Contemporary advances in medical imaging

    Alpana Senapati, Shaden Khalaf, and Mouaz H. Al-Mallah     Houston Methodist DeBakey Heart and Vascular Center, Houston, TX, United States

    Abstract

    Contemporary advances in imaging technology have revolutionized the field of cardiovascular disease with improved detection of disease states coupled with innovative therapeutic interventions. As a result, clinicians have a plethora of diagnostic tools including echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography (CT), cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), and nuclear imaging. Echocardiography is widely available and provides a comprehensive assessment of cardiac anatomy, function, and hemodynamics. Complementary to echocardiography, CMR provides accurate cardiac volumes, function, and noninvasive hemodynamic assessment of valvular disease and flows. Innovations in cardiac CT have provided the ability to noninvasively image the coronary arteries, as well as cardiac structures that are useful in preprocedural planning for cardiac surgery or transcatheter heart interventions. Nuclear imaging has previously been the mainstay of ischemia assessment in coronary artery disease using exercise or vasodilator testing. Advances in CT-fractional flow reserve, CMR with scar imaging, and positron emission tomography (PET) with coronary flow reserve provide an ability to detect ischemia while extracting vital prognostic data for each patient. Recent advances in technetium-99m pyrophosphate, PET, and CMR have improved the ability to noninvasively detect cardiomyopathies such as cardiac amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, and inflammatory or infiltrative diseases. Nevertheless, each imaging modality is complementary to each other and often a multimodality patient-specific approach is needed. Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence within a clinical workflow allows for a safer, time and cost-effective approach to clinical practice and management.

    Introduction

    Innovations in cardiovascular imaging have changed the field of cardiovascular medicine with a significant impact on medical diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes. Contemporary advances in echocardiography (ECHO), nuclear cardiology, cardiac computed tomography (CT), and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) continue to evolve in the 21st century with an improved understanding of cardiac structure and pathophysiology. From the evaluation of basic cardiac anatomy and function, valvular heart disease, coronary artery disease (CAD), and cardiomyopathies, each noninvasive imaging modality adds to the armamentarium of diagnostic tools physicians and cardiologists can utilize to effectively diagnose and treat patients. With constant advances in new therapeutics and catheter-based interventions, such as transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), cardiac imaging plays an integral part in the decision-making process for patient care. Understanding the advantages and limitations of each modality is essential in choosing the proper test and often a multimodality imaging approach is needed. In this chapter, we provide an overview of the contemporary advances in noninvasive imaging while highlighting gaps where artificial intelligence can further advance the field.

    Echocardiography

    History of echocardiography

    Echocardiography is ubiquitous in clinical practice as it continues to be the initial noninvasive imaging test to be ordered. It provides a comprehensive assessment of cardiac structure, function, and hemodynamics becoming one of the most utilized cardiac imaging tests. The origins of ECHO date back to the 1880s with the discovery of piezoelectricity by

    Contrast agents in echocardiography

    The field of contrast ECHO began in 1969 with Raymond Gramiak and Pravin Shah while performing ultrasound on a patient undergoing cardiac catheterization using indocyanine green dye, which produced a cloud of echoes within the heart (

    Three-dimensional echocardiography

    Recent advances in ECHO transducer technology and faster computer processing systems using automated algorithms allow for 3D rendered images for clinical use. Several advantages of 3D ECHO include accurate quantitation of left ventricular volumes, ejection fraction, and a full volumetric dataset that allows for infinite slice planes for direct visualization of specific cardiac anatomic structures (

    Echocardiography strain imaging

    Strain imaging continues to evolve as a novel and promising tool for the evaluation of cardiac function in several cardiac disease states. Speckle tracking ECHO is a recent development utilizing small speckles of reflected ultrasound throughout the cardiac cycle. Strain measures the fractional shortening of two points (speckles) within the myocardium along the circumferential, radial, or longitudinal planes in the 4-,3-, and 2-chamber views. It then calculates an average strain curve in each direction, which is then quantified and displayed as a polar map with more negative values associated with the better myocardial function (Fig. 7.2) (
    There has been immense interest in machine learning and use of artificial intelligence in cardiovascular medicine with new technological advances and a growing population with cardiovascular disease. Noninvasive imaging remains a gatekeeper initial test in the management of patients with cardiovascular diseases. The use of machine learning in echocardiography offers a simplified diagnostic approach by utilizing complex mathematical models to integrate multiple imaging parameters from a high volume and large clinical imaging database (

    Nuclear cardiology

    Single-photon emission computed tomography

    Stress testing is a routinely used noninvasive modality applied to assess patients presenting with chest pain, with the aim of detecting the presence or absence of significant CAD. There are multiple types of stress testing ranging from exercise electrocardiography (ECG) treadmill, stress ECHO, stress CMR, or nuclear stress test. Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is one of the most widely utilized types of nuclear stress testing in the United States and usually uses Technetium-99m or Thallium-201 radiotracers for myocardial perfusion imaging. Combining these stress tests with exercise allows for assessment for functional capacity, chronotropic incompetence, and exercise capacity, all of which have significant clinical and prognostic implications (

    Position emission tomography

    Positron emission tomography (PET) has gained popularity over the past several years owing to multiple factors, including shorter study duration, better image resolution, ability to perform metabolic imaging, and lower radiation exposure. Given the enhanced image quality and absolute quantification of myocardial flow reserve (MFR), PET has higher accuracy for the detection of CAD (Fig. 7.4). MFR is also important for early detection of CAD and a marker for myocardial dysfunction in the absence of obstructive CAD (
    In addition, PET metabolic imaging utilizes the native myocardial metabolic pathway that is normally dependent on fatty acid metabolism. Although inflammatory cells have higher rates of glucose metabolism, infarcted “nonviable” myocardial tissue, on the other hand, experience disturbances in native metabolism. This is the basis for PET’s ability to determine myocardial viability, evaluation of inflammatory conditions, as well as infections of heart valves (

    Technetium-99m pyrophosphate imaging

    Cardiac amyloidosis is a type of infiltrative cardiomyopathy that results from the abnormal amyloid fibril deposition in the heart, with two main types: transthyretin (ATTR) and light-chain (AL). Diagnosis is usually made through serum blood markers along with fat pad biopsy, endomyocardial biopsy, CMR, or technetium-99m pyrophosphate (99mTc-PYP). New advances in noninvasive imaging with 99mTc-PYP imaging have improved the ability to differentiate between ATTR and AL subtypes of cardiac amyloid, which is a critical step for treatment planning (

    Cardiac computed tomography

    Cardiac CT assessment of coronary artery disease

    In the last decade, cardiac CT has gained acceptance as a tool for anatomical assessment of the coronary vasculature. The rapid advances in technology using dual X-ray source and wide multidetectors (320-slice detector scanners) allow for lower radiation exposure while maintaining higher temporal and spatial resolution with isotropic voxels down to 0.3 mm in x, y, and z axes (

    CT fractional flow reserve

    Although cardiac CT provides an excellent anatomic assessment of the coronaries, it has limited accuracy especially in the settings of high heart rates and dense calcifications. A recent technology that allows for the noninvasive functional assessment of the coronary arteries has emerged (

    CT perfusion

    The major advantage of CT perfusion is the ability to simultaneously and noninvasively evaluate coronary anatomy and physiology. Similar to nuclear cardiology, associated coronary perfusion defects during stress testing using pharmacologic agents, such as adenosine or regadenoson, allow for the identification of ischemia and functionally obstructive CAD (

    Cardiac CT in structural heart disease

    Although coronary CT angiography is the most commonly used application for cardiac CT, it is not the only one. With recent advances in percutaneous therapies such as TAVR, mitral valve clip, and transcatheter mitral valve replacement, the clinical applications of cardiac CT in structural heart disease has rapidly expanded (

    Cardiac magnetic resonance

    T1 mapping and late-gadolinium enhancement

    Clinical application of CMR started in the 1980s with the assessment of the cardiac structure, function, and myocardial tissue using T1 and T2 relaxation properties. With the development of contrast agents, myocardial perfusion, and viability assessment with detection of scar ensued in the 1990s. CMR can also be used to assess the aorta, coronary and peripheral vessels (
    With the advent of faster imaging processing systems, CMR has the added advantage of assessing myocardial tissue characteristics using T1 and T2 mapping. Specific myocardial tissue characteristic T1, T2, and T2∗ magnetization relaxation times help differentiate normal tissue from myocardial interstitial fibrosis, edema, and iron deposition within the myocardium. Contrast T1 mapping performed before and after gadolinium contrast can generate values for calculation of native T1 time and extracellular volume fraction, which correlates with the amount of diffuse interstitial fibrosis or infiltration of the heart (
    Contrast-enhanced CMR is well established for noninvasive evaluation of replacement fibrosis for myocardial scar assessment using late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). CMR-LGE is the only noninvasive modality to directly visualize myocardial scar, whereas previously this was only possible through direct evaluation of tissue from invasive endomyocardial biopsies or autopsies (

    CMR stress perfusion

    Coronary artery disease remains the leading cause of morbidity of mortality worldwide. Efforts to select the most cost-effective test for detecting and managing CAD continue to evolve. With significant advances in CMR due to its superior spatial and temporal resolution, stress perfusion CMR has evolved as a novel imaging tool for the detection and quantification of CAD and is comparable to other stress imaging modalities (

    Valvular heart disease

    Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging plays a key role in the evaluation of valvular heart disease and has several advantages including excellent signal-to-noise ratio and being able to image in any cardiac plane. Phase-contrast velocity mapping is used in CMR to assess flow through the systemic aorta and pulmonary artery systems to accurately quantify flow. CMR can accurately assess cardiac function, assess the mechanism of valvular pathology, quantify valvular regurgitation (“leaky valves”), and evaluate its effects on cardiac chamber size and function when ECHO is inconclusive or additional information is needed (

    CMR 4D flow

    Recent advancements in CMR using 3D phase-contrast imaging, or 4D flow, allows for measurement of flow in the x, y, and z planes, instead of assessing flow only in the traditional 2D plane. With advances in image processing, 4D flow datasets that are then imported into a software program for analysis can be acquired in 8–15 min. With a 4D flow sequence, anatomy, as well as 3D flow information throughout the cardiac cycle, can be collected and temporally related to visualize complex flow patterns in normal or structural heart disease (
    The integration of machine learning-based algorithms within clinical CMR can further improve workflow efficiency through faster postprocessing of acquired scans resulting in faster time to diagnose. Automated algorithms assessing cardiac anatomy, cardiac volumes, flow quantification, and 4D flow can result in a comprehensive cardiovascular assessment within minutes (

    Conclusions

    Innovations in cardiovascular imaging continue to evolve with recent and ongoing advances in ECHO, nuclear cardiology, cardiac CT, and CMR. Each cardiac imaging modality has its own advantages and often a multimodality imaging approach is needed in diagnosing complex patients. As imaging technology and understanding of cardiac pathophysiology continue to improve, cardiac imaging will no longer be solely used for disease diagnosis but will expand to incorporate prognostic data that could be useful for decision making and therapy selection. The rapid incorporation of machine learning algorithms within clinical imaging workflows holds promise in improving patient access to cardiac imaging. Multimodality cardiac imaging has and will remain an essential of contemporary approaches to patient-centered comprehensive care.

    Chapter 8: Ultrasound and artificial intelligence

    Brian A. Telfer1, Viksit Kumar2, Aaron D. Aguirre3,4,5, Anthony E. Samir2, and Laura J. Brattain1,2     1Human Health and Performance Systems, MIT Lincoln Laboratory, Lexington, MA, United States     2Center for Ultrasound Research & Translation, Department of Radiology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States     3Cardiology Division, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States     4Wellman Center for Photomedicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, United States     5Center for Systems Biology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, United States

    Abstract

    Medical ultrasound (US) is an indispensable medical imaging modality. It is nonionizing, portable, and can provide real-time visualization of tissue dynamics. In particular, US imaging of the heart, known as echocardiography, has been routinely used in the diagnosis, management, and treatment of patients with heart disease. However, US is highly operator dependent, thus suffering from high intra- and intervariability. Leveraging recent advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning has been applied to circumvent existent limitations of US-based imaging. In this chapter, we highlight the recent progress and discuss remaining challenges as well as future opportunities. The focus is on cardiovascular applications, but common themes and differences for noncardiovascular applications are also summarized.

    Keywords

    Artificial intelligence; Convolutional neural networks; Deep learning; Echocardiography; Intracardiac echocardiography; Intravascular US; Machine learning; Transesophageal echocardiography; Transthoracic echocardiography

    Introduction

    Compared to other major medical imaging modalities such as X-ray, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging, medical ultrasound (US) has unique attributes that make it the preferred modality for many clinical applications. In particular, US is nonionizing, portable, and provides real-time imaging, with adequate spatial and depth resolution to visualize tissue dynamics. The ability to measure Doppler information is also important, particularly for measuring blood flows. The small size of US transducers is a key attribute for intravascular applications. In addition, accessibility has been increased with the use of portable US, which continues to move toward a smaller footprint and lower cost. Nowadays, some US probes can even be directly connected to a phone or tablet.
    On the other hand, US also has unique challenges, particularly in that image quality is highly dependent on the operator’s skill in acquiring images based on the proper position, orientation, and probe pressure. Additional challenges that further require operator skill include the presence of noise, artifacts, limited field of view, difficulty in imaging structures behind bone and air, and device variability across manufacturers. Sonographers become highly proficient through extensive training and long experience, but high intra- and interobserver variability remains. This skill dependence has limited the wider use of US by healthcare providers who are not US imaging specialists.

    The goals of this chapter are to highlight the recent progress, as well as the current challenges and future opportunities. Specifically, this chapter addresses topics such as the following: (1) what is the current state of machine learning for medical US application, both in research and commercially; (2) what applications are receiving the most attention and have performance improvements been quantified; (3) how do ML solutions fit in an overall workflow; and (4) what open-source datasets are available for the broader community to contribute to progress in this field. The focus is on cardiovascular applications (Section Cardiovascular/echocardiography), but common themes and differences for other applications for medical US are also summarized (Section Breast, liver, and thyroid ultrasound). A discussion is offered in Discussion and outlook section.

    Cardiovascular/echocardiography

    Echocardiography is one of the most widely used diagnostic imaging modalities in cardiology. The most common form is transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), with other forms that include transesophageal echocardiography (TEE), intracardiac echocardiography (ICE), and intravascular US (IVUS) (Fig. 8.2). It is the only imaging modality that provides real-time imaging of the heart.
    Two-dimensional echocardiography is ubiquitously used to guide the diagnosis and down-stream management of numerous cardiac pathologies. Detailed analysis of echocardiography, however, is resource intensive, often resulting in visual estimation rather than precise calculation. ML proposes to automate many of these processes. There are already a number of widely adopted commercial software tools developed for the functional analysis of 2D echocardiography data (e.g., EchoPAC by GE Healthcare, QLAB by Philips, etc.), which can perform an assortment of tasks ranging from segmentation and detection of anatomic landmarks to blood tracking. All results from such analyses, however, are wholly dependent upon careful annotation of input data, which is implicitly deferred to the clinician. That is, to use these tools, the physician evaluating the imaging study must manually select the correct study, choose an appropriate window, and specify which parameters to compute. These steps, while trivial in the evaluation of an individual echocardiogram, become limitations when analyzing significantly larger datasets (
    In this chapter, we consider recent applications of ML to transthoracic, transesophageal, intracardiac, and intravascular echocardiography. Fetal echocardiography is yet another specialty topic for which ML is being applied (

    Transthoracic echocardiography and transesophageal echocardiography

    TTE and TEE characterize both structure and function of the heart. TTE is acquired using a probe applied externally to the chest wall with modest pressure. A coupling gel is used to minimize impedance mismatch. Several standard probe locations are used including the left parasternal, apical, and subcostal positions and various cross-sectional views are obtained using tilting or rotation of the probe in these positions. For TEE, an endoscopic probe is inserted through the mouth of the patient, typically under conscious sedation, and passed through the oropharynx into the esophagus. The depth of insertion (e.g., upper esophageal, midesophageal, and transgastric) as well as the angle and tilt of the probe head provides standard views. TEE provides clearer pictures of the upper chambers and can be particularly useful on obese patients or intubated patients.
    TTE is the most commonly used form of echocardiography in the assessment of structural and functional cardiovascular abnormalities. A complete TTE examination consists of a sonographer measuring nearly 30 parameters relating to physical dimensions and flow rates of the heart’s chambers, valves, and aorta. These measurements are based on four primary US views, including both B-mode images and video as well as Doppler. 3D and strain imaging are additional modalities that are becoming increasingly common. Data and measurements from the exam are then reviewed by a trained cardiologist, who adds findings to the report. With the large number of measurements as well as types of data, echocardiography provides a rich problem space for ML. A key difference in echocardiography compared to other cardiovascular imaging modalities is that US image acquisition is highly interactive and operator-dependent.
    The number of recent reviews (
    ML has been and will continue to improve TTE and TEE in several respects:
    1. • increasing accuracy and precision while reducing bias,
    2. • reducing image acquisition and study review times,
    3. • enabling new types of measurements that would be impractical without automation,
    4. • increasing accessibility of more indications,
    5. • increasing accessibility to more patients.
    Although 2D TTE remains the primary source of inputs, the increasing use of 3D TTE has augmented the accuracy of ML approaches by utilizing larger amounts of imagery. In addition, ML combined with portable US has the potential to allow aspects of TTE to be performed outside of a dedicated TTE facility, possibly even by nonexperts. Semiautomated and automated quantification in TTE has been progressing for over a decade in commercial products (
    The top-level TTE workflow is summarized in Fig. 8.3. A sonographer performs an exam in real time on a patient. A typical TTE exam requires about 30 min. During the exam, the sonographer positions the probe for a particular view and makes real-time measurements. After the exam is completed, a cardiologist reviews the images and measurements, and based on a conglomerate of specific findings establishes a particular diagnosis. Most of the published work on applying ML to TTE relates to view classification and measurements of the left ventricle. Little attention has been given to improving image acquisition, although this is a goal of Bay Labs (San Francisco, USA), as noted by

    Quality assessment and view classification

    Significant research has been focused on automated view classification. Typical TTE exams collect at least 70 videos at different views (
    Table 8.2 summarizes 2D view classification results from recent publications. The goal of view classification is to categorize a specific video as being from a particular view. The approach is usually to classify random images from a video and apply logic to classify the entire video.

    The biases (mean errors) of the ML methods compared to the criterion methods in Table 8.3 are small, most often underestimates. However, the 95% limits of agreement (LoAs, equivalent to 1.96 standard deviations assuming a Gaussian distribution) are large compared to values for EDV, ESV, and EF (ranges of mean values noted earlier). The large LoAs make it very difficult to compare performance of different methods. On the other hand, these LoAs are comparable to interobserver and intersite LoAs. For example, one study (
    Insight on the source of poor concordance for specific cases is not generally reported.
    It has been clearly established that automated methods save time. An example of time reduction for 2D TTE of 217 ± 69 to 116 ± 57 s per patient was found using Philips a2DQ software (
    3D TTE has been shown to be more accurate and reproducible than 2D TTE and is recommended by the most recent American Society of Echocardiography and European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging guidelines (
    Various ML approaches have been applied, with a progression over time toward deep convolutional neural networks, with Leclerc and colleagues (
    As a commercial product, the details of the HeartModel algorithm are not well described, but reportedly are based on ML (
    Most methods that use CNNs have taken a standard approach of segmenting the left ventricle and measuring volumes and ejection fractions from the segmented frames. In an attempt to measure ejection fraction for all cases, even those with poor image quality, CNNs have also been used to measure ejection fraction based on estimating contraction coefficients from two images, without segmenting the chamber boundaries (
    Attention is also being directed toward applying ML-based solutions for portable US.
    Finally, although measurement of LV volume has received the most attention in the literature, detailed mitral valve analysis from 3D transesophageal echocardiography has also been reported using automated commercial software (eSie Valve Software, Siemens Healthcare, Mountain View, CA) (

    Disease classification

    In addition to computing standard measurements, ML has been applied to disease classification, which is one of the most important and impactful applications of ML. Recent work has shown that ML can improve the identification of subclinical diseases from echocardiography. For example, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was discriminated from physiological hypertrophy using three ML algorithms (support vector machines, random forests, and artificial neural networks) for TTE measurements (

    Intracardiac echocardiography

    ICE has emerged as a useful tool in the everyday practice of electrophysiology and percutaneous interventions (
    For use, an ICE catheter is inserted into the patient’s vasculature (e.g., femoral vein) and navigated to the heart, where it acquires 2D B-mode images of cardiac structures. Often in conjunction with fluoroscopy, ICE has been used for transseptal interventions (e.g., shunt closure), catheter ablation of atrial fibrillation, and ventricular tachycardia, among other applications. ICE offers direct visualization of the surrounding tissue and is often used for instrument tracking and for assessing tissue/instrument contact. Compared to external US probes, ICE can achieve higher quality views of targets in the near-field with higher acoustic frequencies, reducing aberration and attenuation due to layers of intervening muscle, fat, and other tissues. When compared to TEE, ICE is also associated with decreased procedure length while eliminating the risks of endotracheal or esophageal intubation and general anesthesia (
    The use of ICE, however, requires highly trained operators. For example, although 2D ICE offers a wider cross-section view than a typical TTE/TEE, it has limited thickness along the axial direction. Obtaining the optimal view requires dexterity and experience in manipulating control knobs. Image interpretation also requires a substantial amount of expertise. In addition, the continuous contractile movement of the heart makes it challenging to keep up with the motion while maintaining an adequate view with the use of an ICE probe. Ablation lesion tracking and assessment as well as ablation catheter tracking also demand a high level of training.
    One way to mitigate the thin viewing plane is to compound multiple 2D ICE slices together using robotic manipulation. A GPU-enabled real-time 3D ICE volume stitching and visualization method has been proposed (
    Commercial 3D ICE imaging systems are also emerging. Sequoia US system (Siemens Healthineers) equipped with SoundStar 3D diagnostic US catheter (10F, 90 cm, Biosense Webster, Inc., Diamond Bar, CA) is capable of acquiring US volumes from within the heart. A more recent 3D ICE system, Acuson SC2000 Prime with ACUSON AcuNav (Siemens Healthineers), can provide 2D/3D quantification using AI. The details of the AI methods used are not available.
    Although numerous technical approaches have been investigated over the past decades, few have provided a reliable and reproducible advancement in clinical outcomes. Several recurring procedures are needed to raise the success rate to the 70%–80% range (

    Intravascular ultrasound

    Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) is an imaging modality that has a specially designed catheter with a miniaturized US probe attached to the distal end of the catheter. The coronary arteries are the most frequent imaging target for IVUS. IVUS is used to exam the vessel walls and assess calcification and atheromatous plaque, which cannot be seen by conventional angiography.
    IVUS imaging has also been proven useful in guiding coronary intervention procedures based on a comprehensive assessment of atherosclerotic plaque quantitative and qualitative characteristics, while also proving to be useful for coronary stent evaluation postimplantation (
    Compared to intravascular optical coherence tomography (OCT), which has ∼10× better imaging resolution, IVUS offers much better penetration (∼5×) depth for the assessment of lipid or necrotic plaques (

    Although conventional image processing remains an important approach to facilitate the interpretation of IVUS, ML has shown promise in IVUS tissue classification (TC) and anatomical component segmentation. IVUS TC is largely related to atheromatous plaque and calcification assessment. Earlier efforts focused on texture-based or radio frequency-based feature extractions, followed by using support vector machine (SVM) or random forest (RF) as a classifier for plaque or calcification assessment (
    Over the past few years, DL has been increasingly applied to TC within the IVUS realm. Because of the limited annotations available,
    In regards to segmentation of anatomical components on IVUS, the majority of the work relates to segmenting arterial and media-adventitial (MA) walls.

    Breast, liver, and thyroid ultrasound

    Besides cardiovascular applications, other organs that have been frequently explored with ML algorithms include breast, liver, thyroid, prostate, brain, fetal, and skin. Different anatomical organs have their own unique requirements and challenges. In the past 3 years, as a result of rapid technical advances in DL algorithms, DL-based approaches have been by far the preferred ML approach for the detection of desired tissue, segmentation of desired tissue to perform measurements, and classification of tissue into a specific class. In this section, we will focus on breast, liver, and thyroid, where we have seen a burst of DL algorithm development.

    Breast ultrasound

    Breast tissue cells are prone to cancer and as such breast cancer is the leading cause of death in women aged 20–59 years (
    The application of DL in breast US can be broken down into three broad categories: detection/localization of abnormal breast tissue/mass or tumor, segmentation of breast mass, and classification of breast mass as benign or malignant. Detection or localization of breast masses have special relevance in the absence of mammogram exams and can improve the efficiency and productivity of the screening process especially when the exam is performed by less-skilled users. Segmentation of breast masses is important in identifying certain morphologic features associated with breast cancer such as irregular boundaries, spikes in boundary called as spiculations, and irregular shape. Suspicious breast masses are recommended for biopsy based on the BI-RADS score and are prone to overdiagnosis leading to undue emotional, pain, and economical stress associated with biopsy performance. Classifying breast masses as benign or malignant can reduce the number of unnecessary biopsies. Textural and morphological features extracted from sonographic images have been commonly used in the past few decades with limited success. Deep neural networks have been commonly used for detection (

    Liver ultrasound

    Liver, the largest organ in the body, is prone to cancer and fatty liver disease. Liver cancer is the fifth and seventh most common cause of cancer death among men and women, respectively (
    US has been extensively used as the primary imaging modality for the evaluation of liver disease. Abdominal US exam covering liver, kidney, and spleen is the most common US exam. Acquiring and annotating standard US views is a meticulous task. DL algorithms have been proposed for view classification (

    Discussion and outlook

    Progress in applying ML to ultrasound has accelerated over the last few years, as part of an overall movement to increase automation for medical applications over at least the past decade. As is the case in other domains, DL algorithms and in particular, CNNs, have become the predominant classification methods, overtaking other classifiers operating on hand-crafted features. As in other types of biomedical image interpretation, U-Nets have been found to perform well for segmentation tasks.
    In TTE, most approaches have used variants of CNNs to segment the left ventricle and then measure volumes and ejection fraction from those boundaries. However, in a few cases, CNNs have been trained to operate directly on the US images to make measurements. Most approaches have trained CNNs in standard ways and do not make full use of transfer learning (
    Progress has been made in accuracy, but there is much more to be done. Automated methods eliminate intra- and interobserver variability of the measurements themselves, although variability still exists due to variability in the imaging. Thus, automated methods have improved precision compared to manual interpretation. Automated methods have also been shown to have low biases when compared to manual measurements as the criterion standard. However, LoAs are large. Imagine telling a patient that they have an ejection fraction between 25% and 65% (due to a LoA of ±20% as reported in some results). That would not be helpful. Still, the large LoAs are partially a result of the fact that the criterion standard is manual measurement, which itself suffers from intra- and interobserver variability. In addition, much more work needs to be done to characterize and understand the outlier error cases. This has been done to some level in a couple of investigations, but needs to be performed systematically and routinely. That will lead to improved results.
    Most research has focused on the aspects of the TTE system flow depicted in Fig. 8.3, and in particular on view of classification and left ventricular measurements. The vast majority of published papers have focused on B-mode video processing, rather than the Doppler information that is also available from echocardiography examinations. Electrocardiogram (ECG) data are also collected during TTE, which is particularly useful for determining the underlying rhythm and correlating a particular image to the cardiac cycle. However, ECG data are also not typically used in research on ML for TTE, in some cases for convenience (it is simpler to just analyze US imagery) and in some cases because the focus is on point-of-care US where ECG may not be included. More broadly, there is a rich research space to fuse US information with other sensor modalities.
    Consideration of workflow of an ML system within a clinical environment is an important topic. Commercial products that incorporate some degree of artificial intelligence do address workflow and aspects of workflow, such as provision for manual editing as well as measuring time saved. However, workflow and human factors are typically not evaluated explicitly. In academic papers, the focus is on a particular subfunction, and workflow and the overall system that is needed are typically not considered. Published papers with more of a system view will be valuable.
    A critical aspect of automated echocardiography that has been typically neglected involves aiding nonexperts in acquiring the correct views (guiding probe position, orientation) and high-quality images. For example, it is well reported that automated algorithms are less accurate for poor quality images, even when acquired by trained sonographers. Improving image quality will lead to improved accuracy. Aiding image acquisition and identifying which images to process needs to become a significant topic in future research.
    Finally, approaches to explainable AI are notably missing from the literature. The AI community is increasingly giving attention on how humans gain trust in AI-enabled systems. As echocardiography is image-based, trust can be promoted as the human views segmentations or other annotations on images interpreted by the AI system. For example, the human will learn types of cases that the AI system can measure accurately, and which types of cases need to be scrutinized more closely. Still, trust is an important aspect of a human-machine system, and the research into explainable AI has much to contribute to echocardiography.
    Overall, we expect that the acceleration in ML applications to echocardiography will lead to the following:
    1. • improved accuracy and faster measurements for 2D echocardiography,
    2. • increased adoption of 3D echocardiography (e.g., 3D TTE and 3D ICE),
    3. • increased use of echocardiography for point of care applications by nonexperts (US at the bedside) and eventually even within the home environment,
    4. • increased use of ML for cardiac procedure guidance,
    5. • emerging use of ML for noninvasive, longitudinal monitoring of cardiovascular conditions with biofeedback.
    More broadly speaking, ML has the potential in improving accuracy, speed, and expanding the application of medical US to the nonexpert user. Many discussion points above can also be applied to other organs such as those covered in Section 3. In general, when compared to publicly available nonmedical datasets such as ImageNet (
    Increased automation enabled by ML will free sonographers and clinicians from making low-level measurements, which will allow them to provide more individualized care for more patients and ultimately improve the overall patient outcome.

    Chapter 9: Computed tomography and artificial intelligence

    Damini Dey1, Andrew Lin1, Donghee Han2, and Piotr J. Slomka1     1Biomedical Imaging Research Institute and Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, CA, United States     2Department of Imaging and the Smidt Heart Institute, Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, CA, United States

    Abstract

    In the past 2 decades, significant advances in computed tomography (CT) hardware and software have expanded the clinical utility of CT imaging. Hardware improvements include faster gantry rotation with improved temporal resolution, improved spatial resolution, and greater coverage of the patient, enabling faster acquisition. Concurrently, there have been applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in all aspects of CT imaging—acquisition, reconstruction, analysis, and measurement of novel image features—which may further improve the value and reduce cost. Chapter 9 summarizes the recent advances in AI applied to several key aspects of CT imaging, interpretation, and analysis.

    Keywords

    Artificial intelligence; Computed tomography; Deep learning; Diagnosis; Machine learning; Prognosis
