    Introduction

    In the past 2 decades, significant advances in computed tomography (CT) hardware and software have expanded the clinical utility of CT imaging. In the cardiovascular domain, imaging of the coronary arteries is technically challenging due to their small size and rapid constant motion. Cardiac CT requires high temporal resolution to “freeze” such motion and, therefore, has benefited from steadily increasing CT gantry rotation speeds. Imaging of the coronary arteries also requires high spatial resolution and reconstruction of submillimeter slices. Multiple CT slices need to be acquired simultaneously for complete coverage of the heart in one breath-hold. To meet these requirements, technical advances in CT hardware have focused on improved temporal and spatial resolution and more detectors for increased coverage (

    Terminology

    In general, AI describes a computational program that can perform tasks that are associated with human intelligence, as such learning and problem-solving. Machine learning (ML) represents learning techniques that can give AI the ability to learn, typically progressively from large datasets, without making any prior assumptions. Finally, deep learning (DL) methods, a subset of ML, mimic human cognition by using multiple layers of convolutional neural networks (CNNs); in each layer, convolutional filters perform as feature extractors. In the past few years, the popularity and application of DL methods have expanded dramatically.

    Artificial intelligence in CT image reconstruction

    Given the hardware developments in CT imaging, there is a demand for image reconstruction algorithms to be more accurate and computationally efficient. In addition to well-established analytic and iterative methods for CT image reconstruction, a new wave of data-driven and learning-based methods has emerged, which draw extensively from DL techniques.

    Deep learning approaches

    The power of DL lies in the multilayer approach used to extract and identify important features from an input. CNNs are usually trained by first defining a loss function, which measures the discrepancy between the actual and desired outputs of the CNN for the training dataset. An optimized set of weights for the convolutional layers is then determined using an iterative optimization algorithm (

    Denoising low-dose CT images

    DL approaches have the potential to help reduce CT radiation doses while speeding up reconstruction times. With an estimated 80 million CT scans performed in the United States each year (
    Chen et al. first trained a CNN to reduce noise in CT images by learning a patch-based neural net (

    Improving sparse-view CT reconstruction

    Low-dose CT can also be obtained by reducing the number of projections over the same acquisition arc, also known as a sparse-view protocol (

    Removing image artifacts

    CNNs have also been used to reduce artifacts caused by metal or beam hardening. Metallic implants in patients are highly attenuated, leading to “hardening” of the polychromatic X-ray beams and resultant streak artifacts in reconstructed CT images (
    In summary, the described AI techniques can optimize or even replace modern analytic and iterative reconstruction methods with algorithms learned from big data. They can improve the quality of images reconstructed from insufficient data, as occurring in low-dose or sparse-view CT, or overcome artifacts due to adverse object conditions such as metal in a patient. Although not yet ready for clinical implementation, these algorithms have the potential to enhance CT workflow by providing rapid and computationally efficient image reconstruction.

    Artificial intelligence in cardiac CT image analysis

    The big data generated by precision cardiovascular imaging is heterogeneous and rapidly changing, requiring increasingly sophisticated and efficient computational models for their analysis and interpretation. Noninvasive imaging with coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring noncontrast cardiac CT and coronary CT angiography (CTA) plays a key role in the diagnosis, risk stratification, and management of patients with cardiovascular disease. By facilitating CT image segmentation, measurements, and subsequent clinical pathways, AI may assist physicians in delivering more efficient and personalized care with improved accuracy and reduced costs.

    Image segmentation

    One of the first DL algorithms developed for cardiac CT used marginal space learning—which incrementally learns classifiers in marginal spaces of lower dimensions—to automatically segment all four heart chambers in 3D CT volumes. This method was tested on a large annotated dataset, achieving accurate boundary delineation with an average speed of 4 s per volume (
    Coronary artery segmentation from coronary CTA enables luminal stenosis grading, plaque assessment, and blood flow simulation. The two major steps in this process are coronary centerline extraction and lumen segmentation. Centerline extraction has typically been performed using CNNs as a pre- or postprocessing step for traditional methods (
    Automated segmentation of heart valves has been of recent interest due to the surge in transcatheter valve replacement procedures, which require valve modeling and precise sizing of the implants. Marginal space learning can provide patient-specific modeling and segmentation of all four valves from cardiac CT; this framework incorporates a constrained multilinear shape method to efficiently estimate the patient-specific valve parameters from cine images (

    Semiautomated plaque analysis

    Beyond the detection of coronary stenosis, coronary CTA enables a comprehensive assessment of atherosclerotic plaque, with certain visually determined plaque characteristics conferring an increased risk of future cardiovascular events (

    Automated measurements

    CAC assessed via CT is a direct marker of coronary atherosclerosis and a strong predictor of adverse cardiovascular events (
    The noninvasive detection and quantification of coronary stenosis is the most widely used clinical application of coronary CTA, with current reporting based on a subjective visual assessment by clinicians.
    The hemodynamic significance of a given coronary stenosis can also be assessed using AI techniques. A novel DL algorithm to calculate noninvasive fractional flow reserve (FFR), trained on a large dataset of synthetically generated coronary models, demonstrated similar accuracy and faster execution times (∼2.4 s per case) compared to computationally demanding 3D flow simulations, with invasive FFR as the reference standard (
    Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is a metabolically active fat depot within the visceral pericardium that directly encases the coronary arteries. There is evidence that EAT exerts a local pathological effect on the coronary vasculature (

    Outcome prediction

    ML integration of clinical and cardiac CT data has been shown to improve the prediction of cardiovascular outcomes. In 6814 participants from the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis),
    Coronary CTA measures can also enhance ML risk prediction models. In an analysis of 10,030 patients from the CONFIRM (Coronary CT Angiography EvaluatioN For Clinical Outcomes: An InteRnational Multicenter) registry, an ML model combining 25 clinical and 44 visually assessed coronary CTA parameters (based on lesion location, composition, and stenosis severity) predicted 5-year all-cause mortality with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.79, significantly better than existing clinical or CTA metrics alone (

    Cardiac CT radiomics

    Radiomics is a new field of quantitative image analysis in which digital medical images are converted into mineable high-dimensional data (
    Coronary atherosclerotic plaques consist of distinct histological components with different CT attenuation values; each voxel is a separate measurement of the amount of radiation absorbed in the given volume. This has enabled the noninvasive assessment of plaque characteristics in vivo with coronary CTA. However, as previously discussed, the visual interpretation of plaque features is subject to interobserver variability, and current plaque quantification methods are based on absolute voxel attenuation values without considering the relationship between voxels. Radiomics can provide an objective, mathematical, or AI-based description of plaque that incorporates the spatial distribution of voxels. This approach has been shown to outperform conventional qualitative and quantitative parameters for the detection of high-risk plaque (
    In summary, AI applications have shown great promise in facilitating cardiac CT image analysis, by automating image segmentation and quantification and assisting physician interpretation. Furthermore, the integration of clinical and imaging data using AI models improves cardiovascular risk stratification over conventional methods. Radiomic analysis is a new field that quantifies spatial and textural features from images and utilizes AI approaches to identify novel imaging biomarkers from big data. In the foreseeable future, AI may work in the background of cardiac CT image analysis software and routine clinical reporting, automatically collecting data and enabling real-time diagnosis and risk stratification.

    Artificial intelligence in CT brain for stroke

    Stroke is one of the major causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide (

    Noncontrast CT

    The noncontrast CT scan is an effective and rapid method of CT examination without contrast injection. It is the current standard for the initial imaging of patients who are suspected of having a stroke. The two different types of stroke, hemorrhagic and ischemic, have different treatment strategies. The biggest advantage of noncontrast CT is its ability to detect an intracranial hemorrhage to discriminate hemorrhagic stroke. DL-based AI applications can improve the detection of intracranial hemorrhage. The largest contemporary study consisting of 313,318 noncontrast CT scans evaluated a fully automated (DL) algorithm designed to detect time-sensitive abnormal findings, including intracranial hemorrhage (
    In the case of ischemic stroke, CT findings are often subtle compared to hemorrhagic stroke; thus, training and experience are required for accurate noncontrast CT evaluations. The Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score (ASPECTS) is a 10-point quantitative score that measures the extent of early ischemic changes in brain noncontrast CT images (
    The hyperdense sign in noncontrast CT represents a marker of thromboembolus in patients with acute ischemic stroke. AI-based automated detection of the hyperdense vessel sign in emergency imaging may accelerate the identification of patients with ischemic stroke. This was demonstrated in a study that used an AI algorithm to detect the hyperdense middle cerebral artery (MCA) dot sign (

    CT angiography

    CTA can effectively evaluate the presence and extent of intracranial vessel occlusion in patients with acute ischemic stroke. In addition, CTA enables the visualization of the anatomy of the proximal extracranial vessel and collateral flows, providing information to guide endovascular treatment. Although it is not challenging for expert readers to interpret CTA, the automated analysis of CTA imaging can be used to assist physicians by improving the accuracy and efficiency of their readings. In a study of 875 patients, where 46% of the subjects had large artery occlusions, automated CTA analysis based on a DL algorithm showed an accuracy of 86%, sensitivity of 90%, and specificity of 83% compared to the interpretations of experienced stroke neurologists (
    Another application of AI algorithms to CTA images is to assess collateral flow. Collateral flow is defined as blood flow through a network of preexistent vascular anastomoses. Assessments of collateral flow based on CTA imaging can identify patients who may benefit from an endovascular thrombectomy (

    CT perfusion

    CTP is a series of 3D CT scans acquired after intravenous contrast injection, which demonstrates blood perfusion in the brain. Compared to noncontrast CT, CTP can identify earlier ischemic changes. Prior research evaluated estimates of CTP postprocessing quantitative parameters including cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume, and mean transit time. These perfusion parameters help identify brain tissue characterizations in patients with acute ischemic stroke. Automated and operator-independent imaging processing tools have been used to quantify CTP parameters, providing rapid processing of quantitative CTP parameters within several minutes (
    CTP enables the distinction of potentially salvageable ischemic tissue (penumbra) from irreversibly infarcted tissue (core). The accurate estimation of core and penumbra volume is an important point in CTP image analysis that helps determine the optimal treatment strategy. Core and penumbra volumes evolve over time: the core becomes larger, as the penumbral tissue becomes irreversibly damaged core. These changes depend on various clinical and imaging factors, such as the location of the infarct and the baseline size of the core and penumbral tissues. Prior research has demonstrated that ML algorithms can predict not only core and penumbra volumes, but also how the core volume changes over time (
    In summary, AI applications for CT-based stroke evaluation have performed well in rapid, automated, and standardized analysis of noncontrast CT, CTA, and CTP scans. This information can provide real-time support for clinical decision-making and individualized treatment strategies for patients with acute ischemic stroke. Future studies will need to determine the feasibility and efficacy of integrating these AI algorithms into the clinical workflow of stroke management.

    Artificial intelligence in CT for cancer screening

    Cancer is a group of diseases involving the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells in the body. Cancer remains the most prominent cause of morbidity and mortality, accounting for approximately 1.8 million new cancer cases in 2019; a number that is projected to rise to more than 2.3 million by 2030 (

    Lung nodule detection

    Early detection of malignant lung nodules improves prognosis, and CT is a useful modality for detecting lung nodules. Current guidelines suggest that a low-dose CT scan (LDCT) is an appropriate and effective screening tool for selected high-risk populations (

    Identification of high-risk imaging features

    Pulmonary nodules are incidentally detected in more than 1.5 million adults in the United States each year (
    Radiomics is the process of extracting a large number of quantitative features from medical images and can be used to identify subtle imaging features of malignant lung nodules that cannot be detected by visual interpretation. Once the features have been extracted using dedicated software, a potential challenge for radiomics is to identify and prioritize stable radiomics features. Traditional ML methods can be used for feature selection from a large radiomic dataset (
    Recent advances in DL algorithms have demonstrated promising results for identifying, classifying, and quantifying patterns in medical imaging analysis (
    To summarize, a variety of AI applications have been used to enhance accuracy and efficiency in lung cancer CT screening. The application of such algorithms can assist in the manual identification of pulmonary nodules and reduce physician interpretation time.

    Summary

    In summary, with the increasing sophistication of ML and deep-learning techniques, AI-based algorithms can be utilized to improve medical imaging. When testing the performance of AI algorithms, the test data must be always kept separate from training data, to enable realistic estimates of performance. Further, external validation in data from unseen centers, not just hold-out data from the same center, can be expected to provide the most robust performance. Individualized risk prediction, which explains the AI findings for a specific patient, will be increasingly useful because they can personalize medical therapy. They will also be important for the acceptance of new AI approaches by physicians by overcoming the “black box” perception of AI. From the current data, AI-based algorithms can be expected to improve most aspects of CT imaging—personalized acquisition, reconstruction, image interpretation, and analysis and measurement of novel image features.

    Abstract

    Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) is the best-suited cardiac imaging modality to provide reliable and reproducible information regarding cardiac volumes, function, and tissue characterization. In clinical practice, artificial intelligence (AI) in CMR can be applied to the whole process, ranging from sequence reconstruction, image analysis, and reporting of findings. In sequence reconstruction, the application of AI is mainly focused on the speed of reconstruction, while in image analysis and reporting AI is primarily aimed at automating the process of segmentation of both ventricles as well as fibrotic tissue. Within the realm of tissue characterization, AI can also be helpful in the depiction of tissue abnormalities from noncontrast images. Finally, AI can be useful for prognostic stratification.

    Introduction

    The diagnostic and prognostic role of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing in medicine (
    The aforementioned applications of AI in CMR can be helpful from numerous aspects, especially in relation to workflow optimization by shortening acquisition periods, image analysis and reporting of findings that would help with the institution of patient-specific and disease-specific therapy. In the next section of this chapter, we will provide an overview of the application of AI in CMR.

    Image reconstruction with AI

    In this era, CMR represents the most accurate and reproducible noninvasive cardiovascular imaging technique that allows for the evaluation of chamber volumes and function in addition to tissue characterization of ventricular walls (
    To overcome such a limitation, several strategies have been developed by different vendors. In particular, new sequences have been used for different acquisition and reconstruction of the k-space (

    Role of AI in cardiac MR analysis

    Left and right ventricular function

    Cine images represent an important aspect of CMR examinations. Acquiring cine images in long-axis and short-axis planes provides the ability to evaluate wall motion, chamber volumes and function, anatomy, and valvular disease with high reproducibility (
    The neural networks used for CMR image analysis had been developed on small but heterogeneous populations and comparisons have often been performed to establish the network with the best performance (
    The aforementioned limitation of a small sample size used for the development of a neural network for image analysis was outdated by Bai and colleagues, who used the UK-biobank as the source of data (

    Role of AI in tissue characterization

    One of the main advantages of CMR is the high spatial resolution that allows for the ability to characterize myocardial tissue (
    LGE is typically acquired in clinical practice for the evaluation of replacement fibrosis (
    Moccia et al. developed two algorithms based on a fully convolutional neural network (FCNN) for the detection of LGE in an ischemic cohort (
    Another interesting application of AI in terms of tissue characterization was developed by Baessler et al. using a combined approach of T1 weighted images, texture analysis, and machine learning (ML) on a cohort of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy patients (

    AI for prognostic assessment

    CMR is a useful noninvasive imaging tool that provides valuable information for prognosis and risk stratification (
    The application of ML algorithms for risk stratification has been seen in cohorts undergoing cardiac CT. Motwani and colleagues showed that an ML approach, built with a boosted ensemble algorithm and 10-fold stratified cross-validation, combining clinical data and quantitative atherosclerotic plaque measures, was able to better predict 5-year all-cause mortality compared to existing clinical or cardiac CT metrics alone (
    Recently, an article by Chen et al. studied the role of ML in predicting 1-year cardiovascular events in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy (
    However, randomized trials are the next logical step with this innovative approach that could prove the effectiveness of an AI-based method on risk assessment. The ideal workflow for establishing the prognostic trajectory of individuals using ML is summarized in Fig. 10.4.

    Limitation and future directions

    The major limitation of AI in cardiac MR is represented by the limited insight that is offered to clinicians regarding the inner working of various AI models, traditionally called as the “black box” aspect of AI. Furthermore it is well known that the development of a powerful AI algorithm requires large datasets for training and validation purposes. This aspect is quite challenging as each institution, site, and/or company has its own regulations and policies on data sharing and privacy. Nevertheless, the potential implications for an expanded role for AI within healthcare in general, and cardiac magnetic resonance in particular, promises to revolutionize the field, and future multi-disciplinary collaborations are likely to focus efforts and attempt at reaching solutions for current existent limitations.

    Conclusions

    The application of AI promises to revolutionize and advance the utility of CMR in clinical medicine and across healthcare systems. AI in CMR adds value in regards to image acquisition, reporting of findings, and contextualization of data (Fig. 10.5). At the time being, the application of AI in CMR includes the following:
    • (1) Optimization of the workflow involving CMR image reconstruction and reporting.
    • (2) Extraction of tissue characteristics without the need for additional contrast agents.
    • (3) Improvement in prognostication of outcomes in select high-risk cohorts.
    The ensuing few years promise to result in significant advances in the application of AI in the field of cardiac MR, with the ultimate goal of providing physicians with tools to optimize daily workflow while providing patients with specific and precise risk assessment.

    Chapter 11: Nuclear imaging and artificial intelligence

    Benjamin C. Lee1, Felix Y.J. Keng2, Subhi J. Al’Aref3, and Lohendran Baskaran1,2     1Dalio Institute of Cardiovascular Imaging, Weill Cornell Medicine/NewYork-Presbyterian, New York, NY, United States     2Department of Cardiovascular Medicine, National Heart Centre, Singapore     3Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, Little Rock, AR, United States

    Abstract

    Myocardial perfusion imaging with single-photon emission computed tomography and positron emission tomography has aided in diagnosing the severity of coronary artery disease. Artificial intelligence in cardiovascular nuclear medicine imaging includes various methods such as rule-based reasoning, artificial neural networks, structured machine learning, and deep convolutional neural networks. These artificial intelligence methods have been applied in detecting perfusion defects and other endpoints. Deep learning methods have been applied to nuclear medicine image formation to decrease computation time, improve image quality, and reduce radiation exposure to patients. This chapter summarizes AI methodologies applied to image analysis and image reconstruction for cardiovascular nuclear medicine imaging.

    Myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) has aided in diagnosing coronary artery disease (CAD) particularly in assessing its severity, manifest as ischemic heart disease (IHD). Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is the most widely available and validated nuclear medicine imaging modality (Fig. 11.1D). Positron emission tomography (PET) on the other hand produces higher resolution images (Fig. 11.1E) and has a higher diagnostic accuracy than SPECT and cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (
    Image reconstruction of nuclear medicine images was first performed by the filtered backprojection (FBP) algorithm, an analytical formulation of inverting the projection data in the camera-collected sinograms (Fig. 11.1A and B) to the original image. However, FBP does not account for the inherent Poisson noise model and therefore iterative reconstruction methods were developed to better model the physical process and camera system thus reducing noise and artifacts in the reconstructed image.
    Image analysis begins with the segmentation of the left ventricular (LV) myocardium using polar sampling to get the maximum count circumferential profile of each short-axis slice (
    Artificial intelligence in cardiovascular nuclear medicine imaging has been applied as early as 1985 using reason-based semantic nets and fuzzy logic (
    Recent developments of deep learning algorithms such as the convolutional neural network (CNN) and availability of faster hardware such as graphics processing units have contributed to AI-based image reconstruction of nuclear medicine images, mostly for PET images due to it being a newer and higher resolution modality. These deep learning-based techniques aim to decrease reconstruction time, improve image quality, and reduce radiation dose to the patient.

    Artificial intelligence in cardiac SPECT and PET image analysis

    Application of AI methods for cardiovascular SPECT and PET image analysis to diagnose IHD began with expert systems using a knowledge base and associated rules. Learning-based methods soon followed with artificial neural networks. Due to heavy computational requirements to train a neural network, other machine learning methods such as support vector machines and decision tree-based methods gained more popularity. Attention to neural networks was later renewed due to hardware improvements and new deep learning algorithms in the form of convolutional neural networks. As most of the research in AI for medical image analysis has been to diagnose or predict similar disease indicators or clinical endpoints, the following topics are organized by AI algorithms: nonlearning-based expert systems, structured traditional machine learning, shallow artificial neural networks, and deep convolutional neural networks. The methods reviewed focused on cardiovascular imaging, which were mostly from SPECT systems.

    Nonlearning expert systems

    Expert systems are programmed with known facts and their inferences to emulate the decision-making process and performance of a human expert. The first type is case-based reasoning, which is a process of making decisions based on past experiences. It finds the most similar prior problem in the knowledge base, based on a similarity metric on relevant features, and applies that solution to the current problem.
    A more common type of expert system employs rule-based reasoning, which encodes knowledge from experts into “if-then” association rules. Although rule-based reasoning can be more difficult to implement compared to case-based reasoning, rule-based expert systems are typically more accurate. The earliest SPECT application of a rule-based expert system was introduced in 1985, where
    Later,

    Traditional machine learning

    In contrast to expert systems, learning-based systems, such as supervised machine learning, develop a model of the data only guided by the labeled output as ground truth. The learnable weights or coefficients of a model are iteratively updated in small steps that eventually reduce the error between the model’s prediction and the ground truth output. Any machine learning method that inputs features, hand-engineered by a domain expert from raw data, is considered traditional machine learning. As such, models that input structured or tabular data fall into this category. Specifically, models that are not deep neural networks also fall into this category, like support vector machines (SVMs), decision tree-based ensemble methods, and shallow artificial neural networks. Linear regression and logistic regression, borrowed from statistics, are also part of machine learning because they learn their coefficients from data.
    An SVM is a classifier that separates two classes with a linear boundary that maximizes the margin between the boundary line and the closest data points from each class, known as support vectors (Fig. 11.2A). SVMs can also generate nonlinear class boundaries by warping the feature space into higher dimensions to make the two classes separable by a linear boundary. An SVM with the kernel trick replaces the expensive coordinate transformation with a simpler distance computation to the decision boundary.
    Decision tree-based ensemble methods combine multiple decision trees and are categorized into either bagging or boosting ensembles. Bagging, a contraction of bootstrap aggregating, either averages or majority votes on the outputs of individual models that were trained in parallel on different subsets of the training data. Random Forest is an example that uses bagging on individual decision trees (Fig. 11.2B).
    Boosting is a method that sequences individual weak learning models that perform slightly better than random guessing, with increased weights iteratively placed on the previously incorrectly predicted training cases, thus converting the whole series of weak learning models to a stronger ensembled learning model. AdaBoost, short for adaptive boosting, was the first boosting algorithm to use weak learners like decision stumps, decision trees with a single split. LogitBoost reframed boosting probabilistically using the logistic loss function (Fig. 11.2C) instead of the exponential loss of AdaBoost. Therefore, LogitBoost is less sensitive to noisy data and outliers compared to AdaBoost. Gradient Boosting, also called gradient boosting machine or gradient tree boosting, is a generalization of AdaBoost, where each new weak learning model added reduces the overall model error using gradients to provide the next optimization direction. XGBoost, which stands for Extreme Gradient Boosting, is a gradient boosting algorithm with many algorithmic improvements that reduce overfitting, run an order of magnitude faster than its predecessors, and are well suited on large datasets.
    Both bagging and boosting reduce the variance of the output, producing more stable models. They differ in that bagging is better suited for reducing overfitting while boosting can reduce bias and increase accuracy.
    In the early 2010s, preliminary work on SPECT images used SVMs to detect abnormal perfusion (
    LogitBoost has also been used to predict outcomes in other studies.

    Shallow artificial neural networks

    Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are learning algorithms with interconnected artificial neurons called perceptrons that are loosely based on biological neurons (Fig. 11.4A). Each perceptron or node sums multiple weighted input values and based on a threshold, outputs a single value between 0 and 1, called an activation. This nonlinear operation of limiting the output to a range is performed by a sigmoid or an S-shaped function and allows for input to output mappings that are more complicated than a simple linear combination. A feed-forward neural network propagates the weighted and combined activation signals from one layer of nodes to the next in one direction without cyclical connections. These are also called fully connected layers or multilayer perceptrons. The output at the last layer can output continuous-valued regression results or be binarized for classification. Although current deep artificial neural networks have up to hundreds of layers (Fig. 11.4B), the earliest artificial neural networks consisted of just an input layer, one hidden layer, and an output layer because a single hidden layer was found to be sufficient to approximate any continuous function (
    The perceptron was introduced in the 1950s but an efficient algorithm for training neural networks called backpropagation was not developed until 1986. In backpropagation, the gradients of the output errors generated from a loss function propagate backwards through the layers correcting their weights iteratively (Fig. 11.4A). Shallow ANNs were the earliest traditional machine learning models studied on SPECT images, 2 decades earlier than SVMs and tree-based ensemble methods noted in the prior section.

    Deep learning and convolutional neural networks

    Deep learning is a subset of machine learning in which raw data such as images or time sequences are inputted into a learning model instead of hand-engineered features. Precisely, a deep learning model is a neural network with more than one hidden layer and can be as deep as several hundred layers (Fig. 11.4B). The multiple hidden layers afford the neural network to automate the feature extraction process and create higher-order decision boundaries.
    Convolutional neural networks or CNNs (Fig. 11.5A) are deep learning models that automatically extract features from large 1D, 2D, 3D, or even 4D inputs in the first part of the network consisting of convolutional layers by compressing the data into a set of important features. This is performed by a mathematical operation called a convolution that involves sliding a filter across an image. A moving average filter or a smoothing filter is an example. Any kind of filter may be learned in the training process. Input images filtered over several convolutional layers are transformed into features and are then sent to the final part of the network consisting of fully connected layers like a regular ANN, for the classification or regression prediction step. The convolutional layers allow CNNs to be efficient because only spatially local network connections are considered. The unbiased nature of the CNN’s feature extraction step may lead to never-before-considered and better output-predictive features than hand-engineered ones.

    CNNs have been applied to other conditions in nuclear medicine beyond coronary artery disease. Cardiac sarcoidosis (CS) is an inflammatory disease in which small clumps of white blood cells called granulomas form in the heart.
    One criticism of machine learning is that it is a “black box” where the nonlinearity of the machine learning algorithms makes it difficult to know how and why the algorithm arrived at its decision. It is desirable to understand the algorithm’s feature visualization and feature importance.

    CNNs were originally designed for inputting rectangular natural images of the outside world; however, changing the network architecture of CNNs to better adapt to the desired input data is possible. Projecting the capped cylindrically 3D shape of the LV myocardium to a 2D polar map to input into a CNN introduces spatial distortions where the apical region is compressed, and the basal regions are expanded. Additionally, a 2D polar map image leaves blank regions in the corner of the circumscribed square input image. To avoid these issues,
    CNNs have also been adapted to produce output images. This new architecture is called a fully convolutional network (FCN), which leaves out the fully connected layers of the second half of the CNN and consists of only convolutional layers. The U-Net is a special case of an FCN that mirrors the downsampling convolutional layers of a CNN with succeeding deconvolutional layers that upsample the compressed features to a segmented image of the original size (Fig. 11.5C) (

    Artificial intelligence in cardiac SPECT and PET image reconstruction

    Artificial intelligence in image reconstruction for nuclear medicine has been a recent development due to the relatively recent advent of the convolutional neural network. As most image reconstruction deep learning methods are CNN based, the topics are organized by the goals of the reconstruction. Some of these objectives include directly reconstructing the image from the measurement data without an explicit image measurement model in an end-to-end approach, while others include using the traditional image reconstruction algorithms but generating attenuation maps from non-CT imaging modalities or correcting for motion artifacts. Deep learning has also been applied to the last step of the image reconstruction pipeline that includes noise reduction techniques that allow for either improving image quality or lowering the radiopharmaceutical dosage while retaining the same image quality. Although much of this research in nuclear medicine has been focused on brain imaging, the techniques described here are applicable to cardiovascular imaging.

    End-to-end reconstruction

    In the machine learning context, end-to-end reconstruction refers to estimating an image directly from the raw measurement data of the imaging camera without using conventional filtered backprojection or iterative reconstruction methods like ordered subsets expectation-maximization (OSEM). The measurement data that SPECT and PET cameras ultimately produce are sinogram data (Fig. 11.1B), which are sets of angular projections (Fig. 11.1A). In 2018,

    Attenuation correction

    For PET, varying radiopaque areas of the body can attenuate an emitted positron from reaching its intended sensor causing attenuation artifacts where some parts of the myocardium may incorrectly appear to have lower counts. Incorporating a CT attenuation correction (CTAC) map (Fig. 11.2A) from a PET/CT imaging system into the reconstruction process can correct for this. For PET/MR imaging systems,

    Motion correction

    Motion of the patient during imaging is unavoidable, whether it is cardiac, respiratory, or patient motion. The impact of motion is blurred imaging.

    Denoising and image quality improvement

    Autoencoders are convolutional neural networks that extract the most important information in images by forcing the successive image activations of the network through a bottleneck. Autoencoders are special cases of encoder–decoder networks where the input and outputs are the same. The impact of the bottleneck retaining the most important information is a smoothing or denoising effect.
    Another wide area of deep learning reconstruction research is in denoising low-dose nuclear medicine scans. Many of these approaches generally train an encoder–decoder network with low-dose image inputs and standard-dose image outputs. During testing or running of the model, the low-dose images are transformed into ones with reduced noise. There are many examples of this using different networks.

    Summary

    Artificial intelligence methods have had a long history in nuclear medicine imaging beginning with expert systems using mostly rule-based reasoning, next shallow artificial neural networks, and then traditional machine learning algorithms. Recent deep learning algorithms include convolutional neural networks for classification, U-Net and V-Net for segmentation, encoder–decoder networks for image reconstruction, and generative adversarial networks for image generation. One of the challenges that remain for machine learning in nuclear medicine imaging is training models with sufficiently large numbers of training images on the order of thousands to hundreds of thousands of images to avoid overfitting models. Some strategies to address the small data problem include: (1) data augmentation to increase the training set, (2) employing unsupervised, semisupervised or self-supervised learning to reduce the dependence on expensive manual data labeling, and (3) using a hybrid approach of rules and machine learning to extend the generalizability of these models. The other broader challenge is instilling confidence in machine-learned predictions by adding interpretability to address the “how” and explainability to address the “why.” These are yet unsolved but critical ongoing areas of machine learning research.

    Chapter 12: Radiomics in cardiovascular imaging: principles and clinical implications

    Márton Tokodi1, Attila Kovács1, and Pál Maurovich-Horvat2     1Heart and Vascular Center, Semmelweis University, Budapest, Hungary     2Department of Radiology, Medical Imaging Center, Semmelweis University, Budapest, Hungary

    Abstract

    The rapid technological advancements in noninvasive imaging, coupled with the increasing availability of large datasets and the expansion of computational power, have reformed every aspect of cardiovascular (CV) medicine. As a result, imaging has become an essential part of both clinical practice and research. Day by day, thousands of images are acquired in CV imaging laboratories and are interpreted using a wide range of qualitative and quantitative descriptors. However, radiologic images contain much more information than we can comprehend visually or quantify with simple manual measurements. Radiomics—the process of high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from imaging data—holds the key to unleash the untapped potential of information withheld in imaging datasets and to support personalized diagnostic and therapeutic decisions. In this chapter, we review the principles of radiomics, along with its potential role in CV imaging.

    Keywords

    Cardiovascular imaging; Machine learning; Precision medicine; Radiology; Radiomics; Texture analysis

    Introduction

    Over the past decades, the medical community has witnessed an unprecedented expansion in the arsenal of noninvasive imaging technologies (
    Massive amounts of medical images are acquired along the diagnostic and therapeutic pathway that a CV patient follows. The conventional interpretation of these images is reliant on the compound of basic, guideline-defined geometric quantifiers and qualitative, often subjective, descriptors. Although this approach is sufficient for clinical judgment in most cases, it has substantial shortcomings, and there is much space to improve. Images encompass an abundance of meaningful information that is challenging to quantify, interpret, and link with diagnosis or prognosis using solely conventional metrics. Moreover, visually assessed qualitative characteristics rely on a priori knowledge, have limited capabilities to discern subtle differences, and are hard to reproduce. Therefore, medical professionals are in the pursuit of novel technologies that can augment the interpretation of images allowing more personalized patient management.
    Advanced data extraction and analytic tools might offer a panacea for the limitations above. One of these emerging technologies is radiomics, which can be defined as the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features enabling the conversion of images into structured, mineable datasets. These high-dimensional databases can be supplied to machine learning (ML) algorithms that are capable of simultaneously interpreting myriads of variables to generate and test hypotheses, and ultimately to support clinical decisions. Radiomic features can describe the texture and spatial complexity in detail through the uncovering of patterns that are invisible to the naked eye. Thus, it provides a nearly limitless supply of imaging biomarkers with potential incremental value over conventional descriptors.
    The utility of radiomics-based predictive models was first demonstrated in the field of oncology, where notable success was achieved in tumor classification, prediction of treatment response, and prognostication in multiple cohorts (
    In this chapter, we provide an overview of basic radiomics concepts and workflow, along with its potential role in CV imaging. Besides its strength, we will also review some of the pitfalls that should be avoided while utilizing this state-of-the-art analytic approach.

    Concept of radiomics

    Radiomics is a precision phenotyping toolbox designed to break down radiological images into a multitude of features (

    Process of radiomics

    The practice of radiomics comprises discrete steps (Fig. 12.1): (1) image acquisition, (2) identification of the region of interest (ROI) and segmentation, (3) extraction of descriptive features from segmented ROI, (4) generation of searchable databases, and (5) mining these databases to develop ML-based models.

    Image acquisition

    Images suitable for radiomics analysis can be assessed using different imaging modalities such as cardiac ultrasound, CT, MRI, or nuclear medicine imaging techniques. It should be highlighted that radiomics can be applied on standard, routinely acquired clinical images without requiring dedicated acquisition protocols or additional imaging. Accordingly, radiomics has a real potential for being integrated into the routine clinical workflow as an adjunct to conventional measures.
    Nevertheless, the standardization of imaging protocols across different centers is still lacking. This usually does not hamper the identification and measurement of conventional features used in current clinical practice. However, when images are analyzed in-depth in order to extract pixel-based data, differences in image acquisition, reconstruction, and postprocessing parameters can introduce significant variability that is not caused by the underlying pathological conditions (

    Identification of the region of interest and segmentation

    Following the selection of the images to be analyzed, the next critical and challenging step is the identification and segmentation of image regions (i.e., ROI) containing essential prognostic information. As the radiomic features are extracted from the delineated areas or volumes, variations in contouring that alter the ROI will modify the values of the radiomic features as well. Therefore, it is indispensable to have a consistent contouring technique defined through standard operating procedures. There are various contouring methods ranging from manual to fully automated techniques (

    Extraction of radiomic features

    After the segmentation of the ROI, radiomic features can be extracted through dedicated pipelines developed by individual manufacturers or using open-source packages. Radiomic features can be categorized into four major groups (Fig. 12.2): (1) intensity-based metrics, (2) texture-based metrics, (3) shape-based measures, and (4) transform-based features.

    Intensity-based metrics

    Intensity-based metrics (or first-order statistics) are calculated from individual pixel values without considering any additional information that might be obtained from analyzing the spatial relationship between pixels. The pixel values can be analyzed using the tools of histogram analysis. These metrics are used to quantify different aspects of the distribution, such as central tendency, variation, shape, and diversity.
    The basic mathematical descriptors of central tendency and variation, such as mean, median, minimum, maximum, percentiles, and interquartile range are well known among medical professionals. Although these metrics are simple to calculate and interpret, they do not describe precisely the size and shape of the distribution. As several different distributions may exist with the same central tendency but different shapes, these statistics are not sufficient to characterize a given image.
    The shape of the distribution is most frequently described by variance— a measure of sample variation around the mean— and standard deviation (SD), which is the square root of variance. In normally distributed datasets, the SD quantifies the band around the mean where approximately 68% of the data points are located. Skewness and kurtosis are less frequently used by medical professionals; however, they capture other meaningful characteristics of the distribution. Skewness expresses how asymmetric the distribution is. Negative skewness indicates that the bulk of the data is located to the right of the mean, whereas positive skewness means the opposite. Kurtosis quantifies how close the data points are to the mean. Small values indicate that most values are situated within one SD of the mean, and the dataset contains only a few outliers, whereas higher values imply that a large proportion of data points can be found beyond one SD. In normally distributed datasets, the kurtosis is equal to 3. It is common to compare the kurtosis of a distribution to this value to assess how data points are dispersed around the mean.
    The statistics mentioned above provide information about the average, the variation, and the distribution of the sample but not about the diversity of pixel values. Concepts of information theory can be applied to quantify heterogeneity. Energy measures the overall magnitude of the values, and it is calculated by squaring and then summing them. Uniformity quantifies the similarity of the values, and it is computed by squaring the relative frequency of the given values and then summing them. Entropy measures the information content of the dataset (

    Texture-based metrics

    The preceding parameters neglect all spatial information and use the absolute values of individual pixels solely. In order to consider spatial relationships, more sophisticated mathematical approaches are required. As a promising solution, the field of texture analysis was born in the 1970s, and it has been continuously evolving ever since (
    Second-order statistics
    In 1973, Haralick et al. proposed the idea of gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) for the classification of materials and terrains based on their texture (
    Prior to matrix generation, pixels values are required to be discretized into a given number of bins, as pixels with exactly the same values occur very scarcely. The matrix will have the same number of rows as columns, which equals the number of bins. Next, a direction and a distance are needed to be defined to analyze the texture. The direction is usually described with an angle (Fig. 12.4). Statistics are calculated in four directions only (0, 45, 90, 135 degrees), as the remaining directions are the exact counterparts of the above. As the next step, the transposed matrix is added to the original raw GLCM to receive a symmetrical matrix. Because relative frequencies are more informative than absolute numbers, the matrix should be normalized by dividing each of its elements by the sum of all values in the GLCM. Due to the fact that texture is an intrinsic property of an image, the same results should be obtained even if the image is rotated. Therefore, to achieve rotationally invariant results, statistics are calculated on the four GLCMs and then averaged.
    Higher-order statistics
    Whereas second-order statistics examine the relationship between pairs of pixels, higher-order metrics attempt to describe the link between three or more pixels. Hereunder, we review some of the most widely used concepts (Fig. 12.3).
    Gray-level run-length matrix (GLRLM) quantifies how many consecutive pixels have the same value along a predefined direction (
    Gray-level gap-length matrix (GLGLM) measures the distribution of gap lengths for each gray level in an image (
    Gray-level size zone matrix (GLSZM) quantifies the number of continuous pixels with the same gray level (
    A neighborhood gray-tone difference matrix (NGTDM) is generated by the summation of differences between the gray level of each pixel and its neighborhood within a predefined distance (
    Gray-level dependence matrix (GLDM) determines the number of connected pixels within a given distance that are dependent on the center pixel (

    Shape-based metrics

    Beyond its texture, the spatial distribution, localization, and size of a given abnormality carry additional information with potential diagnostic and prognostic value. Some of these metrics are simple and routinely assessed in clinical practice, whereas others are less known and more challenging to understand.
    One-, two-, and three-dimensional metrics
    One-dimensional (1D) metrics are based on measuring the distance between two points. These parameters are commonly used in daily clinical practice to describe the size of an abnormality. Diameters measured in different directions can be used to derive new statistics that can characterize additional properties (e.g., the ratio of the longest and the shortest diameters describes the roundness or ellipticity of a lesion).
    Two-dimensional (2D) metrics are calculated based on cross-sectional planes and are used to compute different parameters that are based on areas. These parameters are often used to approximate the three-dimensional (3D) properties of the abnormality (e.g., the 1D diameter and the 2D area are all considered approximations of the 3D volume).
    Three-dimensional metrics aim to quantify different aspects of a volumetric shape. The geometrical properties of 3D objects have been thoroughly examined in the field of rigid-body mechanics. All objects have so-called principal axes or eigenvectors. These mutually perpendicular axes intersect at the center of mass. The force applied to the principal axes acts independently, meaning that if we push or rotate the object along or around any of these axes, the object will not move or rotate in any other direction. These eigenvectors also have eigenvalues that can be interpreted as weights proportional to the amount of mass located along that given principal axis. The eigenvectors can be used to quantify different shape-based metrics— for example, roundness, which is the difference between the largest eigenvalues of the smallest enclosing and the largest enclosed ellipse.
    Fractal dimension
    Fractal dimension measures the spatial complexity of an object and quantifies self-symmetry by analyzing repeating patterns at different scales (
    The most simplistic concept of quantifying fractal dimension is the box-counting method. In this analysis, the boxes of a grid occupied by the object are counted repeatedly at different scales. Then, the number of occupied boxes is plotted against the reciprocal of the scale on a log-log plot, and the box-counting dimension will be equal to the slope of the line connecting the data points (

    Transform-based metrics

    Medical images comprise an immense number of pixel values distributed in the spatial domain. These images can be transformed into the frequency domain without losing any data as spatial- and frequency-domain representations of an image carry identical information. However, each emphasizes different aspects of an image; therefore, each enables different analytic options. In the frequency domain, the pattern and rate at which the pixel values change along spatial directions are used to represent the image instead of assigning gray-level values to spatial coordinates.
    Fourier and Gabor transforms
    Fourier transform decomposes the spatial-domain dataset into a fundamental sine wave and its harmonics along the two dimensions of an image. By converting the image into the frequency domain using this transform, spatial information is discarded. The Gabor transform, named after the Hungarian-born physicist Dénes Gábor, is a special case of the short-time Fourier transform, which enables the simultaneous evaluation of spatial and frequency information (
    Wavelet transforms
    Similar to the Fourier transform, wavelet transform also converts the image into the frequency domain, but spatial information is preserved (

    Database building

    The power of predictive models heavily depends on having well-curated, sufficiently large datasets. Radiomics-based modeling can be performed with a few hundred patients as well; however, more extensive datasets would significantly enhance the predictive power and generalizability. Moreover, holistic models incorporating additional, nonradiomic features (e.g., clinical and genomic covariates) tend to be more robust; therefore, researchers should endeavor to capture several other domains of variables as well.

    Modeling

    A detailed description of modeling goes beyond the focus of this chapter; however, a few aspects should be briefly discussed. The process of radiomic feature extraction will yield a virtually unlimited number of parameters, which often exceeds the sample size of the cohort used for modeling. Utilizing all features would inevitably result in overfitting; therefore, one needs to identify an optimal subset of input variables. Feature selection should be performed in a data-driven fashion and should be reported in a transparent manner. Various techniques (filtering, wrapper, and embedded methods) exist to pinpoint features that are robust, informative, and nonredundant (
    Once the final set of input features is identified, one can proceed with building a specific predictive model. Different ML algorithms are associated with distinct inherent strengths and limitations; therefore, the choice of modeling definitely affects prediction performance (
    Emphasis should also be placed on the thorough validation of models as nonvalidated predictive systems are of limited value (
    Noting the high inconsistency in reporting of multivariate prediction tasks in medicine, researchers are advised to follow the recommendations set forth by the TRIPOD statement and the Radiomics Quality score (

    Clinical implications

    The feasibility and potential utility of radiomics have been illustrated in various clinical scenarios. Significant success has been achieved in myocardial tissue characterization, coronary artery calcium quantification, coronary plaque phenotyping, and risk stratification of CV patients (

    Characterization of myocardial texture

    A considerable number of proof-of-concept studies have demonstrated the capabilities of texture analysis to aid clinicians in various diagnostic dilemmas related to patients with suspected hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). In a small cohort,
    In support of the presumptions above, radiomics seems to be capable of capturing subclinical changes in noncontrast cine cardiac MR images of hypertensive patients well beyond the efficiency of conventional image interpretation techniques (
    The precise assessment of MI as well as myocardial viability are two other strengths of cardiac MR, and they account for a substantial proportion of referrals. Although late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) cardiac MR is a well-established and accurate method for the detection of ischemic myocardial scar (
    With its unique capability for tissue characterization, cardiac MRI has become the primary tool for the noninvasive assessment of myocardial inflammation in patients with suspected myocarditis (
    Despite being the most appropriate choice for myocardial tissue characterization, the availability of cardiac MR might be limited, and more accessible screening tools are warranted. Accordingly,
    Other investigators have attempted to detect infarcted myocardium from radiomics-based analysis of 2D echocardiograms as various radiomics descriptors such as first-order statistics (
    If we are looking for alternatives to LGE MR for the detection of myocardial scar, late iodine enhancement CT scans might be an ideal choice as iodine contrast agents have similar wash-in and wash-out kinetics as gadolinium (
    The detection of myocardial scars is fundamental to therapeutic decision-making, risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring; however, the assessment of diffuse remodeling of the extracellular matrix is equally important. Multiple diagnostic strategies have been tested for the noninvasive assessment of diffuse extracellular matrix remodeling as an expanding body of evidence indicates that diffuse myocardial fibrosis is a causative factor of myocardial dysfunction and ventricular arrhythmias (

    Automated coronary artery calcium scoring

    Coronary artery calcifications can be visualized and quantified with CT. The extent of coronary calcification is routinely expressed using the Agatston score, which has been shown to be an independent and robust predictor of adverse CV events (

    Coronary plaque phenotyping

    Although the detection of coronary plaques relies on conventional coronary CT angiography-derived metrics, the comprehensive assessment of the plaque microenvironment, histology, and biology requires a more profound radiomic analysis. The radiomics-based phenotyping of a given plaque can identify high-risk plaque features—the radiological manifestations of complex pathological processes—as alterations in its attenuation histogram and texture.
    Out of the four main CT signatures of high-risk coronary atherosclerotic plaques, the napkin-ring sign (NRS)—a plaque cross-section with a central area of low CT attenuation apparently in contact with the lumen, surrounded by ring-shaped higher attenuation plaque tissue (
    Visually detectable adverse plaque characteristics based on coronary CT angiography show only a modest correlation with intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), optical coherence tomography (OCT), or sodium-fluoride positron emission tomography (NaF18-PET)-derived features (
    Advanced atherosclerotic lesions (early and late fibroatheroma or thin-cap atheroma) are associated with a higher risk of MI (

    Radiomic phenotyping of perivascular fat

    There is an expanding body of evidence that perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) plays a pivotal role in the regulation of vascular function in both homeostasis and disease (

    Valvular heart disease

    The assessment of mechanical prosthetic valve obstruction is challenging as the clinical and radiological signs are much alike, while the etiologies and the subsequent management are different. As part of a multimodality approach, cardiac CT has been suggested to facilitate the differentiation between thrombus, pannus, and vegetation (
    Another interesting approach is the automated assessment of mitral regurgitation severity using radiomics-based ML classifiers. In a study, an SVM model utilizing texture features extracted from a rectangular ROI covering the regurgitant area of echocardiographic images exhibited an accuracy of over 95% in apical two-chamber, apical four-chamber, and parasternal long-axis views as well (

    Intracardiac mass

    Echocardiography is the primary modality of choice for the differential diagnosis of intracardiac masses (
    In patients with atrial fibrillation, transesophageal echocardiography is the gold standard imaging modality for the diagnosis and exclusion of left atrial (LA) and left atrial appendage (LAA) thrombi (

    Risk stratification

    The accurate identification of high-risk patients who might benefit from more intensive therapeutic strategies represents a crucial mission in CV medicine. Radiomics can be helpful in such a scenario, as the extracted quantitative features can be supplied to ML-based predictive models to determine the risk of life-threatening cardiac events, hence providing a window of opportunity for treatment and prevention.
    Coronary artery calcium scoring only represents a small fraction of all information embedded in noncontrast cardiac CT scans. Therefore, a screening method that could integrate the assessment of coronary calcium and other phenotypic elements such as left ventricular hypertrophy would be highly desirable in preventive CV imaging. A study involving almost two thousand participants of the Dallas Heart Study has demonstrated that an automated pipeline using radiomic features extracted from noncontrast cardiac CT scans can achieve an AUC above 0.70 for detecting high-risk left ventricular hypertrophy (
    Although numerous studies have attempted to explore the potentials of radiomics in plaque detection and phenotyping, there is only limited evidence of the prognostic value of coronary CT-derived quantitative intensity-based parameters. Nevertheless, it seems that the addition of quantitative plaque characteristics to clinical risk profile (as assessed by the Framingham risk score) and qualitative expert opinion increases the accuracy of predicting acute coronary syndrome (AUC: 0.64 vs. 0.79, P < .05) (
    Both post-MI and HCM patients are susceptible to ventricular tachyarrhythmias that represent a well-established risk factor of sudden cardiac death. This unfavorable outcome can be prevented by the implantation of implantable cardioverter defibrillators (
    It is a well-known fact that both the presence and the greater extent of LGE are associated with worse prognosis in HCM (

    The future direction of radiomic research

    Radiomics is an appealing novel technology with the potential to expand medical knowledge and reform the field of CV imaging. It has achieved promising results in various clinical scenarios; nonetheless, there is still a long way to go before it transitions to routine clinical practice.
    An inevitable step toward this aim would be the standardization of image acquisition, reconstruction, and postprocessing protocols, as it can be hard to determine whether differences in radiomic features reflect biological alterations or variations in the technical details of the imaging process (
    It should also be highlighted that most of the published results were derived from proof-of-concept studies with relatively small sample size. Accordingly, for the verification of the proposed radiomics-based models and computer-aided diagnostic systems, multicenter and multivendor studies in larger cohorts are warranted. In addition, future investigations should also evaluate the clinical impact of radiomics analysis, as it is still unknown how much the utilization of such models improves patient care and outcomes.
    After proving the generalizability of the models, it should be ensured that radiomics-based decision support tools can be used conveniently without increasing clinical workload. In the CV imaging laboratory of the future, radiomics-based ML models will be directly linked to picture archiving and communication systems, and electronic medical records. Consequently, the extracted radiomic features can be easily compared with the results of previous visits and can be merged with information from different domains of clinical data to enable individualized decision-making.

    Conclusions

    Radiomics represents an emerging image analysis technology with the potential to enhance the accuracy and precision of CV imaging. By unveiling imperceptible patterns in medical images, radiomics is capable of providing a detailed description of disease burden and linking distinct phenotypes to outcomes. In addition, radiomics offers a unique insight into tissue-level pathophysiology, which might facilitate the understanding of disease mechanisms. The utilization of radiomic features also holds the promise to objectify image interpretation, to tailor diagnostic and therapeutic strategies in a more individualized manner, and ultimately, to bring us one step closer to personalized patient management. If current efforts are able to resolve the existing technical challenges, radiomics will become a valuable tool in the clinical arena and will leave a permanent footprint in CV imaging.
