    Chapter 13: Automated interpretation of electrocardiographic tracings

    Mohammad Kachuee, and Majid Sarrafzadeh     Computer Science Department, University of California, Los Angeles, CA, United States

    Abstract

    Electrocardiography (ECG) is frequently used to detect a wide variety of cardiac conditions. Historically, clinicians are trained to analyze ECG recordings and to make a diagnosis based on signal morphologies. However, due to the considerable monetary and nonmonetary costs associated with reliance on human experts as well as issues related to availability and continuous monitoring, there has been great attention toward the automated interpretation of ECG recordings. In this chapter, we present a brief background on ECG signals; then, we explain traditional and modern approaches to the automated analysis of ECG recordings, including methods based on feature engineering and automated end-to-end learning methods. Then, we conclude by discussing the evaluation of these systems and outlining research directions for future studies.

    Keywords

    Classification; Deep learning; Electrocardiography; Machine learning; Pattern recognition; Signal processing; Timeseries; Vital signals
    1. Electrocardiography 
    2. Traditional approach to automated ECG analysis 
    3. End-to-end automated ECG analysis 
    4. Evaluation of ECG classifiers 
    5. Research directions 
    6. Conclusions 
    7. References 

    Electrocardiography

    Electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG) is a recording of the electrical activity of the heart measured using electrodes placed on the skin. Since its invention in the early 1900s, ECG has been widely used as a tool to diagnose various heart conditions, such as arrhythmias, ischemic heart disease, structural abnormalities, heart failure, and pacemaker dysfunction. A typical clinical ECG machine records from 12 leads based on 10 electrode contacts. Each lead provides a unique viewpoint to the electrical stimulation patterns across the heart (
    Fig. 13.1 shows a typical ECG waveform with important key-points and cardiac cycles annotated. The P wave represents atrial depolarization where both atria contract simultaneously. The QRS complex marks the beginning of ventricular depolarization, initiating ventricular contraction. The pause after the QRS complex, the ST segment, marks repolarization of the ventricles. Lastly, the T wave corresponds to the end of ventricular repolarization and the end of ventricular contraction (systole).
    ECG recordings can be used to measure major electrophysiologic characteristics such as rate, rhythm, and axis. The heart rate is a measure of the time it takes for the heart to complete one cycle. The normal resting heart rate is within the range of 60–100 beats per minute. An irregular waveform pattern on the ECG signal can be indicative of different arrhythmias or pacemaker dysfunction. Usually, multiple leads are used to find the electrical axis of the heart. Any physical displacement or structural abnormality of the heart also results in the deviation of the electrical axis. Furthermore, the ECG can be used as a tool to diagnose important heart conditions such as hypertrophy in which myocardial tissue gets enlarged/thickened, causing disruption in ventricular systolic and diastolic function. Myocardial infarction is another important condition in which a part of myocardial tissue becomes ischemic and is replaced by akinetic scar tissue as a result of diminished blood flow, usually as a consequence of coronary artery disease. Further detail regarding ECG recordings and corresponding clinical cardiac conditions are outside the scope of this chapter, and are available in specialized textbooks (
    ECG signals are susceptible to different types of noise and artifacts from various physiological, instrumental, and environmental sources. Baseline wander, powerline interference, muscular activity, and electrode motion are considered as major noise and artifacts impacting real-world ECG recordings. Usually, a preprocessing stage is included in an automated analysis system to enhance the quality of signals before any analysis is performed. For this purpose, different filtering and denoising approaches have been suggested in the literature, spanning from very simple moving average or median filters to complex deep learning models trained to recover the clean signal from noisy inputs (
    • 1. Baseline wander is considered as very low-frequency artifact caused by breathing or slow body movements. A very simple high-pass filter can be used to filter signal components of less than 0.5 Hz. While it is straightforward to remove baseline wander, it is a very important step due to the often-large drifts it may cause to the signal baseline.
    • 2. Powerline interference on ECG circuitry is another source of noise causing 50 or 60 Hz (and their harmonics) sinusoidal interference. Notch filters are usually designed to remove frequencies related to the powerline and its harmonics, and can be used to reduce the impact on signal quality. However, care must be taken as important signal components exist within the same frequency range, and excessive filtering may cause signal distortion especially to low-frequency waves such as P and T waves.
    • 3. Muscular activity originating from the myocardium can cause significant interference with recorded electrical activity on the ECG tracing. From the frequency domain, it is very difficult to distinguish and remove this type of interference. One possible solution is to consider the periodic nature of ECG signals and to use longer signal windows since other muscular activities are not periodic.
    • 4. Electrode motion artifacts are caused by skin impedance changes during physical activity. This artifact has frequency components within the range of 1–10 Hz strongly impacting major ECG signal components. Similar to muscular activity interferences, removing electrode motion artifacts requires more sophisticated filtering and analysis such as adaptive filters, estimating motion signals, wave averaging, and so forth.

    Traditional approach to automated ECG analysis

    Moving average (mean filtering) is frequently used to smooth ECG signals by removing high-frequency oscillations. Median filtering is often useful for removal of noisy samples captured by analog to digital converter (ADC) circuitry. While moving average and median filters are easy to implement and effective in practice, it should be noted that using these filters, especially in large window sizes, may result in oversmoothing or adverse nonlinear impacts for the case of median filters.
    Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters can be used to design different band-pass or band-rejection filters. However, designing a powerful FIR filter requires using large window lengths that may cause considerable latency and require extra memory to store a large signal segment during the process. Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filters are usually much more compact and require very small filter windows; however, the phase response for IIR filters does not have a proper phase response as in FIR filters and may cause distortions to the original signals being processed. One solution to using the compactness of IIR filters without any adverse impact on the phase response is to use IIR filters in a bidirectional forward-backward fashion. A forward-backward filter simply applies an IIR filter on the signal window twice by inverting the signal window across the time axis after the first filtering and inverting again after the second filtering. One possible drawback of this approach is that bidirectional filters are not causal, which in practice is handled by using signal buffers causing a certain amount of latency.
    Time-Frequency domain methods such as discrete wavelet decomposition (DCT) can be used to extract different time and frequency components and to apply different filtering or denoising functions. Additionally, DCT can be used as an effective compression method as the decomposition of natural signals usually tends to be sparse having many zero components and a few large nonzero components. For a more detailed discussion of these methods, we refer interested readers to
    Recently, deep learning methods have been suggested as powerful tools for ECG denoising, imputation, and generation. Denoising autoencoders implemented as either a convolutional encoder-decoder pair or as sequence-to-sequence architectures are natural choices to make denoising models. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are suggested to generate synthesized data, applied to ECG inputs; one can use GANs for data augmentation or as a representation learning objective. Another use case would be to impute missing values which are in this case missing or noisy ECG samples based on partially observed data points (
    Fig. 13.2 shows the general pipeline used in traditional automated ECG analysis systems consisting of delineation, feature extraction, and predictive analysis. In the delineation step, ECG key-points are detected for a signal window at hand, usually P, Q, R, S, and T waves for typical ECG signals. Note that based on certain clinical conditions it may not be always possible to detect all the typical key-points for all leads, or the morphology of waves can be drastically different from normal healthy signals.
    Afterward, based on the detected key-points, different features that are considered relevant to the final prediction task are extracted from the input window. It may include physiologically well-known features such as ST-segment length, the relative amplitude of key-points or any other expert-defined features such as frequency domain features, power spectrum, specific compression coefficient, and so forth (
    As the final processing step, extracted feature vectors are fed to a predictor model. In the literature, various model families have been used to learn the target feature relationship including logistic, support vector machine, decision tree, and random forest classifiers. As introducing different machine learning models is not the focus of this chapter, we refer interested readers to recently published review work (

    End-to-end automated ECG analysis

    As discussed in the previous section, traditional automated ECG processing techniques require finding important signal key-points within a certain processing window. However, due to different signal morphologies, it is not always straightforward to detect these key-points. For instance, based on specific clinical conditions, certain points may not appear in ECG signals or may appear in different forms as they usually appear in a normal population. As an example, a heart axis inversion may cause R waves to appear as minima in certain ECG channels, or an elevated ST segment may impose waveform changes that are far from normal morphologies (
    From another perspective, recent advances in pattern recognition suggest that even a completely accurate delineation followed by hand-engineered feature extraction would lead to nonoptimal solutions (
    Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are among the main drivers of advances in the field of deep learning. In the image recognition domain, where CNNs are becoming ubiquitous, CNNs exploit intrinsic properties of natural images such as scale, location, and rotation invariance of objects appearing in images (
    For the case of 1-D convolution, we can formulate each convolution layer as:
    where and denote the input signal and the convolution kernel (i.e., filter weights), respectively. The output, , is the result of applying the kernel on the output signal. Usually, for a given signal frame, multiple kernels are applied at a certain convolution layer, each creating a different feature map providing different higher-level feature representations. The convolutional layer outputs also can be interpreted as the results of different pattern detectors applied to a certain input.
    A typical CNN architecture consists of several convolution layers, each followed by nonlinearity, normalization, and pooling functions, as well as one or two classification layers. For instance, batch normalization (
    Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are models that read an input sequence one at a time while holding a state representation which is a function of inputs observed by the model from the initial state to the current input. RNNs can be implemented based on different input/output sequence timing. For instance, an RNN may take in all the input sequence and generate another output sequence one step at a time, or alternatively, it may generate outputs at each time-step while reading each input.
    From the functional perspective, in general, each RNN hidden state is a function of the previous hidden state and the current input (Markov assumption). Similarly, each output is a function of the current hidden state and the current input:
    where is the hidden state at time-step , and is a set of parameters defining the state transition and output generation functions.
    The main drawback of RNNs stems from the limitations of gradient-based learning which effectively prevents RNNs from capturing representations from more than a dozen steps due to severe vanishing gradient issues. Note that to train an RNN, the computation graph of the recursive operations is unrolled, so the resulting networks are at least as deep as the number of time-steps. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) have been proposed in order to circumvent the issue by using gating mechanisms to help holding the internal state representation (
    Architectures discussed earlier require a fix-sized input; however, ECG signals are usually recorded in varying lengths. Also, due to modeling and computational reasons applying learning models on very long signal sequences would be impractical. More specifically, it would cause massive memory usage and model complexity in CNNs or severe vanishing gradient in RNNs. In the literature, ECG records are commonly split into smaller fixed-size windows or segments. The size of processing windows usually spans from a single heartbeat to less than a minute based on the sampling rates, dataset sizes, and most importantly clinical conditions to be detected. It is well known that certain heart conditions may cause a consistent impact on ECG (e.g., myocardial infarction), while others only cause transient changes such as certain arrhythmia or pacemaker dysfunction. Also, each signal window can be aligned and preprocessed, or it can contain raw signals without any initial preparation.
    Certain models only permit a limited input length. For instance, LSTMs and GRUs are only effective in processing up to 50 time-steps and rapidly decline in performance for lengthier sequences. On the other hand, the size and distribution of the training dataset at hand determine how complex the trained prediction models can be. If only a relatively small set of data is available for the training, using a smaller window size and a more compact model would result in better final performances. Another factor to be considered is the sampling frequency. ECG signals are usually sampled at rates as low as 100 Hz to as high as 4 KHz. It is often very helpful to resample the raw signal to a reasonable sampling rate that provides the necessary signal features while minimizing the number of samples in each window. Lastly, the window size directly impacts the amount of memory and compute required to make predictions, as well as the classification latencies. To summarize, the following factors should be considered in selecting the proper window size:
    1. • Model architecture
    2. • Dataset size
    3. • Sampling frequency
    4. • Cardiac conditions to be detected
    5. • Computational, memory, and latency limitations
    It is worth noting that CNN and RNN models are often combined such that an initial CNN network summarizes the usually lengthy input sequence to a set of more compact features while an RNN takes in these compact features as input to make the final predictions. This architecture can be particularly useful for detecting certain conditions that require considering a large signal window that simple CNNs or RNNs would usually fail at. Such a network is trained in end-to-end error signal backpropagating from the classification layers to unfolded RNN layers as well as CNN layers.

    Evaluation of ECG classifiers

    Evaluation of ECG analysis systems can be very challenging due to different factors such as limited quantity and quality of expert annotations, huge class imbalance, and coexisting health conditions to name a few. Another important aspect that is mostly unanswered in the current literature is considering the importance and severity of medical conditions in the evaluation of diagnostic systems. For instance, a system that is detecting several different diseases should be evaluated and compared based on the importance of weighted average of these disease types rather than simply using the average performance across all conditions (
    In terms of the number of True Positive (TP), True Negative (TN), False Positive (FP), and False Negative (FN) predictions, typical evaluation measures including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score are defined as:
    Intuitively speaking, Accuracy measures the ratio of correct predictions to the total number of predictions. Precision measures the ratio of positive predicted cases which are detected correctly to the number of all predicted positive cases, showing what percentage of samples predicted as positive are actually positive samples. Recall is the ratio of correctly detected cases to the number of actual positive cases, basically measuring how reliable a system is in detecting a less frequent positive condition. F1 score is reporting a harmonic mean of precision and recall values, which is quite helpful in comparing different systems using a single value rather than considering different measures at the same time (
    Apart from these numeric measures, other more illustrative evaluation tools are often adopted in the literature. Confusion matrix is one of the most well-known evaluation measures that are frequently used in multiclass classification problems. In a confusion matrix, each row represents the number of actual samples in each class and each column represents the number of predicted samples for each class. Ideally, a perfect classifier would have zero elements for nondiagonal positions that are representing incorrectly classified samples. Furthermore, off-diagonal values can be used to investigate how different classes are being classified incorrectly with respect to other classes, i.e., confused or mixed-up with each other. Please refer to (
    Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve demonstrates the rate of true positives (TPR) versus the rate of false positives (FPR) to visually evaluate the operation of a binary classifier at different decision threshold settings. Here:
    Intuitively, the ROC curve shows the trade-off between the ability to detect positive samples versus the rate of samples detected as positive by error. Often area under the ROC (AU-ROC) curve is used to measure how close a certain model is to the ideal case, where high recall (or, TPR) is achieved without inducing any false positives, in which the AU-ROC approaches to one (Fig. 13.6).
    Alternatively, the precision versus recall curve has been used to illustrate the precision-recall trade-off and the area under this curve is used as a quantitative performance measure to compare classifiers. There is evidence suggesting that the precision-recall curve is more informative in binary classification tasks with a considerable class imbalance (

    Research directions

    In the previous sections, we presented different approaches for automated analysis of ECG recordings. Many of these approaches rely on machine learning models that require training based on a dataset. Practically, the training dataset determines the complexity of models to be trained which translates to the complexity of patterns to be detected and the final performance of the model. A common approach that is widely used in the deep learning literature is to augment a dataset with altered samples from the original dataset to effectively produce a larger training set. For instance, imaging data can be augmented by horizontal flipping, randomly cropping different parts of an image, changing pixel colors, etc. However, data augmentation for ECG signals is more challenging and most of the studies either use no data augmentation or use very basic augmentation such as adding a small Gaussian noise. A more comprehensive study on data augmentation for ECG signals can potentially unlock the use of more powerful and more complex architectures compared to the models being used today.
    While the number of annotated recordings is usually very limited due to limited access and the costs associated with human experts, there are ample unlabeled recordings available. For instance, Physionet MIMIC III (
    Another avenue of research is using attention-based models for ECG analysis. Attention models are currently considered state-of-the-art for tasks that require detecting patterns within long intervals. Also, the attention mechanism can be used to reduce the computational load of processing signals. For example,
    Interpretability is considered one of the main challenges for any automated learning-based health analytic system. There are many legal and ethical concerns associated with block-box models that only provide statistically appealing performances but do not provide any reasoning based on each analyzed instance. There have been many recent endeavors to address this by either using models that provide insights about their operations or modeling dynamics of a black-box model. However, the case of timeseries input domain is more challenging than usual tabular data as explanations for a signal window should present visually appealing and yet accurate interpretations. This requires extensive research in the interpretation of timeseries models. A recent work by

    Conclusions

    In this chapter, we presented an overview of the methods used for the automated interpretation of ECG records. We covered basic concepts about the ECG signal as well as different established signal processing, feature extraction, and recognition approaches. In the end, this chapter presents a few directions for future research that the authors believe to be promising avenues of extending the current literature.

    Chapter 14: Machine learning in cardiovascular genomics, proteomics, and drug discovery

    Ming Wai Yeung1, Jan-Walter Benjamins1, Pim van der Harst1,2,3, and Luis Eduardo Juarez-Orozco1,3     1University of Groningen, University Medical Center Groningen, Department of Cardiology, Groningen, The Netherlands     2University of Groningen, University Medical Centre Groningen, Department of Genetics, Groningen, The Netherlands     3Department of Cardiology, Division Heart and Lungs, University Medical Centre Utrecht, University of Utrecht, Utrecht, The Netherlands

    Abstract

    This chapter discusses the current status and challenges in applying machine learning in three closely connected fields, namely genomics, proteomics, and drug discovery. Usage of machine learning methods are described and compared in the context of respective fields through selected literature. The current performance of implemented machine learning methods is described in comparison to traditional statistical methods. Finally, this chapter discusses potential future perspectives for implementation of machine learning in genomics, proteomics, and drug discovery.

    Keywords

    Cardiology; Cardiovascular disease; Drug discovery; Genomics; Machine learning; Proteomics
    1. Acknowledgements 
    2. Introduction 
    3. Machine learning in genomics 
      1. Molecular genetics 
      2. Population and complex genetics 
    4. Machine learning in proteomics 
    5. Machine learning in drug discovery 
    6. Summary 
    7. References 

    Introduction

    Modern cardiovascular medicine and research have seen the development of novel state-of-the-art techniques and analytics. This convergence is currently helping unravel the mechanistic determinants, pathways, and potential therapeutic targets in cardiovascular diseases.
    On the one hand, three decades of refinements (including the completion of the Human Genome Project) in the study of genomics and its downstream influence into the study of proteomics have provided notions of the deterministic but also dynamic nature of this continuum (see Fig. 14.1) in cardiac health and disease. On the other hand, the recent advent of modern machine learning (ML)-based artificial intelligence has provided the opportunity to explore, integrate, and analyze large amounts of data in terms of their inherent complex interrelations and nonlinear dependencies.
    In essence, the very-high-throughput nature of -omics data at different analytical and mechanistic levels represents a suitable target for ML and is expected to boost our capacity to generate valuable insights in the study of cardiovascular disease. This chapter summarizes and interprets the current evidence on the application of ML in the genomic-proteomics horizon and in modern drug discovery initiatives.

    Machine learning in genomics

    ML involves use of computational algorithms for a specific task, which is usually achieved through extracting characteristics/patterns from data. One key feature of ML is that the performance of the learner or model (also called classifier when the objective is data classification, i.e., a binary output) is expected to improve with exposure to more data (experience). Thanks to the increased availability of genomic data in recent years, various ML algorithms are being adopted to help identify “patterns” in the genome and to predict functional consequences of specific genetic variations.

    Molecular genetics

    ML algorithms, using supervised and unsupervised learning methods (where the output label for the output is known or unknown, respectively), have yielded fruitful results in annotation of genomes ranging from identifying various genomic elements to predicting their functional consequences (
    The choice of the algorithm should be made based on the task to be solved but also the characteristics of the data at hand. Importantly, data transformation (i.e., generation of features to represent the data) is also critical for the end-performance of the models. For example, Pertea et al. developed a decision tree-based model called GeneSplicer to classify splice sites in Arabidopsis thaliana and in the human genome (
    While elaborate feature engineering incorporating extensive domain knowledge can improve performance, it may be not always efficient/feasible due to time constraints or limited understanding of the underlying mechanistic structures of the subject at hand. In recent years, ML methods with capability to learn features from data such as Deep Learning are gaining popularity (reviewed by
    Besides functional annotation of a specific genomic region, ML can also be applied to predict the biological effect of individual genomic variations. Pathogenicity prediction is highly relevant in cardiovascular clinical research, especially in rare genetic diseases. Annotations of the variation in different contexts including evolutionary conservation and location on genomic level, regulatory information on transcription level, and functional change on translation/protein level have served as input features for training ML methods (
    Thus far, benchmarking studies have been carried out to compare the performance of different in-silico prediction tools for variants involved in different classes of diseases like cancer (
    Conversely, studies have also been carried out to build specific prediction models with the aim of achieving a better performance than generic predictors.
    Unsupervised ML may be an alternative if a reasonable labeled training set is not available. In a recent paper by

    Population and complex genetics

    The role of genetic markers in cardiovascular disease risk is an active area of research in population genetics. Multifactorial or complex diseases are those that are influenced by both genetic and environmental factors in contrast to Mendelian disorders whose cause can be attributed to single mutations with large detrimental effects. Complex diseases are often linked to multiple genetic variants, which are usually weaker in effect as compared with those discovered in Mendelian diseases. Associations between complex disease and genetic variants are discovered by genome-wide association study (GWAS) which look at the difference in allele frequency of variants between cases and controls.
    Many cardiovascular disorders such as coronary artery disease (CAD), atrial fibrillation (AF), hypertension (HTN), and stroke are complex diseases (
    In recent years there has been interest in personal disease risk profiling using genetic information (
    Since complex diseases are influenced by both genetic and environmental factors, it is sensible to combine information from all aspects such as genetic risk profile, clinical risk factors and lifestyle to maximize the predictive power of risk models (
    Finally, ML can be used in genomic analysis beyond predictive purpose. Comparisons of diverse ML methods give new biological insights, such as the genetic architecture of complex diseases. Deep learning, for instance, is a method capable of abstracting nonlinear relationships that can be deployed to model gene-gene interactions (epistasis) (

    Machine learning in proteomics

    Following the line of modern system-levels approach to cardiovascular disease, emerging molecular profiling technologies such as proteomics could provide new insights into the pathophysiology of cardiovascular disease.
    However, implementations of ML in proteomic studies have not yet witnessed an accelerated advance comparable to the exploratory initiatives described in genomics. It is possible that this discrete (although steadily increasing) development relates to the position of proteomics within the continuum of translational research and medicine (genomics—proteomics—metabolomics—clinical implementation). In this sense, either from a bottom-up or top-bottom perspective, proteomics lies further down the line as ML optimization of data-driven tasks permeates into the analytical arsenal at our disposal. Clearly however, high-throughput molecular (protein) profiling data represents fertile ground for deep profiling of such varying molecular entities in relation to cardiovascular disease.
    Proteomics deals in multifaceted and dynamic profiles with complex signaling pathways and high levels of interconnectivity. In this sense, the potential of ML to explore nonlinear dependencies between large amounts of variables and to select, integrate, and interpret complex variable structures can ultimately refine classification and predictive performance, facilitating timely applicability in the evaluation of proteomic data. Fig. 14.3 depicts the continuum of applicability of ML in proteomics research. However, it is useful to contextualize that comprehensive data evaluation in this regard can benefit from a fair combination of statistical and ML approaches.

    An emerging aspect within the horizon of ML application in proteomic analyses is that of method standardization and quality control. Previously in this chapter, it has been explained how a comprehensive ML workflow comprises organized sequential steps that guarantee the robustness of the resulting models as well as their generalizability. One of such stages is adequate feature selection, which allows the user to reduce the dimensionality of the data, focus on consequent variables, and reduce computational needs to optimize training times. Very-highly correlated input variables may represent redundancy and hamper optimal workflow and modeling unnecessarily, while very weak classifiers (variables) may increase the risk of overfitting unduly. Since this balance in the input structure tuning is crucial, efforts have begun to discuss, experiment, and converge in general recommendations that guarantee seamless flow in ML workflows dedicated to high-throughput omics data (i.e., genomics and proteomics).     Furthermore, proteomics research also contemplates the analysis of a very large number of protein sequences for experimental functional characterization (e.g., using Gene Ontology), and ML-based approaches are expected to help in this multiclass and multilabel niche.
    In summary, the implementation of ML in the field of cardiovascular proteomics research has witnessed the progression between integration of high-dimensional classifiers (mostly through SVM) and modern deep learning approaches for high-throughput identification and function-prediction proteomic data. The suggested classifiers have been based on established software that could improve the identification of patients with cardiovascular disease (including CAD, DVT, HF, and cardiomyopathies), cardiovascular risk factors (dyslipidemia), or risk of adverse cardiovascular events, including death. However, such studies have been restricted in sample size and novel interest in analytical standardization and quality control for adequate ML model training and validation is only recently reemerging. On the other hand, Deep Learning-based approaches to proteomics are being explored as tools to optimize pattern recognition and functional identification/prediction, but only marginally in cardiovascular research. Considering the advancing technologies of molecular profiling, proteomics is eventually expected to consolidate as a standard component of our approach to cardiovascular disease characterization that could be routinely generated from patient samples processed and integrated into, for example, biomarker signatures that convey clinically relevant insights through ML analytics.     Machine learning in drug discovery

    Over the past century, drug discovery has evolved in multiple phases from the coincidental discovery of disease-treating substances—extracted from plants or found otherwise in biological organisms such as fungi—through a knowledge based, but manual approach to a fully automated industry. Following the initial extraction of active substances from plants, a first step in biochemical synthesis was taken to create the active molecular structures, isolated from their native organisms of origin. In the following decennia, wide ranges of chemical compounds were screened for activity in cells, without a prior chosen biological target, such as an amino-acid or protein. After discovery of a compound, a proper target playing a role in disease was then searched. This is what is known as phenotypic drug discovery or “classical” pharmacology. More recently, drug discovery has shifted toward a target-based approach, in which the disease modifying biological targets are first identified, followed by the search for chemical compounds with the required effect on the given targets. Based on available chemical property databases a preselection of chemical compounds can be made for inclusion in multiple screening rounds in which slight molecular modifications are made to optimize target modification and to minimize effect on closely related structures.
    In de novo drug design, “in-silico” virtual prescreening is performed with computer models. Chemical properties of molecular substructures are thereby tested against the intended target, aiming for optimally targeting synthesized models. Most of these computer models are based on chemical compound descriptors, such as quantitative structure-activity relations (QSARs), giving an indication of how a synthesized molecule will alter biological targets.
    Despite tremendous developments as seen in drug discovery over the past century, including the migration to a more target focused design process, the rate of positive treatment of disease is still relatively low. For example,
    Drug discovery also entails minimizing activity of synthesized substances in nonrelated biological targets, meaning to maximally reduce side-effects. In currently prescribed drugs, side-effects are numerous, and in some cases, serious adverse events (AEs) occur. An example is given by Schmidt et al. investigating side-effects in PCSK9 inhibitors. The investigators report that lipid lowering PCSK9 inhibitors are more effective than statin in lowering short- and mid-term LDL-C levels, as well in reducing long-term risk for CVD, showing no significant effect on mortality (
    Warfarin is an anticoagulation drug, known for its increased risk for bleeding and hemorrhage (
    Additionally,
    Spironolactone is a diuretic that prevents dropping potassium-levels while facilitating excretion of water from the body.
    Overall, the one-size-fits-all nature of most commonly used drugs lays the primary basis for reduced effects in parts of the addressed patient population, and for undesired, adverse side-effects reported frequently in literature.
    Individual biological structures in humans differ due to individuals’ genetic makeups and their dependent protein profiles. This not only affects their individual risk to develop cardiovascular diseases, but also their individual drug metabolisms, thereby determining the way they respond to their treatments, and what complications or side effects they face. Therefore, a more patient-tailored and better disease targeting approach is required in the development of new cardiovascular drugs to solve issues seen in current drug therapy. As described before, software models are currently used to perform a prescreening of components with potential disease target modifying chemical properties, with none or minimal activity toward non-targeted biological structures at the same time. Expert coded rules and traditionally simplistic regression or classification QSARs are used to predict chemical properties of newly synthesized substances in relation to their activity toward a drug target.     ML and particularly deep learning techniques have the ability to “see” patterns in complex data structures, allowing humans to uncover information from complex data that would be otherwise hidden to the human eye. Thereby deep learning models may represent a powerful extension to traditional statistical models, such as linear and logistic regression models that perform well on one or a handful of independent variables, but gracefully fail to uncover dependencies in high-dimensional data.

    It should be noted that, even with more precisely targeted drugs, identification of a patient’s genetic profile in relation to the targeted disease will remain crucial in administering drugs in a personalized way. Presently, the only part of a total solution seems to be to identify patient groups that are most likely to respond to a drug, and that are most unlikely to have any AEs in any of the non-disease-related, nontargeted biological structures, based on their genetic profiles.
    Applying ML techniques may help to both improve patient selection and patient specific targeting of the disease, by development of personalized medications, improving overall patient outcomes, and preventing side-effects and adverse events induced by pharmacological treatment. Fig. 14.5 summarizes the continuum in drug developments where ML implementation offers potential benefit.
    Where the first steps have been taken to improve gene-based patient selection for certain drug treatment, and the first ML models have been used for biochemical feature learning as well as feature selection, huge improvements are to be expected, if ML models will be applied further on integral multiomics data, to gain knowledge of mechanisms underlying disease, and to improve identification of disease-related biological drug targets. Finally, combined improvement of disease-targeting medications and selection of responders should not only improve patient outcomes but also positively affect the economic burden of healthcare costs on society, by lowering unnecessary hospital admissions as well as readmissions.

    Summary

    Adaption of ML varies in the field of genomics, proteomics, and drug discovery in cardiovascular research. Drug Discovery. ML is widely used in the study of genomics in cardiovascular research for various purposes from variant annotation to disease risk prediction. It is less popular in proteomic analyses due to current limits in performance. ML has been used for QSAR analyses with a generally superior performance over simple rule-based and statistical methods, such as linear/logistic regression. While traditional ML methods namely SVM and random forest remain the most popular methods, emergence of deep learning in this field is expected with increasing data availability in the field. Efforts of developing better prediction/classification models with ML for disease status/risk have been seen in all three fields. An integral workflow/framework combining these data could be a promising approach to further enhance the predictive performance of ML models.

    Chapter 15: Wearable devices and machine learning algorithms for cardiovascular health assessment

    Abdallah Elshafeey, Omar Mhaimeed, Jamal Al Ani, and Mohamed B. Elshazly     Department of Medicine and Medical Education, Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar, Doha, Qatar

    Abstract

    The rapid improvement in wearable technology and its increasing sophistication is providing endless opportunities for progress in societal wellbeing and healthcare institution. Chapter 15 discusses the evolving field of digital medicine, specifically smart wearables, and its application to both cardiovascular health and disease. It begins by first introducing some of the currently used sensors and detailing their underlying mechanisms of action. Thereafter, it explores the concept of machine learning and how it allows for the rapid and meaningful analysis of the millions of bytes of data collected by these sensors on a daily basis. Further, we delve into some of the ways wearables are being used to monitor cardiac health and disease, including: disease prevention through lifestyle management, screening for disease, and disease management. Lastly, this chapter provides a discussion of some of the challenges facing this rapidly evolving field.

    Keywords

    Cardiovascular health; Digital medicine; Machine learning; Smart wearables; Technology
    1. Introduction 
    2. Types of data collected 
    3. Machine learning (ML) 
    4. Uses of smart wearable data 
      1. Lifestyle management in the general population 
      2. Screening for CVD 
      3. Disease management in CVD patients 
        1. Management of atrial fibrillation 
        2. Detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) 
        3. Postmyocardial infarction management and recovery 
        4. Detection of hyperkalemia in heart failure patients 
        5. Monitoring chronic heart failure prognosis using physical activity 
    5. Current challenges 
    6. Conclusion and future directions 
    7. References 

    Introduction

    Smart wearables are smart, consumer-grade devices that can be worn on the body either as an accessory or part of clothing. They include clothing, ear-wear, watches, headbands, rings, sociometric badges, and wristbands. Smart wearables incorporate high processing power, advanced software, sophisticated sensors that can track activity, Global Positioning System (GPS), and biometric data. In the rapidly proliferating technological world of our modern day, the plethora of smart wearables in the market has made it rather difficult for one to keep up with this field. However, recent advancements in technology have begun to have implications on smart wearables and their role on human health, and investing in the pursuit of the virtues of smart wearables may very well be a worthwhile endeavor.
    Medical wearables date back to around 1286, when the first wearable eyeglasses were made by Salvino D’Armate (
    In the past few years, the smart wearables industry has been centered around the wrist, particularly in the form of smart watches, which have contributed to its massive growth (
    Another major driver for the smart wearables market is healthcare. Wearables are significantly improving in their ability to capture and record real-time user activity and biometric data, and have an appeal in the healthcare sector as they allow for daily monitoring of activity and a number of clinical parameters (
    Smart wearables also allow for remote patient monitoring of biometric data by measuring an individual’s pulse throughout the day across a number of various activities. Additionally, some can monitor the blood pressure and may even record a patient’s heart rhythm through a single-lead electrocardiograph (ECG). Although this is not as accurate as the typical 12-lead ECG used in the clinical workplace, it can still provide invaluable information of a patient’s heart rhythm (
    A systematic review of 22 subjects conducted in June of 2019 by a team in Germany concluded that mobile health devices can aid in the early diagnosis and treatment of atrial fibrillation (AF), and that successful application of mobile health technologies could significantly contribute to reducing the cost of illness associated with AF (
    Smart wearables can also aid in the issue of medication adherence. In case of adults with chronic illnesses who are prescribed medications, 30%–50% of the medications are not taken as prescribed (

    Types of data collected

    Smart wearables have evolved over the years and have become capable of monitoring a multitude of organs, thereby providing real-time information about the various functions of the human body. These include devices that collect epidermal, ocular, intracochlear, dental, biochemical, and physiological parameters that can subsequently be processed and analyzed by complex algorithms and artificial intelligence (AI) software (
    There are many different types of sensors, each of which can collect unique data about the human body such as heart rate, blood pressure, activity levels and much more. Some examples of such sensors include:
    1. • Accelerometers, altimeters, and GPS systems that can determine characteristics such as acceleration, speed, pace, and altitude. This information can then be combined with age, sex, weight, and height to give an indication of activity levels at any point in time. This is done through complex machine learning algorithms that can determine parameters such as the number of calories burned, number of steps taken, distance walked, and others.
    2. • Heart rate sensors that can continuously measure heart rate at rest and during exercise. Most devices use a technology known as photoplethysmography (PPG), which consists of a light-emitting diode that emits green photons toward the skin. The light interacts with blood and gets absorbed at various degrees based on the blood flow, and the reflected light is then received by a photodiode and interpreted by the receiver. Again, machine learning algorithms that detect time from pulse peak to peak are able to determine heart rate (
    3. • ECG sensors that can provide single lead ECG recordings whenever needed, or on a regular basis. Most sensors like the one used by the Apple Watch do this through utilization of a vector between the left and right arms when the patient places a finger on the watch.
    4. • Sensors that can measure blood pressure when prompted. These include devices that utilize PPG technology. Some other watches (Omron Heart Guide) use an inflatable cuff around the wrist to measure blood pressure.
    These are only a few of the multitude of sensors currently available. Others include oxygen saturation sensors, respiratory rate sensors, and many more (Table 15.1) (

    Machine learning (ML)

    The collection of data is the first part in this process. Technology and progress have permitted the gathering of enormous amounts of data while simultaneously allowing for the safe storage. The challenge, however, lies with the effective utilization of the data and turning it into clinically meaningful parameters to consumers and patients. This is where the implementation of machine learning comes into play.
    ML is the complex interplay between computer science and mathematics, more specifically statistics (
    Supervised learning is the type of learning a computer does to which the outcome is already known and well established. They are all tasks that a trained person can do well, and the computer simply tries to replicate the same outcome reached by humans. These can range from simple to complex tasks, and mostly involve recognition and classification. Examples of these include classifying documents based on their content, or even just recognizing whether an image shows a cat or a dog (
    On the other hand, unsupervised ML is much more open-ended and has limitless possibilities. In this type of learning, there is no specific outcome being measured. The computer simply aims to manipulate the data in limitless ways, in hopes of identifying patterns or specific groupings that can later be tested using a supervised algorithm in order to determine its clinical use, if any (

    Uses of smart wearable data

    Now that we have discussed the multitude of different types of data that can be collected by smart wearables, as well as the different ways in which they can be manipulated and interpreted, we can delve into how smart wearables can be useful for cardiovascular health. The uses of wearable data can be broadly split into three different groups: lifestyle management in the general population, screening for cardiovascular disease, and disease management in patients suffering from cardiovascular diseases.

    Lifestyle management in the general population

    Several modifiable causes of cardiovascular disease (CVD) have long been identified. These include hypertension, obesity, smoking, and diabetes mellitus among many others (
    The field of smart wearables and machine learning is relatively young, and there has only been a small amount of research into it. However, there is one study that has looked at exercise data and attempted to link it to several diseases including diabetes and hypertension. This study is known as the Henry Ford Exercise Testing (FIT) project (
    One challenge that arises when considering wearable technology as a primary tool for lifestyle management in the general population is the notion that many individuals may not be motivated enough to actively keep track of their fitness level on a daily basis. Behavioral change in general is extremely difficult to instigate. The Framingham Heart Study could provide some insight on how this issue can be tackled (
    This goes to show that individuals get increasingly motivated when a competitive component is included. This notion could be further exploited to encourage members of the population to actually use smart wearables, and in doing so, increase physical activity. In fact, this is already implemented by Apple in their Apple Watches. The activity app in the Apple Watch allows users to challenge friends or family, and whoever has the most steps by the end of the week earns a virtual trophy. Users can also work their way to different trophies by meeting their daily step goals.
    Lifestyle management in the general population to prevent the incidence of CVD has been a constant challenge facing the healthcare system. However, as was demonstrated, wearable technology can play a vital role in how the healthcare community approaches such an important undertaking of disease prevention. Precision behavioral change may be difficult to accomplish; however, future endeavors must focus on identifying the most suitable, evidence-based, and personalized primordial prevention strategies to implement as early as possible in childhood, when behaviors are more pliable, and likely to last a lifetime.

    Screening for CVD

    With the prevalence of smart wearables across the general population, and the intrinsic feature of continuous data collection of those smart wearables, there is a wealth of data being acquired by these electronics that could prove instrumental at identifying certain diseases and pathologies. Continuous heart rate monitoring can allow these devices to screen their users for cardiac arrhythmias, and when asked to conduct an ECG, they can additionally screen for atrial fibrillation (AF) or long QT syndrome, for example. Asymptomatic AF presents with the same risks and complications as symptomatic AF, such as heart failure, kidney disease, stroke, coronary artery disease, and death.
    Using their smartwatches, Apple launched the prospective Apple Heart Study in 2017, which aims to investigate the concordance of recorded pulse irregularities with simultaneous ECG recordings, and to assess the time it takes for the user to contact a healthcare provider within 3 months of pulse irregularity detection. The data collected by the Apple Watch, using a combination of LED (light-emitting diode) lights and light-sensitive photodiodes, measured the changes in blood flow to generate a photoplethysmogram that is subsequently used to estimate the pulse by recording intervals between photoplethysmography signal peaks (PSP) and producing a tachogram. The photoplethysmogram waveforms are then fed to an algorithm developed by Apple, the Irregular Pulse Notification Algorithm, to identify irregular pulses possibly indicative of AF. In the case of an irregularity that meets inclusion criteria, the algorithm will prospectively and opportunistically scan for photoplethysmography irregularities when there is minimal arm movement. Upon 4 serial conformations of an irregular photoplethysmography, the participant is informed of the irregular pulse. Out of a study population of 419,093 participants, an irregular pulse was detected in 0.52% of smartwatch wearers. About 34% of those with an irregular pulse were diagnosed with AF after wearing an ECG patch for up to 7 days. The results of this study showed a positive predictive value of 84% (participants who received a notification of an irregular pulse and also had an ECG showing AF) (
    Devices that screen for hypertension, such as the Omron HeartGuide, present numerous benefits, given the high rates of hypertension among the general population. The value of such devices lies in their function of conducting serial blood pressure measurements during the course of the day, and hence developing an extensive record of a user’s blood pressure. This record can be used by a user’s primary care physician with the assistance of ML algorithms to patients at risk for developing hypertension, and possibly predict cardiovascular events in patients with an established diagnosis of hypertension.

    Disease management in CVD patients

    Beyond the multitude of opportunities that data gathered by smart wearables have in lifestyle management within the general population, the data being collected also has the potential to be utilized in the management of patients with preexisting cardiovascular diseases. Examples of such opportunities that will be discussed in this section are monitoring for cardiac arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, detection of myocardial infarctions, and guiding postinfarction care, and monitoring as well as managing heart failure.

    Management of atrial fibrillation

    AF is one of the most common cardiac arrhythmias, particularly in older patients, and is characterized by an irregular heartbeat and loss of atrial contraction, consequently resulting in blood clots, stroke, and heart failure. There are several risk factors that predispose individuals to developing AF, such as increasing age, hypertension, obesity, and other underlying cardiovascular diseases. In the United States, it is predicted that the number of individuals expected to be diagnosed with this arrhythmia will reach up to 6 million by 2050, posing a significant pecuniary burden on the healthcare system (
    There has been significant progress recently in the development of wearable cardiac rhythm recorders that can record rhythm strips using smartphone technology. After the initial success of AliveCor’s single lead Kardia Mobile device in 2017, the company introduced the Kardia Band (KB), the first FDA-cleared Apple Watch accessory that patients can use to record 30 s rhythm strips. The KB operates synchronously with an application that uses machine learning ECG-recognition algorithms to provide an instant diagnosis of AF, informing the patient of the diagnosis, and providing them with the option of sending the results to their physician (Fig. 15.2). Further, this technology has numerous applications in patients with previously established AF. A promising use to this technology in AF patients is confirming their AF status prior to a scheduled electrical cardioversion appointment, allowing them to make an informed decision on whether they should come to the hospital or not. On its own, the application’s ML algorithm is able to accurately identify cases of AF up to 93% of the time, and electrophysiologists using the KB recording were able to accurately identify in up to 99% of AF cases. Not only does this help patients determine whether or not they should go to the hospital, but it can also help the hospital save valuable time and resources if a scheduled procedure such as direct current cardioversion is no longer necessary (
    Other beneficial applications of this technology is ECG monitoring in patients postcardioversion and ablation procedures that are common in AF, as there is an estimated recurrence rate of up to 50% within the first year following these treatments (

    Detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)

    Another significant application of smart wearable technology is the detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), a possibly life-threatening cardiac event that requires urgent revascularization and is diagnosed largely using an ECG. In the United States, the occurrence of a coronary event in 2019 is expected to occur in about 1,055,000 individuals (
    Smart wearable technology, such as the Kardia Mobile, allows at-risk individuals to obtain an ECG earlier when presenting with STEMI, reducing their time for diagnosis and receiving critical intervention. The ST LEUIS pilot study used an adapted version of the Kardia Mobile device consisting of two wire leads, allowing the device to reconstruct a 12-lead ECG from serial lead measurements. The study showed excellent concordance of the reconstructed 12-lead ECGs with standard 12-lead ECGs for detecting an STEMI as well as non-ST elevation myocardial infarctions (NSTEMI), as seen in table 2 (

    Postmyocardial infarction management and recovery

    A significant factor in recovery of any cardiovascular event is education and compliance after hospital discharge. Unfortunately, most of this often occurs hastily during the discharge process, and considering the pervasiveness of technology in our lives, it seems intuitive to integrate technology in this process, and capitalize on the advantages artificial intelligence has to offer. The application Corrie Health, developed by a group at Johns Hopkins, is an example of how technology and smart wearables can be integrated into the hospital discharge process, and transform it into a patient-centered approach.
    The target age group of Corrie Health are individuals between the ages of 40 and 85 years who are recovering from a myocardial infarction in the acute setting. The application accounts for this target cohort by working with Apple to create an optimal user interface. Some of the features of the Corrie Health application include informing users of their daily tasks, such as taking their prescribed medications and measuring their heart rate, blood pressure, and weight (
    Importantly, Corrie Health integrates with smart wearable devices and uses wearable data such as daily step or stairs count to provide personalized guidance to each patient. This information can be very valuable in structuring home-based cardiac rehabilitation programs that push patients to gradually increase their submaximal exercise capacity. Biometric wearable data, particularly heart rate, may even be used to optimize beta-blocker dosing in patients with chronic coronary artery disease, and correlate this data with their angina symptoms.

    Detection of hyperkalemia in heart failure patients

    Another innovative application of smart wearables is the detection of hyperkalemia from smartphone ECGs. Hyperkalemia is prevalent in multiple pathologies, including congestive heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and as an effect of several medications used to treat these conditions. Normally, the detection of hyperkalemia requires an invasive blood test, since only relatively severe hyperkalemia causes evident changes on an ECG. At mild to moderate levels, the PR interval is prolonged, and there is the development of peaked T waves (
    In a recent 2018 study, Mayo Clinic developed an algorithm utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) that was trained to detect hyperkalemia using ECG leads I and II from a training group of 484,310 patients admitted between 1994 and 2017 with a serum potassium collected within 12 h of their ECG. After an extensive learning phase, its performance was evaluated on an initial testing group of 224,690 patients. In the initial test group, the AUC was 0.87 (sensitivity 85%, specificity 72%). A secondary performance evaluation was conducted prospectively on 10 patients undergoing hemodialysis wearing the portable AliveCor smartphone ECG device. The sensitivity was 94% and specificity 74% across 5.4 h of ECG data in the hyperkalemic state and 44.1 h in a nonhyperkalemic state (

    Monitoring chronic heart failure prognosis using physical activity

    Similarly to how cardiac rehabilitation significantly improves recovery in post-MI patients, patients with chronic heart failure are seen to have low tolerance to physical activity, preventing them from engaging in daily tasks. Moreover, decreased physical capacity in heart failure patients portends a worse prognosis, with increased rehospitalization and mortality risk (
    These functional capacity tests, however, only occur in a hospital setting by scheduled appointments, and thus cannot pick up on health deteriorations that may occur between appointments. Smart wearables can close this gap by utilizing in-built accelerometer to calculate a patient’s 6MWT score, and additionally, send the results to the patient’s providers to monitor their progress. The benefit is that many smartphones currently have accelerometers built into their devices, making it even easier to collect and use the data necessary to assess a patient’s functional capacity. Accelerometers were found to have high accuracy in detecting physical activity in heart failure patients, demonstrating their clinical applicability in performing out-of-clinic 6MWT that would allow for continuous patient monitoring and early detection of health deterioration. These results have instigated a multicenter trial to assess whether a smart wearable-based intervention improves functional capacity in patients with chronic heart failure with reduced (HFrEF) and preserved (HFpEF) ejection fractions (

    Current challenges

    As with any novel medical advancement, the principle of using smart wearables and artificial intelligence processed data to prevent, detect, and manage CVD is not without limitations. The first limitation that comes into play is the feasibility of collecting all this data for millions of people. The data for one person could exceed thousands of gigabytes, so how feasible would it be to collect and store all this data for an entire population? This would require lots of new data infrastructure that could accommodate these massive amounts of data. This is not something beyond reach but does need a lot of prospective planning before anything is implemented nationwide. This brings us to the second challenge we face which is confidentiality and privacy. With so much personal data being collected every second, patients deserve to know where that data goes and who has access to it. These are issues that companies need to be fully transparent about in order to maintain the everlasting trust between patients and the healthcare community.
    Another important challenge will be deciding which types of data will be actually useful to collect and use in algorithms to predict CVD. Not all data is actionable and some of it may be redundant and the key to improving population health is generating clinically meaningful data. For example, is 24/7 monitoring of heart rate for the entirety of life meaningful? ML algorithms work more effectively when data is preoptimized. This can only be achieved through trial and error, as is the case with any development throughout human history. A lot more focus is shifting toward this novel field and more information will come to light in the coming years regarding which types of data are most useful and which types of algorithms work best. This also ties in with the next challenge, which is the need for extensive validation studies into the findings that preliminary studies report. These studies will come with time and will allow to further refine the methodology to achieve the most efficient data collection and analysis.
    The final challenge is the economic aspect of an endeavor of such a scale. Studies and trials would need significant funding, since it is plausible to assume that individuals would require smart wearables in order to collect data, which is an expensive task. This will require a lot of reconsideration of national research funding allocation. It might also take time to convince health administrators and policy makers that this is a worthwhile national endeavor to pursue. To consider an example, the recently published Apple Heart Study recruited approximately 400,000 Apple Watch users over 2  years. Although this trial was the first of its kind and proved that such large-scale and rapid recruitment is possible, it had significant problems with retaining patients wherein 79% dropped out in the first few months. One has to be creative regarding improving such potentially revolutionary trials through integration of various clinical platforms and encouragement of patient involvement.
    After that comes the huge challenge of applying what is discovered through research and trials to clinical practice and healthcare in general, especially disease prevention. Providing everyone in a population of 300 million with a smart wearable is not cheap. The research phase will be important in providing strong evidence as to whether or not a large-scale investment could potentially save healthcare providers’ costs over the long term by lowering the incidence of CVD and lowering readmission rates for CVD patients.

    Conclusion and future directions

    The advent of smart wearables constitutes the latest trend in health technology. With improvements in computation and technology allowing for the incorporation of AI and ML, their clinical utility is only expected to rise. The design and implementation of sensors such as glucose, sleep, and breathing sensors would provide new and clinically significant health-related data. Parameters measured using different modalities can be used to expand already existing datasets in order to make ML algorithms more accurate in the detection of disease. These datasets can then be used in large studies in order to assess their effectiveness and their utility. Once the virtual infrastructure containing these parameters is built, physicians and healthcare professionals should be trained to retrieve and interpret the data from smart wearables. It is also imperative that cheaper, smart wearables are manufactured in order to be accessible by those of lower socioeconomic status.
    Smart wearables undoubtedly add a new dimension to healthcare, and when utilized properly, have the potential to be extremely beneficial in a healthcare setting. They allow patients to take charge of their own health, be more engaged in the pursuit of good health, and build healthy habits. This can be achieved in numerous ways such as simply ensuring medication adherence and physical activity. With the extremely high rates of obesity and associated noncommunicable diseases such as CVD and cancer, physical activity would undoubtedly be a worthwhile endeavor, and help curtail the significant morbidity and mortality associated with such diseases. Their implementation in the clinical space would result in a paradigm shift, as the focus of disease can be aimed more toward prevention. Smart wearable technology is also ready for prime-time integration in the management of many cardiovascular diseases; however, we still need to improvise ways to streamline big data analysis, while making result visualization meaningful and seamless to both the physicians and patients.

    Chapter 16: The future of artificial intelligence in healthcare

    Nathan Radakovich1, and Aziz Nazha2     1Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine, Cleveland, OH, United States     2Cleveland Clinic Taussig Cancer Center, Leukemia Department, Cleveland, OH, United States

    Abstract

    The field of artificial intelligence (AI) has witnessed significant advances in the last decade in terms of computational power and the ease of implementing AI in domain-specific settings. The medical field, in particular, contains many prominent examples of these advances. AI has already taken a foothold in some specialties such as radiology, and is likely to continue expanding into other clinical realms, altering established approaches for disease diagnosis, research conduct, and patients interaction. This chapter provides an historical perspective and background on recent computing advances that have set the stage for the emergence of AI in healthcare, describes the burgeoning trends in AI’s clinical implementation, and considers some of the challenges that will face healthcare providers as AI makes its way into day-to-day clinical practice.

    Keywords

    Artificial intelligence; Computer vision; Electronic health records; Interpretability; Machine learning; Neural network; Time series analysis
