    Introduction and historical perspective

    Intelligence is a difficult to encapsulate concept, one for which scientists and philosophers have proposed myriad definitions and metrics over the years. It is unsurprising, given the difficulty of reaching a consensus regarding our own intelligence, that a firm definition of artificial intelligence (AI), a term first coined by the pioneering AI researcher John McCarthy in the 1950s (
    Modern applications of AI fulfill previous definitions to various degrees. Autonomously driving cars, for instance, have debuted with some success, and have featured software both programmed a priori to understand and obey the rules of the road, as well as software whose driving abilities and decision-making is derived from observing hours of human driving. In these two different approaches to the same task, we see two data-processing and judgment-making faculties that we deem as signs of intelligence: the ability to learn the rules governing a task and then implement those rules; and the ability to learn from experience, thereby coming to an inductive understanding of a previously unknown task.
    Turing’s definition of AI required a computer to match human abilities, but in certain realms AI has begun not only to match human abilities, but to surpass them. Computational power, which has increased exponentially since the advent of microprocessors in the 1960s (
    With the diverse and rapid developments in AI, it is unsurprising that healthcare, which comprises one-fifth of the United States’ economy and has data repositories measuring in the petabytes, has been a recent hotbed for AI research. The notion of computers as powerful tools—or rivals—for physicians is by no means recent, however. In a 1970 commentary, “Medicine and the Computer: The Promise and Problems of Change,” in the New England Journal of Medicine, Dr. William Schwartz, an early advocate of AI in healthcare, envisioned not only the “housekeeping” role that computers would play in the form of electronic health records (EHRs), but the more direct role they would play in the intellectual work of medicine (

    Supervised and unsupervised learning

    AI tasks can be described as “supervised” or “unsupervised” according to the output desired by the user. In supervised learning tasks, an algorithm is given input data to make a prediction, which can be categorical (e.g., “does this biopsy contain malignant tissue?”) or numerical (e.g., “what is the predicted survival of this patient, given their disease status and comorbidities?”). Source data are used to generate initial predictions by the algorithm. Predictions are then compared to actual outcomes, and the algorithm is iteratively refined based on the discrepancies between the two, yielding successively more accurate predictions (

    Neural networks: a brief overview

    Neural networks are amongst the most widely used and successful tools in contemporary AI. Neural networks’ namesake and inspiration come from biologic neurons, and in particular from the way that action potentials between neurons are used as the basic unit of communication in the nervous system. Neural networks process information by propagating data along a series of interconnected nodes, or “neurons,” starting with some external input and generating an output after relaying the data through many layers of neurons (
    Because of their ability to create more abstract representations of data in hidden layers, neural networks are also capable of integrating several different types of data into a single model. Distinct types of data are fed into separate inputs, processed through several parallel hidden layers, and then connected by subsequent layers prior to yielding an output. This is of particular utility in medicine, where images, laboratory values, and free text reports all play a role in decision-making and patient care; rather than considering different data types in isolation, interactions between data can be captured.

    The pace of change in AI research

    The pace of innovation in healthcare-related AI is accelerating, and is on pace to continue doing so. A PubMed search of terms “deep learning,” “machine learning,” “artificial intelligence,” or “neural network” reveals a consistent increase in both the absolute volume of AI-related research, and in the proportion of the medical literature that it constitutes. In the year 2000, 1838 articles (0.38% of all articles published in 2000) met the aforementioned search criteria. In 2010, there were 5491 such articles (0.74% of all articles), and in 2018 there were 15,240 (5.20% of all articles) (Fig. 16.2).
    These trends reflect the increasing recognition of AI’s utility and promise in healthcare, as well as ongoing improvements in the hardware and software that facilitate increasingly sophisticated AI algorithms. They also reflect the democratization of the tools used to implement AI. Most industry-standard AI packages are freely available online, and cheap online computing power can be accessed for computationally demanding projects, eliminating the need for costly upfront capital investments. The convergence of these factors has lowered the threshold for successfully using AI, thereby allowing clinician experts to begin implementing AI across a wide array of domain-specific applications.

    Computer vision

    Computer vision is the use of AI to interpret and extract data from images. No medical application of AI has seen as much recent progress, or garnered as much popular attention, as medical image processing, especially in the fields of pathology and radiology. This progress has been facilitated by the advent of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a subtype of neural network designed to process images in a manner similar to human sight. CNNs begin with basic patterns and textures such as horizontal and vertical lines, then build successively more complex and abstract representations based on those initial steps, thereby learning a more generalizable version of the object in question (3,5). This allows CNNs to learn from training data, and to effectively apply what they have learned to previously unseen examples. The advent of transfer learning, which uses models that have already been trained to recognize basic shapes and contours, allows powerful models to be trained efficiently and effectively on novel tasks, facilitating the expansion of computer vision to increasing numbers of novel applications (

    AI in radiology

    CNNs are approaching the point of clinical usefulness in several tasks in radiology, and in some cases have already passed that threshold. Routine screening mammography, detection of abnormalities on chest radiographs, bone age assessment, pulmonary nodule detection, and tuberculosis screening have all been successfully performed by CNNs, to name a few notable applications (
    Image segmentation, a tedious but important task used to identify areas of interest in images such as individual organs, tumors, fluid collections, or injured tissue, can also increasingly be performed by AI (Fig. 16.3) (
    Beyond achieving remarkable performance on existing tasks in radiology, AI has demonstrated the potential to extract novel, clinically meaningful information from images. In lung cancer, AI has shown promise in using CT images to predict the invasiveness of tumors, assess tumors’ response to chemotherapy, and distinguish between indolent and aggressive tumors (
    Generative adversarial networks (GANs), a type of neural network designed to generate de novo data that resemble real data, have also found a foothold in radiology (Fig. 16.4). GANs have shown promise in several realms: reducing noise artifact in images, thereby making them more interpretable for human observers; synthesizing images across modalities, such as different MRI sequences; and creating synthetic instances of training data that can be used to improve the generalizability of image classifiers (Fig. 16.5) (Armanious et al.;

    AI in pathology

    Pathology has seen similar improvements as radiology in the use of AI for common tasks. While efforts to apply AI to tasks such as routine pap smears date to the early 1990s, contemporary work has yielded highly accurate and specific models capable of detecting abnormalities on routine smears (

    Dermatology and ophthalmology

    AI has also taken a foothold in clinical specialties, namely in ophthalmology, where AI is increasingly used to interpret fundoscopic images, and dermatology, where it is employed in classifying skin lesions. Importantly, recent work in these fields has also included implementation of AI into regular practice. In a 2018 trial, an AI-based diabetic retinopathy detection tool achieved 87.5% sensitivity and 90.7% specificity in a primary care setting, subsequently becoming the first AI-based system to gain U.S. Food and Drug Administration authorization (
    Prospective, implementation-oriented studies in ophthalmology demonstrate the potential for AI’s generalizability and practical integration into clinical workflow, two factors that represent barriers to more widespread utilization of AI in medicine. Crucially, they also address an unmet healthcare need. Time, expense, and provider scarcity are barriers to success in any form of preventative care, and the patients affected by those barriers experience poorer health as a consequence (
    AI has made similar strides in dermatology, namely in classifying skin lesions. CNNs have continually improved over the last decade, with the latest generation of algorithms achieving parity with dermatologists in melanoma and multilabel lesion classification tasks (
    Beyond single pictures of lesions, a logical next step in lesion imaging is longitudinal monitoring, since change over time is a consideration when evaluating potentially cancerous skin lesions. Dermatologists’ sensitivity is only 80% for detecting melanomas when viewing a lesion at a single point in time, so even models that outperform humans will likely miss a significant number of melanomas, and interval monitoring may be required to improve screening (35). Prospective data are needed in order to create the datasets necessary to develop such a tool (

    Time-series analysis

    Understanding the chronology of patients’ diseases is an integral part of the practice of medicine. Time-series analysis, which employs AI to process sequences of events, has seen significant strides in recent years. Time-series problems abound in medicine, from single variable tasks such as interpreting the pattern of voltages recorded in an electrocardiogram to complex multivariable predictions, such as determining whether an ICU patient is improving or deteriorating based on trends in vital signs, labs, written notes, and day-to-day physical exam findings.
    Much of the recent research in time-series analysis has to do with event prediction. In the ICU setting this includes risk-stratifying patients by likelihood of mortality and promptly identifying sepsis (

    Mobile device applications

    Medical data are traditionally collected either in clinics or the inpatient setting, but for most patients this represents a small fraction of their lives. When we observe a tremor or assess a patient’s gait in the clinic, it is with the assumption that we are seeing a representative sample of their daily lives, but this may not always be true, such as in patients with masked hypertension, or in Parkinson disease patients who experience fluctuations in symptoms throughout the day. With the advent of inexpensive and accurate portable monitoring devices, it is now feasible to directly gather information about patients’ day-to-day activity outside of a medical setting, thereby greatly expanding the pool of potentially useful data about patients (
    This wealth of data has been studied in many settings, such as monitoring for fall risk in the elderly (

    AI in medical research

    Classification of disease

    While much popular attention is directed toward AI’s applications in clinical practice, it also promises to alter how physicians research disease. For example, unsupervised clustering of asthma patients was able to group patients into distinct clinically meaningful cohorts that varied based on asthma severity, resource utilization, responsiveness to bronchodilators, and biologic variables such as eosinophilia, circulating inflammatory markers, and exhaled nitric oxide (
    Not only do such clusters, which are generated without any a priori designation of outcomes or patient phenotypes, identify clinically relevant subpopulations of patients, they have clear diagnostic and therapeutic ramifications. Clustering approaches could be used in clinical practice to fine-tune aggressiveness of therapy, avoid ineffective treatments, and to identify those most likely to respond to novel targeted therapies. AI-based clustering may also inform future clinical trial design. In fields like oncology, where many new agents are designed with disease-specific biology in mind, AI may facilitate more targeted selection criteria. In cases where there is a strong biologic rationale for those selection criteria, this may allow for smaller trials to be conducted while still achieving statistical power, thereby reducing trial costs and sparing unnecessary interventions for those unlikely to benefit.

    AI as a tool in data gathering

    One of the challenges in clinical research that draws from EHRs is accurately sifting through disorganized data. Important information about patient outcomes often comes in the form of unstructured text in pathology reports or clinician notes, and such data need to be extracted manually in order to be incorporated into outcomes research. Obtaining information through manual review of EHR is time-consuming, and may place practical constraints on sample size. Conversely, methodologically convenient but less granular methods of chart review, such as querying International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes without manual review of individual charts, facilitate larger sample sizes at the expense of detail. Natural language processing (NLP), another field where AI has yielded important strides, could be used in the future as a means of collecting data with the speed and throughput of computerized queries.
    Traditional rule-based methods of natural language processing require explicit programming on how to extract information. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), a type of network designed to take previous inputs into account, are capable of more flexible, context-sensitive performance, and can be applied to NLP; CNNs have also been used effectively in this setting (

    Future challenges in implementation

    Much of the focus on AI in healthcare has been on the development of AI models themselves: how to more accurately identify objects, classify sequences, or deal with the subtleties and inconsistencies of interpreting written language. However, as progress continues in each of these realms, thought also needs to be given to other factors that will impact the clinical utilization of AI.

    Practical considerations

    Broadly speaking, the enthusiasm for AI in healthcare is driven by two hopes: that AI will improve the quality of care that physicians deliver, and that it will do so in a way that improves patient and physician experiences. Thus, in arenas where AI achieves or surpasses human performance, the question turns from one of theoretical usefulness to one of practical implementation. Even if an AI-based model performs exceedingly well, it will not provide any clinical benefit unless it can reasonably be integrated into physicians’ workflows. For many applications this likely means integration into existing EHR systems, which carries the attendant requirements of securely handling patient data, reliably standardizing the input data used by AI systems, and likely the ability to interface with other EHR-based AI programs (

    Interpretability

    Any AI that plays a significant role in guiding patient care will have to include mechanisms for making its predictions explicable to clinicians and patients. Simple models such as logistic regression are easy to interpret because each variable is considered in isolation, making interpretation straightforward. However, simplistic models are rarely adequate, and medicine provides many examples of the adage that “for every complex problem there is an answer that is clear, simple, and wrong.”
    Medical data are never considered in isolation, and medical decision-making is almost never simple. For example, the same heart rate could have very different implications depending on patient comorbidities, other vital signs, and numerous other factors, all of which are implicitly or explicitly considered by human clinicians when delivering care and choosing a course of action. Moreover, clinicians are able to describe how they interpret complex sets of data and why they draw certain conclusions. If AI is to gain widespread acceptance by clinicians and patients, it will have to manage to be sophisticated while remaining similarly accountable.

    Testing and overdiagnosis

    The risk of overdiagnosis needs to be considered as AI-based diagnostic tools become increasingly sensitive. Overdiagnosis occurs when a test correctly identifies the presence of disease, but there is no benefit from intervening on the disease (
    Outside of the scope of existing screening, overdiagnosis also needs to be considered as new sources of health information, such as wearable devices, become increasingly common. In some cases, such as atrial fibrillation or atrial high rate episodes in ambulatory patients, even asymptomatic events have unfavorable prognostic implications and require intervention (

    Barriers to implementation

    Beyond practical barriers, the impact of AI on physicians themselves must be considered. It is often assumed that better technology necessarily improves the lives of its users, but studies of physician satisfaction with EHR and computerized order entry belie this assumption. Indeed, the use of computerized records and orders is an independent predictor of physician burnout, and if EHR-integrated AI increases the time spent interacting with EHR and detracts from physician-patient interactions, it could in turn become a contributor to the burnout problem (
    Precautions about burnout aside, fluid and user-friendly EHR integration is also crucial to the successful uptake of AI. Numerous best practice alerts (BPAs) to warn clinicians about drug-drug interactions, adherence to guidelines, or health maintenance are already incorporated into EHR systems, with varying degrees of success and uptake, which in turn determines how much patients ultimately benefit from such tools. In cases where BPAs do not provide benefit, a major contributor is physician alert fatigue, which is driven in part by the sheer volume of BPAs encountered (
    Despite posing potential problems, clinical AI may also offer solutions for physicians’ struggles with burnout and burdensome EHR. The use of human scribes is known to ameliorate burnout and increase physician job satisfaction without detracting from patients’ experiences, but their widespread use is limited by cost and scarcity (
    NLP in medicine currently functions as a dictation tool, and while dictation may be more efficient than typing, it does not substantially alter the current workflow for physicians; with or without dictation, a sizable amount of physician time is spent on documentation rather than actual patient care. This may change with the advent of increasingly sophisticated language-processing technologies. A system that can summarize physician-patient discussions and generate summary statements about patients problems would be able to capture the unique aspects of an individual visit, thereby freeing physicians from having to recapitulate an entire visit when writing or dictating a note (

    The challenge of accurate source data

    AI models’ performance will only be as good as their source data, and if flawed data are used, flawed predictions should be expected. For instance in cases such as pulmonary nodule classification where intraobserver variability is high, it is difficult to assign accurate labels to training data without a tissue diagnosis, limiting the ceiling of an algorithm’s usefulness (
    Beyond the accuracy of source data, the same precautions about external validity need to be taken as with any other form of research. Many AI models achieve exquisite accuracy on internal datasets, but fail to recapitulate that accuracy when validated externally, meaning that stellar performance in one setting could be unacceptably, even dangerously, flawed in another (
    Beyond the prospect of inaccurate data, AI has the potential to unintentionally adopt human bias and prejudices. Photo recognition software, including some models developed for medical use, performs more accurately on light-skinned individuals than on dark-skinned ones due to underrepresentation in datasets; more troublingly, minority individuals are more likely to be viewed unfavorably by AI systems such as crime-prediction or loan-approval algorithms (

    Will AI make physicians obsolete?

    The emergence of increasingly useful, clinically viable AI brings with it uncertainty about the future role of human physicians, including fears of being displaced or even replaced. This has been especially true in radiology, where much of the recent progress in medical AI has occurred. The majority of medical trainees anticipate that AI will reduce the workload required of radiologists, and in one study half of students contemplating careers in radiology cited this as a source of trepidation (
    Practicing radiologists have expressed similar views in commentaries, acknowledging AI’s incorporation into clinical practice as inevitable while simultaneously predicting that AI will support radiologists and augment their skills but not supplant them (
    Meanwhile, complex decision-making remains the purview of human physicians, and AI systems capable of taking an active role in clinical decision-making have had decidedly mixed success. IBM’s Watson, which attracted widespread attention for its ability to interpret semantically nuanced questions and compete on the TV quiz show Jeopardy, underwent several years of pilot testing as a decision support system in clinical oncology. However, after a period of use at select major cancer centers in the United States, Watson for Oncology (WFO) was discontinued, although it continues to be studied in several East Asian countries (
    Retrospective comparisons between WFO’s recommendations and those of a multidisciplinary tumor board show that WFO’s missteps occur more commonly in elderly patients, intermediate-staged disease, or in malignancies where there are significant regional or national variations in standards of care (
    Nonetheless, the prospect of AI as a partner in clinical decision-making remains appealing, especially when considering the gaps in care provided by human clinicians. Medical error incurs billions of dollars in costs annually, and is estimated by some to be the third-leading cause of death in the United States, a sobering reminder of our own limitations (

    AI in medical education

    As AI becomes integrated into clinical practice, medical school and residency curricula will need to adapt in order to ensure that clinicians approach it in an informed manner. Since the reforms in medical education prompted by the Flexner report, one of the cornerstones of medical education has been literacy in research methods and statistics, as well as careful review of scientific literature (
    A knowledge gap likely already exists in the medical community. When surveyed about their understanding of AI, medical students’ self-assessment of their level of knowledge outstrips their ability to actually answer questions about the basics of AI, suggesting that awareness and popular coverage of the topic alone does not confer a deeper understanding or the ability to critically appraise AI-based research (

    Conclusion

    The degree of computing power available in the modern era and the sophistication and diversity of artificial intelligence that has followed would have been unthinkable in prior decades. Modern AI has already made significant inroads in the fields of pathology and radiology, and is poised to become a routine part of clinical practice within the decade, with other branches of medicine likely to follow suit as the technology continues to mature. Beyond automating and improving on many existing tasks that physicians perform, AI also holds the promise of yielding new insights from the vast amount of medical data now available. As AI becomes more widespread, care needs to be taken to ensure that it is implemented thoughtfully, with an eye to unintended consequences, and to ensure that medical education promotes a basic working knowledge of AI for future physicians.

    Chapter 17: Ethical and legal challenges

    Emily Tat1, and Mark Rabbat2     1Department of Internal Medicine, Columbia University Medical Center, New York, NY, United States     2Medicine and Radiology, Division of Cardiology, Loyola University Chicago, Chicago, IL, United States

    Abstract

    As the technology of artificial intelligence (AI) grows in cardiovascular medicine, so do the ethical and legal challenges that come with it. Currently, the medical community is ill-informed of what these challenges entail, and policy and ethical guidelines are lacking. Physicians and policy makers should be informed of these issues to minimize harm and promote patient care. Three overarching themes relating to the data, the algorithms, and the results comprise the foundation of these challenges and will be discussed in this chapter. The introduction of big data raises concern for patient privacy and security, with issues of data quality and inconsistent medical records. There is also risk for biases in the algorithms that could worsen health disparities or skew results for financial gain. Finally, the archetypal “black box” algorithm, questions of legal liability, and what happens when humans and machine disagree are discussed in depth. Ultimately, a code of ethics in the coming integration of AI is needed to ensure the preservation of human rights.

    Keywords

    Artificial intelligence; Autonomy; Big data; Black box; Ethics; Informed consent; Liability; Privacy; Safety

    Introduction

    Artificial intelligence (AI) has significant potential to transform the field of cardiovascular medicine. Major advancements are seen throughout all subsets of AI from machine learning algorithms and neural networks, natural language processing, and robotics to cognitive computing computer vision. There is promise for these advancements to improve the morbidity and mortality associated with cardiovascular disease, from better disease surveillance, improved diagnostics, novel treatments, and an era of truly personalized medicine (
    The contents within this chapter will examine some of the most pressing ethical and legal challenges that healthcare providers must be informed of in this new era of medicine. One major theme that will be addressed is big data and the issues involving its integration. This includes threat to patient privacy and safety, the limits of inconsistent electronic health records, and the catch-22 of balancing reductionism and holism, that is, which and how many input variables are required to ensure accurate results. A second theme that will be discussed is the potential for biases within the algorithms. In particular, bias that can worsen health disparities and bias by way of an algorithm’s intent to either improve patient care or for financial gain. The final theme of the chapter discusses the algorithm’s accuracy and the consequences of decisions made from its results. Specifically, the dilemma of the archetypal “black box” algorithm, liability in the face of adverse events, and the question of what to do when humans and machines disagree will be elucidated.
    Underlying each theme is the emphasis for transparency in the algorithm and a need for a code of ethics and clear guidelines to promote patient safety and minimize harm. Most importantly, there is a large fear of AI’s potential to replace the human physician and disrupt the physician-patient relationship (

    Big data

    The current state of big data

    From whole-genome sequencing to wearable biometrics, physicians are now tasked with making sense of an enormous amount of data in an increasingly limited amount of time. Enter AI systems, well-oiled algorithms that are designed to interpret and operationalize larger volumes of health information in a fraction of the time it would take for a human physician.  Using a machine learning based model, a personalized effect of health behavior on blood pressure can be derived (
    1. • “Don’t collect data unless it has a non-zero chance of changing your actions.”
    2. • “Before you seek to collect data, consider the costs of processing that data.”
    3. • “Acknowledge that data collected isn’t always accurate and consider the costs of acting on data that isn’t correct.”
    These principles translate well to the use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. In the face of big data, information is of low utility unless it can improve clinical outcomes. To collect data for the sake of collecting data skews the balance of enormous costs outweighing the benefit of clinical outcomes. The distinction for accurate data should also be emphasized. Incorrect results and predictions in the realm of healthcare can lead to severe consequences, and meticulous quality reporting must be protocolized into AI development to ensure reproducible results. However, professional associations, government agencies, and AI developers may be unaware of how to proceed in this new era of uncharted AI territory.

    The effect of AI on healthcare expenditure

    The logistics of how AI can be integrated into medicine require a discussion of cost. Healthcare costs in the United States currently surpass all other countries. The United States spends over $10,000 per capita or 18% of its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on healthcare with costs projected to increase at an annual rate of 4.1% from 2017 to 2021 (

    Privacy and security

    In the transference of such large amounts of data, questions of confidentiality and security arise. An efficient and accurate AI system cannot be built in solidarity confined to a single hospital network. This is reminiscent of current electronic medical records that are limited to the institution’s hospital network, which greatly impact the efficiency of outside hospital transfers and the like. Given how extensively patient data would be shared across an AI system, existing practices of obtaining consent would be unrealistic. The alternative option also proves difficult. The privacy rule in the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) of 1996 allows the use of deidentified patient-level data without consent (
    An incident involving Google DeepMind and the Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust occurred in which identifiable patient records were transferred across the entire Trust without explicit patient consent (
    Google introduced Federated Learning in 2017, a “distributed machine learning approach which trains machine learning models using decentralized data residing on end devices such as mobile phones” (
